items.title: Heartwood
items.text:
Heartwood is an open-source research agent system for biomedical research environments. You describe work on a project folder in ordinary language; an OpenHands agent proposes commands and file changes; the Heartwood gateway decides which proposals need you, records every decision, and keeps a verifiable audit history.

Start Your First Project Choose a Platform

items.title: Components
items.text:
• The gateway owns project state, policy, action review, authorization of operations outside the agent, session records and audit.
  • The agent loop and coding tools come from OpenHands and run either in the Heartwood process or as a complete worker inside an OpenShell sandbox.
  • The terminal, browser and notebook interfaces present the same gateway contract, so a session, its settings and its review decisions look the same in each.
  • Research Skills, bounded research specialists and staged research workflows run inside the same session, review and records.

items.title: Roles and Responsibilities
items.text: Role Decides Starts with Researcher The task, the model where a choice is offered, and every proposal that waits for review Your First Project Operator How Heartwood runs: the deployment manifest, protected state, review-mode ceiling, worker profile, credentials and checkpoint signer Deploy Heartwood Platform Identity, storage, network controls, compute and inference, under its own authority Platform Contract

items.title: Local Launch
items.text:
Run heartwood in a project folder. The current directory is the project, and Heartwood keeps configuration, sessions, models and audit records in .heartwood/ inside it. Every action set waits for you; Review Changes can be selected for the running process when the model route allows it, as described in Review Modes.

Agent tools run with your operating-system permissions. An allowed terminal command can read anything you can read and can change .heartwood/, including session and audit files, so a local launch is a reviewed assistant rather than an isolation boundary. This is the shape used on workstations, in containers, on Terra and on Stanford Carina.

items.title: Operator-Bound Deployment
items.text: An operator starts the gateway with heartwood gateway serve --deployment and a manifest that binds the project to protected state outside the research folder and sets the policy and review-mode ceiling. With a [worker] section, each session runs in a sandboxed OpenShell worker on an operator-controlled Linux Docker host. The worker receives selected read-only inputs and verified Skills; protected state, provider credentials, the Docker socket and signing keys stay outside it. Operations outside the worker, and the release of their results to it, are authorized only by a researcher decision bound to the exact content reviewed, in every review mode. No production outside-service adapter ships and gateway serve installs none; these operations are available only through an embedding launcher. See Projects and Private State and Security and Controlled Data.

items.title: Support Levels
items.text: Container, GPU container and Terra images and native installers are built and tested in CI for each release commit. The isolated worker passes native qualification in CI on Linux Docker with synthetic workloads, and the evidence is bound to the commit. Heartwood-managed model configurations are qualified per platform as listed in GPU Compatibility. Support and Compatibility gives the level of each configuration, and Security Limits states what the controls do not cover. Use synthetic or non-sensitive files until the institution has approved the deployment for a data class.

items.title: Product Boundaries
items.text: Heartwood is a research agent system built around an OpenHands coding agent. A gateway owns project state, policy, action review, outside authorization, records, and audit; the OpenHands agent worker proposes and runs actions, either in the gateway process or inside an OpenShell sandbox; terminal, browser, and notebook interfaces render one gateway contract. Heartwood reuses OpenHands for the conversation loop and coding tools and does not maintain a parallel agent loop or tool implementation. System Architecture describes the components and the trust boundary between them.

items.title: In Scope
items.text:
• one current-directory research project with private state, locally in .heartwood/ or in external state bound by an operator deployment manifest;
  • terminal, browser, and notebook interfaces over one gateway contract;
  • OpenHands conversations run locally or by a managed native worker in an OpenShell sandbox, with admitted, attempt-bound, budgeted worker traffic and revocation;
  • complete-set action review with gateway-decided review modes under an operator ceiling;
  • content-bound researcher authorization of outside operations and result releases;
  • persistent sessions, replay, tamper-evident audit export, and signed, retained audit checkpoints;
  • reviewed research stages with independent artifact checks, experiment records, task tracking, and bounded research specialists;
  • verified and explicitly installed Skills;
  • platform-aware model discovery and Heartwood-managed model planning;
  • generic, Terra, and Stanford Carina platform adapters and a versioned Heartwood–platform contract with offline conformance checks; and
  • container, native, worker, and qualification artifacts built from pinned inputs, with native qualification evidence bound to a commit.

items.title: Outside the Product Boundary
items.text:
Heartwood does not:

  • discover, authorize, or validate a real biomedical dataset;
  • determine whether a provider or platform may process a particular data class, or claim readiness for sensitive data;
  • replace operating-system, container, scheduler, or cloud isolation; the local backend runs tools with the researcher's identity and isolates nothing;
  • ship a production OpenShell gateway or outside-service adapter;
  • guarantee model output, code correctness, statistical validity, or reproducibility;
  • approve third-party Skills or model licenses on behalf of an institution;
  • provide a multi-user authentication service for the browser; or
  • approve individual tool calls separately when OpenHands supplies them as one action set.

items.title: Design Principles
items.text:
1. Reuse the agent platform. OpenHands owns agent reasoning, conversation persistence, and coding tools.
  2. One product contract. Every interface uses the same gateway commands, events, configuration, and project state.
  3. The gateway decides. Worker output is data; approvals, outside effects, and records require the gateway's own admission and decisions.
  4. Keep platform differences at the boundary. Adapters define capabilities and policy without forking the workflow.
  5. Prefer clean pre-1.0 contracts. Superseded commands and state layouts are removed rather than maintained as parallel paths.

items.title: Experiment Records
items.text: Scientific execution records describe declared code, inputs, parameters, environment, and outputs. They are separate from the session audit, which records agent decisions and action permissions.

items.title: Research Workflow Records
items.text:
Research workflows record each stage before asking the agent to work. The definition binds the stage to its workflow version, input fingerprints, previously accepted artifacts, and declared output paths. Generated Python artifacts are identified as code, so a later verification stage can reference the exact program accepted earlier.

A stage receives a successful record only after its independent checks and any required researcher review pass. The outcome links to the recorded tool proposals, action decisions, tool results, and reproduction evidence for that stage. It does not invent a process exit code: stage acceptance and an individual command's exit status are different observations. Cancelling a started stage records cancellation; cancelling before a stage starts does not imply execution occurred.

items.title: Correction Lineage
items.text:
Corrective work preserves the original stage execution as failed and records each new attempt separately. Its definition contains the correction attempt identity, original reviewed inputs and code, and fresh output paths. The workflow retains the verified findings, exact source snapshot, permitted attempt count, and each independent recheck. It shares the original stage's usage and deadline; starting another attempt does not reset either limit.

A correction experiment succeeds only when its declared replacement files pass the supported defect rechecks. This narrower outcome does not mean the complete workflow stage passed: the normal stage checks and researcher gate still apply. Only independently checked replacement paths enter the current stage's artifact binding, and previously accepted stages are unchanged. The original failed record is never rewritten as a successful execution.

Attempt intent and experiment start are journaled before model dispatch. Recovery can finish an interrupted assessment from recorded evidence but cannot silently repeat execution or begin the next attempt. Tool proposals still use the existing action-review policy; correction consent is not approval of a command or file modification.

items.title: Inspect and Export
items.text:
Inspect Experiment Records in the browser's Research tab, enter /experiments in the terminal, or read NotebookViewModel.experiments in a notebook. All three use the same gateway-owned session projection. The notebook widget also includes an Experiment Records section. For all sessions and recorded scripts in the project, expand Project Experiment Records in the browser's Research tab. Refresh reads current project state; Export Records downloads the gateway's canonical JSON Lines and displays its digest. The export is project-local scientific metadata, not a signed audit checkpoint. The notebook exposes the same collection and export through session.experiment_records() and session.export_experiments().

The start and outcome are committed with their workflow transitions in the existing paired session and audit journal. Their content-minimized fingerprints are included in the security audit; the full scientific records remain project-private. Project queries rebuild experiments.jsonl in the bound state directory from those verified source events using idempotent appends. Rebuilding never reads newer artifact contents or repeats model calls or tool actions.

The gateway's experiment_records() and export_experiments(), and the authenticated routes GET /research/experiments and GET /research/experiments/export, serve the same collection and export. The project collection also includes analyses explicitly recorded through the Python API and command-line recorder below.

items.title: Record a Command-Line Analysis
items.text:
From your project directory, declare the input and new output files before the script name:

heartwood experiments record --input data.csv --output results.json analysis.py --seed 42
heartwood experiments list
heartwood experiments export > experiment-records.jsonl

Heartwood uses its installed Python by default and passes everything after analysis.py literally to the script. Use repeated --input, --output, and --code options for additional files; the script itself is always included as code. Output directories must already exist, and declared output files must not exist. The command prints a run identity and leaves the analysis's output visible in the terminal without copying it into the journal. It returns the script's nonzero exit status when execution fails; a zero exit alone is not success if files changed or declared outputs are missing.

This is an explicit user-run analysis, not an autonomous OpenHands tool or a sandbox. The script has the current user's ordinary filesystem and network permissions. Use normal Heartwood conversation actions when an agent proposes executing code so that the action-review policy applies.

For another interpreter, use --runner bash or --runner Rscript and supply --environment-sha256 with the complete digest of your maintained environment specification. That fingerprint is a declaration, not proof that the external interpreter matches it. Heartwood does not substitute its own Python environment as evidence for another interpreter. For example, a shell script can be recorded with:

heartwood experiments record --runner bash --environment-sha256 DIGEST --input data.csv --output results.json analysis.sh

Replace DIGEST with the actual 64-character SHA-256 digest; do not use a placeholder as reproducibility evidence. The same file-boundary checks and versioned record schema apply to Python and command-line analyses. Raw arguments, environment-variable values, and process output are not stored in the record. Arguments may still appear in shell history or the operating system's process list; never pass credentials or protected values this way.

heartwood experiments list --json returns the gateway's project collection schema. heartwood experiments export writes verified canonical JSON Lines to standard output; protect the exported file like other project metadata. For an abandoned script, heartwood experiments recover RUN_ID and heartwood experiments cancel RUN_ID follow the recovery rules below without stopping processes or deleting files. Use --run-id RUN_ID when automating an initial command whose retries must retain one identity: reuse is rejected rather than repeating work.

items.title: Record a Python Analysis
items.text:
Use the Python recorder around the call that runs your analysis. Run from the project directory, declare every relevant input and code dependency, and choose output files that do not already exist. Create their parent directories before recording.

from heartwood.gateway import ProjectContext
from heartwood.gateway.experiments import ExperimentRecorder

recorder = ExperimentRecorder(ProjectContext.current())
definition = recorder.describe(
    actor_ref="researcher-001",
    entry_point="analysis.py",
    inputs=("data.csv",),
    outputs=("results.json",),
    parameters={"seed": 42},
)

with recorder.record(definition) as run_id:
    from analysis import main

    main(seed=42)

run = next(item for item in recorder.runs() if item.run_id == run_id)
print(run.status)
print(run.outputs)

The recorder observes the declared files before entering the block and checks that inputs and code remain unchanged afterward. If the Python environment was observed, its fingerprint must also remain unchanged. Successful completion requires every declared output to exist and be readable. Missing outputs, changed inputs, and exceptions produce a failed record; a keyboard interruption produces a cancelled record. The original exception is propagated without putting its text in the journal. The recorder does not execute the script, supply parameters to it, or infer undeclared dependencies. The caller remains responsible for connecting the declaration to the actual analysis call.

File hashing uses bounded, streaming reads through the same project boundary as workspace inspection. The default limit is 1 GiB per file; pass max_file_bytes to ExperimentRecorder to change it deliberately. Hashing large files requires reading their bytes and can add noticeable I/O time on shared storage.

items.title: Record Contents
items.text:
The versioned ExperimentEvent schema in heartwood.schemas.experiments is language-neutral. Its shared reducer produces ExperimentRun summaries.

Field Meaning Run and event identifiers Stable identities for execution and idempotent record appends Actor reference A caller-declared identifier, not authenticated proof of identity Code and input files Project-relative paths, SHA-256 digests, and byte counts Parameters and invocation Digests of the explicit declarations, without raw values or arguments Environment A digest and whether its description was observed or declared Git revision and cleanliness Optional explicit context; unknown values remain unset Workflow stage Optional session, workflow run, definition fingerprint, stage, and tool association Evidence links Source session-event identities, kinds, and fingerprints, without commands or results Outcome Attempt number, timestamps, status, exit code when known, and observed outputs

The default Python environment digest covers interpreter identity, operating-system family, machine architecture, and installed package names and versions. It excludes installation paths, package source URLs, credentials, and environment-variable values. It does not capture external executables, native libraries, a GPU driver, or the complete contents of an installed package. For research stages, it describes the gateway's Python environment, not a remote model server or an independently attested execution environment. Independent Result Verification separately captures an isolated Python process through a reviewed probe and rechecks its versions immediately before the reviewed analysis command. That execution witness supplements the stage record; it does not turn package metadata into binary or platform attestation. The gateway, heartwood experiments environment, browser export, and NotebookSession.verification_environment() share the same metadata capture. The terminal and notebook accept an explicitly selected analysis interpreter; the browser export describes server Python and does not execute arbitrary client-supplied executables. The local Independent Result Verification workflow reconstructs a wheel-only pylock.toml with uv in a fresh .heartwood/runtime/ environment through a reviewed tool action. That local workflow is not permission to expose protected runtime state to an isolated worker; remote execution requires separately qualified workspace and evidence handling. Its execution witness binds the original lock and inputs to the observed environment artifact, then guards that artifact before analysis execution. Package installation uses a private lock snapshot and cache without inherited credentials, installer overrides, source builds, or automatic interpreter downloads. Metadata probing and analysis execution also exclude inherited environment variables so Python startup hooks do not receive provider credentials. This isolates dependencies; it is not an operating-system sandbox or an attestation of dependency safety. An explicit ExperimentEnvironment can instead identify a declared container or environment description.

items.title: Persistence and Recovery
items.text:
Records live in experiments.jsonl under the bound state directory and use the existing private JSON Lines append journal and native file locks. The directory is local .heartwood/ or the operator-bound external state root. Project initialization registers the experiment formats in that directory's state.json without rewriting existing session, audit, or experiment records. Supported older project manifests are upgraded atomically; unknown or altered format declarations are rejected rather than relabeled. A hash chain detects modification or reordering within the available record history. Exact event retries do not append a second record; changed retries and invalid transitions are rejected. One shared reducer supplies summaries and exact output-path/digest producer queries.

The Python recorder reserves a run before entering user code and holds its ownership lock until it exits. Reusing a run identifier with record() never enters the code block again, even after process loss. An unfinished started record means that execution may or may not have occurred; reading it does not repeat the work or infer success from files left behind. An unfinished resumed record has the same uncertainty for its later attempt. Terminal outcomes cannot be replaced.

items.title: Recover an Interrupted Script
items.text:
First check whether the original process or any subprocess it launched is still running, and inspect partial outputs and external effects. recorder.recover(run_id) requires the recorder's ownership lock to be free and marks the attempt interrupted without executing anything. It does not stop detached processes, remove files, or establish that retrying is safe. Calling it again leaves the same interrupted record unchanged.

Choose one of these actions after inspection:

  • recorder.cancel(run_id) closes the abandoned record without undoing or deleting anything.
  • recorder.resume(run_id) explicitly starts another attempt under the same run identity and original declaration.

A resumed attempt requires unchanged code, inputs, and any observed Python environment. Declared outputs must be absent; Heartwood never deletes partial results to make a retry possible. The caller must establish that repeating any undeclared or external effects is safe and handle partial outputs deliberately. Changed parameters or dependencies belong in a new experiment, not a resumed one.

After recovering and verifying that a retry is safe:

with recorder.resume(run_id):
    from analysis import main

    main(seed=42)

The resumed intent is persisted before the block runs, and its attempt number increases while the original input declaration and start time remain unchanged. An interrupted resume is not automatically retried. These script APIs cannot recover, cancel, or replace gateway-owned workflow stage records; use the workflow's normal session controls for those.

recorder.export() returns a deterministic, verified JSON Lines snapshot. An export is not a signed checkpoint or deployment-owned immutable record. An operator can bind its exact bytes to the existing audit checkpoint with heartwood audit checkpoint --include-experiments. This retains a verified project snapshot separately from the content-minimized audit and uses the deployment's existing signer and retention controls. The ExperimentSink contract separates ordered, idempotent appends from their storage implementation; the implemented backend is project-local storage.

items.title: Evidence Boundaries
items.text:
These records do not establish scientific correctness, independently authenticate the actor, or prove that a declared script generated an output. Workflow actor references are hashed session-command actor identifiers, not independent identity attestations. Boundary fingerprints detect ordinary changes, not adversarial change-and-restore between observations. Someone who can rewrite project state can rewrite the records and recompute their chain; an intact suffix can also be deleted without an independently retained reference.

Paths, actor references, and metadata can be sensitive even when file contents are excluded. Digests are not anonymization: a small set of possible parameter values can be guessed and hashed. Keep protected values out of declarations, and apply the project's access and export policies to scientific records independently of the security audit.

items.title: Sessions and Audit
items.text: Heartwood separates presentation state from durable session evidence. The gateway reduces one ordered event stream into the authoritative session projection used by terminal, browser, and notebook clients.

items.title: Command Flow
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Interface
    participant Gateway
    participant OpenHands
    participant Tool
    User->>Interface: Submit task
    Interface->>Gateway: Typed session command
    Gateway->>OpenHands: Continue conversation
    OpenHands-->>Gateway: Typed state and transient tokens
    Gateway-->>Interface: Shared session projection
    alt Review mode allows the complete set
        Gateway->>Gateway: Persist gateway decision with mode and rule
    else Researcher decides
        Interface-->>User: Review complete action set
        User->>Interface: Allow the complete set once or reject it
        Interface->>Gateway: Confirmation command
        Gateway->>Gateway: Persist complete-set decision
    end
    Gateway->>OpenHands: Resolve callback
    OpenHands->>Tool: Execute only when allowed
    Tool-->>Gateway: Result
    Gateway-->>Interface: Updated shared projection

items.title: Persistence
items.text: Session directories contain metadata, event records, audit records, exports, and OpenHands persistence for that conversation. Session identifiers are validated before any state path is created, and read-only replay of a new session creates no project state; the first mutating command registers the session. The gateway incrementally translates persisted OpenHands messages, actions, observations, lifecycle, task, usage, specialist, and error state into Heartwood events. While a run is executing or publishing its final events, its live publisher owns event delivery, and read-side reconciliation waits for it so it cannot consume an observation before live reproduction evidence is recorded. After the publisher exits, reconciliation can recover persisted events without claiming that replay observed their execution. Except for a service's first read, reconciliation reads the backend without the session command lock and journals what it read only if no event was appended and the worker attempt was neither fenced nor replaced meanwhile. The session command lock is granted in the order it is requested, so reads that follow one another cannot keep a command, fencing, or revocation waiting. Token deltas stay in process memory.

items.title: Writer Ownership
items.text:
The gateway acquires an interprocess writer lease before mutating a session and keeps it until it closes that session service. A second process cannot reconcile or mutate the session until the owner releases the lease or exits; distinct sessions have independent leases. If a worker does not stop during shutdown, the gateway keeps the lease rather than let another writer continue. A closed session service rejects further commands and discards later backend callbacks; this fence does not terminate an independently running worker. Mutation acquires the writer lease before the paired-snapshot lock, and recovery and replay never wait for a writer lease while holding that lock.

Managed worker attempts use the same lease and journal; their launch, fencing, revocation, reconciliation, and replacement are described in Worker Attempt Ownership. Launch, revocation, and service shutdown are serialized apart from command and event handling, so shutdown cannot release writer ownership while a launch may still return. Events and tokens from a revoked attempt's callbacks are discarded because they do not hold the current lease.

items.title: Maintenance and Migration
items.text:
An internal maintenance context holds the session-root admission lock and every existing session writer lock; an active writer prevents it from starting. Migration staging additionally excludes gateway startup and requires every registered gateway lifetime lease, and an unresolved inference launch intent also blocks it. Staging verifies paired session and audit histories and command receipts, copies their original bytes into a private directory on the destination volume, verifies the copy again, and records file hashes and session heads in a receipt. Pending append recovery, unresolved commands, corrupt records, symbolic links, and existing destinations prevent staging, and worker recovery state, writer metadata, and derived exports are not promoted. A retry uses a fresh staging directory and never adopts an earlier partial copy.

heartwood project migrate --deployment MANIFEST builds on that copy, validates configuration, experiment history, and installed Skill content, and stages the remaining canonical state and model artifacts. It refuses active or unresolved work, including recorded Python experiments, which hold the same project lifetime lease as gateways and inference runtimes. After verifying the staged bytes it records recovery evidence, fences local startup, retires the original directory into a protected backup, and publishes the external state. Managed startup then requires the exact operator binding and a matching completion receipt; the local fence can deny local startup but cannot authorize external state. heartwood project recover-migration --deployment MANIFEST resumes an interrupted publication or restores the preserved original while the target is unchanged; neither path removes the backup. Gateway versions that do not use these locks must be stopped before maintenance.

items.title: Storage Requirements
items.text: Session state must reside on storage that implements process-shared native advisory locks. Heartwood disables existence-lock fallback because it cannot provide the same automatic release after process termination. Local disks, attached persistent disks, and qualified project filesystems are the intended locations; object-store and file-transfer mounts are not session stores unless their native-lock behavior has been qualified.

items.title: Command Receipts
items.text:
Every command has an opaque identifier and a durable receipt. An exact retry of a completed command returns its original event range without repeating a model call, confirmation callback, or tool action, and reusing the identifier with different content is rejected. If a process stops after accepting a command but before recording its completion, Heartwood refuses to execute that identifier again unless durable state establishes its exact outcome. An interrupted approval is completed automatically only when its recorded intent and OpenHands state prove whether the complete action set was resolved. Otherwise the session rejects further mutation, so a second approval or task cannot repeat an uncertain side effect; verify the evidence and continue in a new session.

Outside decisions distinguish authorization from dispatch: an authorized record proves the native call has not started, and a submitting record means its outcome may be uncertain. When checkpoint evidence is configured, in either mode, the authorization checkpoint must be retained before submission is recorded. An authorization that could not be sent is dispatched only by an exact retry of its own approval command, with the same identifier and content, a live matching worker, and renewed input, policy, and expiry checks. Denying the same review withdraws it, and an authorization that outlives its validity interval is recorded as expired; both close the original approval command so the session can continue. Reconciliation records only such expiry and never turns an observation into submission authority.

items.title: Append Recovery
items.text: Each session event and its audit record are committed through a private recovery journal. After an interrupted append, the next writer verifies the journal, hash links, and existing records before completing only the missing write; malformed or inconsistent recovery state fails closed. After process loss, a persisted OpenHands RUNNING state is reported as an unknown outcome and is never resumed or repeated automatically.

items.title: Persisted Schema Compatibility
items.text:
Every current independently persisted Heartwood envelope declares a schema version. Supported legacy inputs are migrated before typed validation. The project state marker records the current versions for project configuration, session events and metadata, command receipts, commit recovery, writer ownership, audit events, Skill metadata, and OpenHands state. A shared migration registry provides one deterministic, forward-only path for each supported older version without mutating its input.

Project-state migration runs under the initialization lock and replaces metadata atomically. Domain loaders apply the same registry before typed validation, so migration routing cannot bypass the record owner. Unknown versions, migration cycles, nondeterministic transforms, malformed records, and unsupported fields fail closed without including persisted content in error messages.

OpenHands persistence records the exact SDK version and Heartwood content-minimization policy that wrote the state. Heartwood validates that marker before reading or rewriting conversation events. An SDK change therefore requires an explicit, tested migration instead of silently adopting possibly incompatible state. When no migration is supported, Heartwood leaves the saved OpenHands records unchanged and reports HW-AGENT-013. The session history remains available for inspection; new work can start in a new session in the same project. SDK profile and provider-connection storage is scoped to private conversation state rather than a global OpenHands installation.

items.title: Action Decisions
items.text:
OpenHands can supply several proposed tool calls through one confirmation callback. Heartwood displays every member as one action set and applies one decision to the complete set; it does not imply that members can be approved independently. The complete proposal and confirmation request must already be durable before the gateway accepts a decision. If native pending state arrives ahead of its live publisher, a decision is rejected without resolving the callback; a fresh command can be submitted after publication. The gateway commits that complete-set decision before OpenHands can continue into model or tool execution. The pending set is reconstructed from unmatched OpenHands actions after restart rather than from a separate Heartwood cache. Its identifier contains a full SHA-256 digest of the ordered tool-call identifiers, native action identifiers, tool names, action kinds, and exact structured arguments. Canonical JSON makes object-key order irrelevant while preserving list and action order. Changed arguments, substituted tools, or added actions require a different decision even when tool-call identifiers are reused. Advisory risk labels and presentation summaries are not execution authority and do not change this binding. The gateway and backend both compare the current binding before resolving a decision. This binds the proposed action content; it does not freeze files referenced by a command or establish an outside security boundary for local tool execution. An approval identifier without the complete action-content binding is invalid; preserved history does not authorize new execution.

An action is recorded as approved only when the session holds a recorded decision for its action set. A gateway decision under a review mode is such a record: an accepted command and an approval.recorded event with the actor gateway and the applied mode and rule, followed by the same checkpoint boundary, digest check, and resolution events as a researcher decision. The projection labels an action as decided only from these records and names the rule for a gateway decision. If a backend reports executing an action without one, the session records an error and fences the worker attempt.

Each OpenHands proposal becomes one heartwood.action-record.v1 projection correlated by stable action and tool-call identifiers. The same record accumulates its group, decision, execution state, bounded result, and typed affected-path evidence across replay. Terminal, file-editor, Task, and other actions use typed variants, while the exact OpenHands arguments remain available for review. Gateway-issued outside operations and result releases use their own typed variants, which carry the destination or model route and the size, digest, and bounded preview of the content being sent. Each record states whether its summary was written by the model or issued by the gateway. Unknown outcomes fail closed and are never converted into a successful result by an interface.

items.title: Audit Integrity
items.text:
Audit records are chained so replay and export detect corruption, and any modification, reordering, or removal made without recomputing the chain. The chain uses no key, so a process that can write canonical state can rewrite records and recompute it. With the local backend, an approved command runs with the gateway's identity and can reach .heartwood/; a managed worker is admitted only without mounts that overlap the external state. The trusted gateway can still write its state, so external placement does not replace independently retained checkpoints. Only a signed checkpoint binds the history, and only as it stood when the checkpoint was signed. Each content-minimized audit record also authenticates the corresponding complete session event by hash; replay requires matching counts, sequence, type, time, chain link, and event hash. The recovery journal repairs a verified interrupted two-file append before replay, while tampered or unexplained mismatches fail closed. Standalone JSON Lines appenders serialize writers with a native lock and use a durable journal to recover an absent, partial, or completely written final record without duplication. Normal append validates the chain head needed for the next record; replay, verification, export, and checkpoint operations verify the complete available history. The export path is itself recorded as an event.

A deployment can create a canonical checkpoint outside the project through the provider-neutral CheckpointSigner contract. The signed payload binds the audit digest, event count, terminal hash, session, deployment identifier, creation time, retention declaration, signer identity, key identity, key version, algorithm, and public-key fingerprint. Managed deployments resolve an approved HTTPS signer and independently trusted public key from one deployment-owned registry; project state stores only the selected profile identifier. The explicit development and offline fallback uses the same contract through an authenticated Unix socket in an owner-only directory, with an owner-only Ed25519 key. Verification requires the active deployment profile or a public key obtained through an independent trust path and rejects noncanonical or unexpected bundle content. The chain and signature cannot prove that an intact suffix was not deleted before checkpoint creation. An operator-bound evidence controller additionally verifies the complete independently retained checkpoint history and requires each successor to extend the retained audit prefix. This detects rewriting or truncation of that prefix; it does not authenticate unobserved events or prove the completeness of activity after the last retained checkpoint. The managed evidence contract defines publication, retention observation and required-mode recovery. The retention declaration also does not implement storage lifecycle controls; the deployment records system remains responsible for authoritative storage and policy enforcement.

Exact action arguments, commands, affected paths, file content, patches, tool output, and failure text stay out of the content-minimized audit payload. Scientific code, input, environment, and output declarations belong in separate experiment records, not in the security audit payload. An operator-requested checkpoint can retain their exact project export as a separate file, with only its digest, byte count, filename, and binding version recorded in the terminal audit-export event. The existing signature then binds that snapshot through the audit hash, without changing the signer protocol or asserting scientific correctness. The log still cannot make every operational identifier, decision, classification, count, or timestamp non-sensitive. Deployments must define retention, access, export, and deletion policy. See Audit Checkpoints and Retention for the operator contract.

items.title: Long Conversations
items.text:
The OpenHands SDK backend receives explicit model input and output budgets. A rolling-history condenser uses the same authorized model route to summarize older history before the active context exceeds the configured budget, while recent events and the condensed summary remain available to the agent.

Agent and condenser calls use separate usage identifiers and do not bypass model-route policy. The shared projection reports each purpose and a combined total without storing completion content in usage events.

items.title: Tasks and Specialists
items.text:
OpenHands Task Tracker updates supply the title and status of each plan item. Free-form task notes are not copied into Heartwood session or audit events.

Specialist work is represented with its specialist name, task identifier, status, parent session, and parent action. The parent OpenHands conversation remains authoritative and receives the specialist result before continuing. Each invocation uses its child conversation UUID for task identity, preventing usage and lineage collisions after the parent restarts. Sequential execution is the default. Qualified parallel advisory reviews use the same workflow journal and grouped action policy. The journal binds consent to the workflow revision, artifact snapshot, reviewers, budget, and qualification evidence. Before dispatch, the gateway rechecks that binding and records the exact native event and tool-call identities with action fingerprints. The security audit contains the review record's digest, not delegated instructions or returned prose.

Admission uses the existing paired event and audit append recovery protocol. An interrupted admission can be recovered as a durable record, but is never permission to dispatch the same batch again. Late callbacks must still own the active session lease and must not be cancelled; they cannot reacquire a released lease.

items.title: Move Between Interfaces
items.text: Heartwood enforces one writer for each session. Close or stop the active terminal, browser gateway, or notebook writer before continuing that session from another process. The next process can then acquire the lease and continue the same authoritative event sequence. Use distinct session identifiers when interfaces must remain active side by side.

items.title: Skill Trust and Distribution
items.text: Heartwood uses the standard Agent Skills directory format and the public OpenHands Skill loader. It adds a distribution and activation boundary for research environments; it does not create a second Skill format or agent runtime.

items.title: Ownership
items.text:
Owner Responsibility heartwood-skills Curated Skill directories, strict OpenHands validation, complete-tree policy, deterministic archives, and catalog generation Skill source operator TUF root, signing roles, metadata expiry, target publication, revocation, and source availability Heartwood deployment Trusted roots, permitted sources, exact controlled-data approvals, platform policy, and network reachability Heartwood gateway Source refresh, verification, inspection, explicit approval, atomic project activation, audit records, and the shared interface projection OpenHands Skill loading, conversation behavior, and coding tools after Heartwood supplies verified active directories

The Heartwood release pins one exact heartwood-skills Git revision as a submodule. Packaging verifies that the initialized directory is clean and matches that gitlink, then archives that revision into native and container artifacts. Release creation additionally verifies that the pinned revision is published on the protected heartwood-skills/main branch. Bundled Skills are governed by that Heartwood release; withdrawing bundled content requires a new Heartwood release. Heartwood also pins the complete-tree digest of each bundled Skill in its gateway source. Before it lists, loads, or projects bundled Skills, the gateway verifies that every pinned Skill directory is present with its pinned digest, and it refuses all three operations otherwise. Other entries in the bundled directory, such as .DS_Store, are never selected or loaded; the gateway logs them and heartwood doctor reports them. A mismatch fails heartwood doctor and the browser's readiness view as HW-SKILL-002, the Skill and specialist settings return the cause instead of a server error, and the browser keeps the rest of the project readable. Verification ignores no file inside a Skill directory, because a stray file such as cached bytecode for a helper module could execute with the Skill. Installations therefore must not write bytecode into the bundled Skill trees: the candidate image installs the Heartwood application wheels without bytecode compilation, and every image sets PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE. Signed catalog revocations govern catalog-installed content and do not silently rewrite release-bundled content.

Curated packages live directly under skills/<skill-name>/; directory names do not encode review or publication state. Other operators may publish their own compatible signed catalogs without moving content into heartwood-skills. Every catalog target contains the complete immutable Agent Skill package, rather than a mutable Git, marketplace, branch, or archive reference, so inspection, approval, verification, replay, and revocation refer to the same bytes.

OpenHands also provides installed-Skill and marketplace APIs for its general-purpose runtime. Heartwood does not use those APIs as a second installation registry because they do not carry deployment TUF roots, exact-digest controlled-data approvals, signed revocation state, or project-scoped audit evidence. Heartwood instead verifies and activates a Skill once in its gateway-owned project store, then loads each verified active Skill directory individually with the public OpenHands Skill loader. Installation decisions and lifecycle results use Heartwood's existing recoverable, scrubbed, hash-chained audit log rather than a Skill-specific logging format.

items.title: Signed Source Flow
items.text:
flowchart LR
    Registry["Deployment source registry"] --> Root["Independent trusted TUF root"]
    Root --> Metadata["Signed and unexpired metadata"]
    Metadata --> Catalog["Catalog target"]
    Catalog --> Archive["Immutable Skill archive"]
    Archive --> Verify["Complete-tree and OpenHands verification"]
    Verify --> Review["Researcher review of exact digest"]
    Review --> Store["Atomic content-addressed project store"]
    Store --> Gateway["Gateway Skill projection"]
    Gateway --> Interfaces["CLI, browser, and notebook"]
    Gateway --> OpenHands["OpenHands active Skill directories"]
    classDef heartwood fill:#0b694d26,stroke:#2b8268
    classDef platform fill:#3f5b7426,stroke:#6f8fae
    class Verify,Review,Store,Gateway,Interfaces,OpenHands heartwood
    class Registry,Root,Metadata,Catalog,Archive platform

The deployment and the Skill source operator supply the registry, trusted root, signed metadata, and archives, shown in blue; Heartwood owns verification, review, installation, and activation, shown in green.

Heartwood refreshes signed metadata again during installation and compares the current tree digest with the digest presented for approval. For a local unreviewed Skill, it reinspects the source after approval and verifies the same digest again after the atomic copy. It refuses expired metadata, missing targets, substitutions, archive-manifest differences, unsafe paths, symbolic or hard links, special files, unsupported tools, undeclared network requirements, incompatible platforms, and revoked content.

Installed catalog artifacts are addressed by the complete tree SHA-256 digest. The activation index records the source identifier, full source commit, catalog target, version, review status, and revocation status. One project-scoped native lock serializes source refresh, download, activation, removal, and runtime revalidation across CLI and browser processes. Heartwood revalidates the signed source, installed tree, and matching activation event in the verified audit chain before exposing an active catalog Skill to OpenHands. Runtime selection rereads the installation index after refreshing signed sources, so a newly observed revocation excludes the package from that same selection. It also reevaluates tool, network, and platform compatibility for the current deployment, so project state moved between environments cannot activate an incompatible Skill. The projection likewise reports controlled-data approval for an installed Skill from the current deployment registry, not from the retained installation record.

items.title: Agent Selection
items.text:
The agent context contains the release-bundled Skills compatible with the current deployment and the verified active installed Skills, and nothing else. The local gateway and the worker projection use this same selection. The gateway loads each selected Skill from its own SKILL.md; it never passes a parent directory to OpenHands for discovery. When it creates the conversation, it first rechecks each selected Skill's complete-tree digest, so content changed between selection and loading is refused. Scripts and references that the local agent reads or runs later in the conversation are not rechecked; the worker path instead mounts a read-only, digest-bound projection. A selected Skill that has changed or fails to load stops conversation setup rather than being skipped. Research specialists receive the Skills their definitions name from the compatible release-bundled part of this selection, loaded and rechecked the same way. The worker image applies the gateway's deployment platform, which the launcher passes to it, so both build the same specialist catalog.

Each content-addressed slot artifacts/sha256/<tree-digest>/ holds exactly one Skill directory. Anything else in that slot, such as a directory written beside the Skill or a staging directory left by an interrupted installation, has neither a verified digest nor an activation record. Heartwood does not load or project that content. The installed Skill's summary lists each unexpected path: the CLI and browser Skill lists show it, the notebook bridge returns it, and heartwood doctor reports it as HW-SKILL-001. The gateway also logs an error naming the entries whenever it selects the Skill. Removing the unexpected entries clears the report; the verified Skill remains available meanwhile. Entries are compared by file identity, so a case-insensitive file system that stores the Skill directory under another spelling of its name reports nothing.

items.title: Worker Projection
items.text:
SkillManager.stage_worker_skills creates a temporary projection containing only compatible release-bundled and verified active installed Skill packages. It refreshes signed sources and checks activation audit records under the existing lifecycle lock, then uses the catalog's verified tree copier to bind every copied package to its selected tree digest. Installation indexes, source registries, trust roots, signatures, and audit records remain outside the projection. The snapshot digest binds the selected names and complete-tree digests; native Skill objects use /skills/<name> locations instead of gateway filesystem paths. Automatic user, project, and marketplace discovery must remain disabled in the worker's agent context.

The trusted launcher owns the private staging directory outside the project, verifies the transferred snapshot, and mounts it read-only at /skills before admitting the worker. The projection accepts at most 256 packages and 64 MiB of content, in addition to the catalog's per-package limits. The staging context removes its directory after transfer or failure; an abrupt process exit can leave unused staging data that recovery must discard. A snapshot records a selection at one point in time; it does not revoke an already running worker when source metadata later changes. The launcher must fence and revoke that worker before replacing its context, and must select and validate a new snapshot for the replacement attempt.

items.title: Offline Use
items.text:
An offline source is a transferred TUF repository containing metadata and targets plus its independently obtained trusted root. The same Python-TUF client performs signature, rollback, freeze, length, and hash checks without network access. The offline path is not a bypass for unsigned directories.

An operator can still install a complete local directory through the explicit advanced path. Heartwood labels that content Local and unreviewed, copies it without following links, and binds approval to the exact complete-tree digest.

items.title: Catalog Publication
items.text:
The Skill repository produces deterministic Agent Skill targets. A separately administered deployment publishes those targets through a TUF repository; Heartwood never trusts a mutable Git branch, workflow artifact, archive URL, or GitHub attestation as an update channel.

Publication follows this boundary:

  1. merge the Skill change through protected main after repository validation and code-owner review;
  2. run Build Catalog Candidate from the protected main branch;
  3. confirm that the workflow rebuilt and tested the complete catalog and produced a GitHub build-provenance attestation;
  4. import that exact candidate into a TUF signing event;
  5. publish the resulting signed metadata and content-addressed targets over HTTPS; and
  6. verify the deployed repository with a clean Python-TUF client before adding or updating a Heartwood deployment source.

Repository code builds and tests the candidate without an identity token; a separate job attests the resulting files without checking out or executing repository code. The candidate workflow does not sign TUF metadata or publish content. This keeps repository write access separate from the update root of trust.

Use upstream TUF-on-CI workflows and signing tools instead of maintaining a Heartwood-specific signer. Keep root keys offline and use a signature threshold appropriate for the maintainer group. Store online snapshot and timestamp keys in an approved key-management or hardware-security service with GitHub OpenID Connect authorization and a protected publication environment.

The initial root ceremony records role keys, thresholds, expiry windows, and repository endpoints. Distribute the resulting trusted root to Heartwood deployments through a channel independent of the hosted TUF repository.

items.title: Revocation and Rotation
items.text:
The Skill source identifies a withdrawal in revocations.toml by Skill name and exact complete-tree SHA-256 digest. Catalog generation rejects unknown names and digest mismatches, preventing a name-only withdrawal from silently applying to replacement content.

After review, build a new candidate and publish newer signed targets, snapshot, and timestamp metadata. Heartwood applies the signed revocation during refresh and rechecks it before exposing installed content to OpenHands.

Metadata and target retention must allow clients with an older trusted root to complete the TUF update sequence. Do not delete historical root versions required for rotation.

items.title: Separate Decisions
items.text:
Repository review answers whether the package met the curated source's code, policy, and test requirements. Installation approval answers whether a researcher accepted the exact package and declared permissions for one project. Controlled-data approval is deployment evidence for one exact digest.

None of these decisions grants a tool, expands the project boundary, supplies a credential, or overrides action confirmation. The active OpenHands tool set and deployment policy remain authoritative.

items.title: Interface Contract
items.text: The gateway owns one SkillSummary projection for bundled, available, installed, revoked, unsupported, and local-candidate content, including declared tools, network use, data access, and dataset types. The CLI, REST API, browser, and notebook bridge render that projection and submit the same inspect, refresh, install, and remove operations. They do not parse catalogs, validate files, or infer trust independently.

items.title: System Architecture
items.text:
Heartwood has three parts: a gateway that owns project state and every decision, an OpenHands agent worker that proposes and runs actions, and terminal, browser, and notebook interfaces that render the gateway's projections. The worker runs either in the gateway process (the local backend) or as a managed native worker in an OpenShell sandbox. Everything the worker returns crosses a trust boundary at the gateway before it can change a session, reach an outside service, or reach the model.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Interfaces
        CLI["Terminal"]
        Web["Browser"]
        Notebook["Notebook bridge"]
    end
    subgraph Host["Gateway host"]
        Ingress["Ingress policy and launch capability"]
        Gateway["Session gateway"]
        State["Project state: configuration, sessions, audit, Skills, models"]
        Manifest["Operator deployment manifest"]
    end
    subgraph Sandbox["OpenShell sandbox"]
        Worker["OpenHands agent server"]
        Projections["Read-only /inputs and /skills"]
    end
    Web --> Ingress --> Gateway
    CLI --> Gateway
    Notebook --> Gateway
    Manifest --> Gateway
    Gateway --> State
    Gateway -- "admitted requests and events" --> Worker
    Worker --> Projections
    Worker --> Model["Model endpoint"]
    Gateway -- "authorized outside operations" --> Service["Outside service"]
    Gateway -- "checkpoints" --> Records["Records service and signer"]
    classDef heartwood fill:#0b694d26,stroke:#2b8268
    classDef platform fill:#3f5b7426,stroke:#6f8fae
    class CLI,Web,Notebook,Ingress,Gateway,State,Worker,Projections heartwood
    class Manifest,Model,Service,Records platform

Green marks what Heartwood supplies and blue marks what the operator, research environment, or provider supplies, as in the Platform Contract. The local backend has no sandbox: the agent's tools run in the gateway process with the researcher's operating-system identity.

items.title: Gateway
items.text:
SessionGateway is the only path from an interface to an agent. It owns:

  • the project context, persisted configuration, and the effective policy profile;
  • one SessionService per session, with its command receipts, paired event and audit journal, and writer lease;
  • action review decisions and the review modes;
  • authorization of outside operations and result releases;
  • worker attempts, their admission, and revocation;
  • audit export and checkpoint evidence;
  • the Skill, specialist, workflow, model, and workspace services described under Gateway Services; and
  • the session projection and researcher-facing labels that every interface renders.

OpenHands owns the agent loop, conversation persistence, coding tools, Task Tracker, and specialist execution. The gateway configures it through the public SDK and does not keep a parallel agent loop, pending-action cache, or tool implementation. The default tool list is the terminal, the project file editor, Task Tracker, and the sequential Task tool, with a global tool concurrency of one. Model switching, Model Context Protocol servers, critic refinement, and automatic model routing are disabled. OpenHands is the only retry owner for model calls, with at most three attempts for a remote route and two for a local one.

items.title: Process Ownership
items.text:
Project configuration writes take a project-scoped interprocess lock. Each gateway registers a lifetime lease for the project before serving calls; leases of different gateways are independent, so separate sessions run concurrently. Session mutation takes a separate writer lease, held by the gateway process that first handles a command for that session until its session service closes. Two processes therefore cannot fork one session; interfaces continue a session sequentially or use different session identifiers. Writer metadata left by a stopped process is treated as stale only after the operating-system lock is acquired. These locks coordinate gateway processes; they do not stop older binaries or separately supervised inference runtimes.

Shutdown closes admission to the gateway API, waits up to five seconds for accepted calls, and then stops model transfers and session services. If work is still active, shutdown reports failure and keeps session ownership and the gateway lease so it can be retried; REST requests to a stopped gateway return 503.

items.title: Agent Worker
items.text: Both execution modes implement the same backend contract, so session commands, review, journaling, and projections do not depend on where the agent runs.

items.title: Local Backend
items.text:
The local backend creates an OpenHands LocalConversation over the research directory in the gateway process. It is the default for heartwood, heartwood gateway serve without --deployment, and the notebook bridge.

The local backend does not isolate anything. An approved terminal command runs with the researcher's operating-system identity and can read or change any file that identity can, including .heartwood/ state, audit records, and model credentials available to the process. The audit chain detects accidental damage, but such a command can rewrite records and recompute the chain. For that reason review-outside-effects is never in force outside a sandbox, and review-changes applies only when the model route needs no credential or uses a qualified platform-isolated transport (Model Credentials).

items.title: Managed Native Worker
items.text:
heartwood gateway serve --deployment MANIFEST selects the managed worker when the deployment manifest contains a worker table with driver = "openshell-docker". No other launch path selects it, and a managed session never falls back to the local backend.

The worker is the OpenHands agent server from the Heartwood worker image, started by images/worker/launch.py as user 10001. Before starting the server it registers the image's own verified advisory specialists. It runs in an OpenShell sandbox created through OpenShell's Docker driver, with /inputs and /skills mounted read-only and /workspace as its working directory. The sandbox has no network of its own (network=none); its only routes are those the OpenShell policy and supervisor permit.

The gateway reaches the worker through an openshell forward service tunnel on loopback and authenticates every request with a per-attempt SESSION_API_KEY. The remote conversation uses Heartwood's agent settings and tool construction; gateway-local parallel-review executors are not installed in the worker, so specialists there run sequentially. Admission refuses a worker whose mounts reach protected state, the research directory, the native configuration home, or the Docker socket.

items.title: Trust Boundary
items.text: The managed worker and everything it returns are untrusted. The gateway admits a worker, binds it to one durable attempt, bounds what it may send, and validates each response and event before the SDK or the session sees it. Four things cross the boundary: the launch and admission of a worker, the attempt binding that every request carries, the budgets and deadlines on worker traffic, and the admission of individual responses and events.

items.title: Worker Admission
items.text:
Launch happens once per session service, on the session's first backend read:

  1. The session policy evaluates the worker's inference endpoint, credential reference, and capability tier; a denied route reaches no platform callback. The route must also equal the manifest's profile_id, model, and model_endpoint.
  2. The gateway stages the manifest's inputs (at most 128 files, 16 MiB each and 64 MiB in total) and a Skill projection into a private directory under the state root. One input identity digest binds the inputs, the Skill selection, the specialist catalog fingerprint, and any client-tool specifications.
  3. The session journals the attempt intent before any sandbox exists.
  4. The launcher connects to the registered OpenShell gateway with its mutual TLS identity and reads its reported version through the SDK health call. A version outside the manifest's gateway_versions stops serving at start with HW-WORKER-001, and stops a later launch or reconciliation before any sandbox, volume, or deletion request.
  5. A short-lived preparation container copies the staged snapshots into two attempt-owned Docker volumes. It runs only the image's chmod with no network, a read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped except FOWNER, and no-new-privileges.
  6. OpenShell creates the sandbox with the pinned image digest, the operator's policy, the provider attachment, CPU and memory limits, and attempt labels.
  7. The launcher admits the sandbox only when OpenShell reports the expected identity, labels, ready phase, main-process generation, and an accepted configuration whose policy hash equals sandbox_policy_sha256.
  8. Docker inspection of the worker container must report the pinned image, NetworkMode: none, no privilege, no added capability, and exactly one read-only volume at each of /inputs and /skills.
  9. A probe inside the worker must report the expected file digests, read-only projections, no /workspace/.heartwood, user 10001, the expected specialist catalog fingerprint, and an openshell:resolve:env: inference placeholder.
  10. The forwarded API must answer with the attempt key and refuse a request without it, and the sandbox is admitted once more before the binding is returned.

The operator's policy file must match policy_file_sha256, require Landlock as a hard requirement, run as 10001:10001, and list /inputs and /skills as read-only.

Container inspection accepts only listed confinement values: the container's own process and user namespaces, a private or absent IPC namespace, and security options that keep the default profiles, add no-new-privileges, or select the default AppArmor profile. An SELinux label is accepted only for the standard confined type (container_t, or its former name svirt_lxc_net_t) or a single sensitivity level with individual categories. Every field must be present in Docker's report; an absent field fails admission. A mount whose host source overlaps the research directory, protected state, native configuration home, or Docker socket is rejected. Sources are compared as written, after normalization, and as resolved on the gateway host; a runtime that reports paths from another filesystem namespace is checked only in the written forms. Inspection does not restrict other mounts the OpenShell supervisor adds.

The gateway version check compares the operator's declaration with the gateway's own report. It catches a misconfigured deployment, not a gateway that misreports its version or lacks the behavior Heartwood's revocation evidence depends on. The patched OpenShell gateway Heartwood builds exists only for qualification (Build and Qualification).

items.title: Worker Attempt Ownership
items.text:
A worker attempt is a durable record in the paired session and audit journal with the phases prepared, active, fenced, and revoked. Its intent binds the project, session, native conversation, image digest, deployment policy, sandbox policy, and input identity. Records contain no worker credentials.

The launcher returns a runtime binding (sandbox identity, process generation, endpoint, image, and policy), and the session issues a process-local lease for it. Every HTTP request, event connection, and session callback requires a live lease that still owns the session writer. The lease reobserves the sandbox through OpenShell before admission, reusing a passing observation for at most one second; a changed sandbox, generation, configuration, or a stopped forwarder fences the attempt. Fencing closes HTTP, event, and callback admission at once, including responses already in flight.

The gateway fences an attempt when it observes an exhausted response budget, a missed request deadline, a failed admission or runtime observation, execution reported without a recorded decision, or session close. Fencing starts revocation on its own short-lived thread, so no control-plane call runs under a session lock or on a transport thread. Revocation waits for a session command in progress and is bounded by the control-plane timeouts: 15 seconds to observe the sandbox, 90 seconds for the delete request, and 90 seconds to observe its absence. It deletes the sandbox through the control client connected at launch, stops the forwarder, rechecks the native configuration, requires Docker to report no attempt-owned worker container, and removes the attempt's volumes before the session records revoked with its evidence. Revocation is attempted once. If it fails, the attempt stays fenced and the writer stays owned, and the worker can keep running until the session closes, the gateway stops, or the next gateway start reconciles it. A fence is raised only when the gateway observes the condition, so a worker the gateway is not exchanging data with is not detected by this path.

A gateway that ends without revoking leaves its attempt in the journal. heartwood gateway serve --deployment calls SessionGateway.reconcile_workers before serving: it fences each unrevoked attempt, deletes the sandbox only when its name, labels, and any retained sandbox identity match, verifies absence, removes owned volumes, and records the evidence. Sessions whose revocation was not observed are reported and stay fenced until a later start. Reconciliation uses the control plane and Docker daemon named by the current manifest; an operator who points the manifest at other infrastructure must first remove the earlier worker, because absence on the new infrastructure would otherwise be recorded as revocation. OpenShell deletion is name-scoped rather than conditional on a generation; unique attempt names and identity checks do not replace control-plane authorization.

After a recorded revocation, a gateway configured to launch workers can start one replacement attempt with a new identity, key, placeholder, and response budget in a new sandbox. The replacement starts a new conversation in an empty workspace; the session projection marks where it became active. Replacement is refused while the journal holds work only the revoked worker's conversation could finish: an unsettled run, an unended pause, an action awaiting review, an unrecoverable outcome, or a non-terminal outside operation or result release. A gateway without a worker configuration refuses commands for a revoked session instead of running it locally; the session stays readable.

items.title: Budgets and Deadlines
items.text:
Every worker attempt has one response budget shared by HTTP responses, connection attempts, and received events. It allows bursts of 1,024 responses and 32 MiB and refills at four responses and 1 MiB per second. Each response is charged its size or 16 bytes per parsed value, whichever is larger; received events are charged by size. Resetting the HTTP client does not replenish the budget, and a replacement attempt receives a new one.

Each request has one wall-clock deadline of 120 seconds from connection to the last body byte, so slow status lines, headers, interim responses, or chunk framing cannot extend it. A response body is limited to 4 MiB, or 16 MiB for a branch snapshot, and to 524,288 JSON values counted before parsing. A walk through paged history ends when a page identifier repeats or after 1,024 pages or 32 MiB. Exhausting the budget, missing a deadline, or returning a history that does not end fences the attempt.

These limits bound what the gateway receives, about 70 MiB of peak memory for one response; they do not bound work inside the worker. The event connection has no deadline of its own: it is idle while a session waits for its researcher, its handshake is limited to ten seconds, and keepalive closes a connection whose peer stops answering. After the first backend read, which can launch the worker, reconciliation reads the worker without holding the session command lock or the gateway state lock. A command's own request to the worker still runs under both locks, within the request deadline.

items.title: Response and Event Admission
items.text:
Responses must be uncompressed UTF-8 JSON with unique keys and finite numbers, on the configured origin, without redirects, ambient proxies, or server-selected client tools. Every event in a page or snapshot must validate as a native OpenHands event before the SDK receives it. The returned tool registrations must equal the exact tool-name and module pairs and client-tool specifications from trusted configuration on create, attach, resume, and fork.

Conversation metadata is admitted field by field against the creation request the gateway sent. Fields the request sets, including the agent, security analyzer, confirmation policy, hooks, workspace, iteration limit, and secret registry, are admitted only when they equal the sent values. A fixed set of reported fields such as status, usage, identifiers, and timestamps is admitted as data, and any other field is rejected. A worker therefore cannot select the agent implementation, model route, analyzer, or secret source the gateway constructs.

The event connection permits only the origin's canonical conversation endpoint without credentials in the URL, query, or fragment, verifies TLS against bundled certificate authorities, limits messages to 4 MiB, and queues at most four frames. Binary messages and completion-log events are rejected. Admission errors never include worker response content.

A worker acknowledgement means a proposal was dispatched, not that an outside effect was authorized or completed. Admission failure does not stop the worker; revocation through the sandbox control plane does.

items.title: Model Credentials
items.text:
The managed worker receives only an openshell:resolve:env: placeholder; the provider credential stays in the OpenShell control plane, which resolves it at request time. Credential expiry, model allowlists, and tenant restrictions are provider and inference-service settings; the selected model name and a provider attachment do not enforce them against a compromised worker.

For the local backend the gateway classifies the route against the platform capability as credential-free, application-scrubbed, or platform-isolated. An application-scrubbed route keeps provider material out of tool inputs, durable state, and projections, but the model client and the tools still share one operating-system identity, so every action is reviewed. A platform-isolated route requires a separately authorized transport and live synthetic qualification.

items.title: Action Review and Review Modes
items.text:
OpenHands pauses before every action set (AlwaysConfirm), and the session service decides whether the set waits for the researcher. The OpenHands policy-rail and pattern analyzers rate each action from its typed content; a rating can send an action to the researcher but never allow one, and the model's own risk field is not an input. A decision applies to the complete action set and is bound to a digest of its exact content (Action Decisions).

The gateway classifies each action from its type: a file-editor view of a path it resolved inside the project is read, a Task Tracker update is plan, any other file-editor or terminal action is workspace, and everything else is other. Terminal commands are never classified by their text.

Mode The gateway allows a set without the researcher when Available review-all never always; every fail-closed path falls back to it review-changes every action is read, or every action is plan, with a low or medium analyzer rating in a sandbox, or locally when the model route needs no credential or is platform-isolated review-outside-effects every action is read, plan, or workspace with a low or medium rating, in an admitted sandbox only while the session's worker attempt is active and admitted

A set always waits for the researcher when it contains an outside operation, a result release, or a tool bound to an outside service, when its proposal is not yet durable, when the researcher paused the session or the run stopped, or when the worker's admission failed. Any unknown classification or unreadable setting selects researcher review.

The researcher selects a mode with --review-mode, /permissions, browser settings, or PUT /settings/actions/review; without a selection the mode is review-outside-effects in a sandbox when the ceiling permits it, and review-all otherwise. The policy profile's allowed_action_review_modes is the ceiling; Deployment Ceiling describes the built-in defaults and how manifest and project lists combine.

A gateway decision is recorded like a researcher decision: an accepted command and an approval.recorded event with the actor gateway and the applied mode and rule (read.file-view, plan.task-tracker, or sandbox.contained), followed by the same checkpoint boundary and resolution events. If the worker reports executing an action without such a record, the session records an error and fences the attempt. Under review-outside-effects, containment of automatically allowed actions rests on the OpenShell policy and on outside-operation admission, not on per-action review. The action-review evaluation is the evidence a deployment needs before listing a mode.

items.title: Outside Operations and Result Releases
items.text:
An outside operation is a worker tool call that would change state in a platform service. A result release sends an outside observation back to the worker's model. Both always require a researcher decision bound to exact content; no review mode allows them automatically.

The outside service adapter (ExternalActionAdapter) is a trusted dependency an embedding launcher supplies to SessionGateway through external_actions_factory. heartwood gateway serve installs none; native qualification uses a synthetic authenticated MCP service. The Platform Contract defines the messages an adapter exchanges.

An outside operation proceeds through these steps:

  1. The worker proposes a call to a tool the adapter lists. The adapter resolves it into a canonical request of at most 64 KiB with at most 16 immutable input references totalling at most 16 MiB, without performing an effect.
  2. The gateway issues an ExternalActionProposal binding the operation identity, the worker attempt, the proposing event, the service policy digest, the request, and a validity interval, and presents it as an action with an unknown rating.
  3. The researcher's decision binds the proposal's SHA-256 digest and permits one use. An approval is journaled and must be retained as checkpoint evidence before any dispatch.
  4. Before dispatch the gateway rechecks the live worker lease, the policy digests, the adapter's policy and actor entitlement, expiry, and the input bytes, then records submitting and calls the adapter once.
  5. The adapter's observation must name the same proposal, operation, project, and service. An uncertain dispatch is recorded as unknown and later resolved by status lookup, never by resubmission.

Only an exact retry of the approval command that recorded an authorization can dispatch it; a status read, reconciliation, another command, or an automatic decision cannot. Denying the same review withdraws an undispatched authorization, and an authorization that outlives its interval is recorded as expired.

A result release is a separate proposal that binds the operation digest, the observation event, the sanitized content, the destination model route, and a validity interval. After approval the adapter independently authorizes disclosure to that route, the worker must be idle with no pending review, and the gateway submits the content once as a user message wrapped in an outside-result envelope.
