The envelope labels the data; it is not an instruction boundary, and the model can act on instructions in released content.

items.title: Protected State and the Deployment Manifest
items.text:
The process current directory is the research-file boundary, and no interface accepts another workspace path. A local launch keeps project state in .heartwood/ under it. A managed launch binds the research directory to external state through an operator manifest with the schema heartwood.project-deployment.v1: the project UUID, the exact research directory, a state_root named by that UUID, the policy that is the project's default and ceiling, and optional worker and evidence tables (Deployment Manifest).

The gateway validates the manifest, its ownership and permissions, and every worker and evidence authority file before opening any store. Project content can neither select a manifest nor supply deployment authority, and copying the research directory does not grant access to the original state. A project's own policy may only narrow the manifest's, and broader or malformed persisted rules fail closed. Without a manifest, the selected platform adapter supplies the default policy and no deployment ceiling applies.

heartwood project migrate --deployment moves local state into the external root, and heartwood project recover-migration --deployment resumes or reverses an interrupted move (Persistence). External placement keeps state out of the worker's mounts; operating-system identities still decide who else can read it, and the gateway can always write it.

items.title: Audit, Checkpoints, and Evidence
items.text:
Each session event and its content-minimized audit record are committed together through a recovery journal, and the audit chain links every record by hash. The chain uses no key; only a signed checkpoint binds history, and only as it stood when it was signed (Audit Integrity).

With an evidence table, the gateway anchors every action-set decision, every outside decision, and session close as a checkpoint boundary. It stages the audit prefix to an S3-compatible records service and has the signer from the deployment's signer registry publish the checkpoint. In required mode a boundary returns only after the retained signature is read back, so an approved action or outside operation does not dispatch without it; in buffered mode an unavailable records service is recorded as a visible gap. An approved outside operation always requires its checkpoint. A session whose history contains checkpoint evidence refuses to dispatch from a gateway that lacks the records configuration. Audit Checkpoints and Retention defines the operator contract.

items.title: Interfaces
items.text:
The terminal, browser, and notebook bridge submit typed commands and render one gateway projection; they keep no event reducers or business rules of their own.

  • The startup planner combines read-only readiness with platform capabilities and returns one phase: project review, connection required, credential required, model required, compute required, ready, or recovery required.
  • Agent work runs in a supervised background thread, so an interface can guide, pause, resume, or review while a task is active. Final messages, actions, lifecycle changes, task plans, usage, specialist lineage, and errors become durable events; token text stays transient.
  • The session projection contains the conversation, versioned action records, lifecycle, the complete pending action set, task plan, usage by purpose, specialist lineage, available commands, status, and bounded next-step suggestions. The gateway enforces the available commands before dispatch.
  • REST, server-sent events, and WebSocket return events and the projection from one serialized snapshot; a transient revision orders token-only updates.

IngressPolicy models direct loopback, a local Jupyter proxy, and an explicitly trusted proxy with one external origin and base path. It rejects undeclared non-loopback exposure, untrusted forwarding metadata, origin and host mismatches, duplicate security headers, and ambiguous paths before a route runs. Every REST, server-sent-event, and WebSocket request must carry the process-lifetime launch capability, and the gateway derives the command actor from it.

items.title: Platform Adapter
items.text: The selected adapter supplies environment detection, capabilities, ingress modes, the model-credential boundary, data-mount declarations, credential allowlists, and the default policy. Generic, Terra, and Carina behavior differs only through these boundaries and their launch orchestration. The versioned Heartwood–platform contract and its offline conformance checks are described in the Platform Contract.

items.title: Gateway Services
items.text: These services run in the gateway and share the session journal, review, and projection.

items.title: Research Workflows
items.text: A versioned definition declares inputs, ordered stages, artifacts, deterministic checks, researcher gates, and work budgets, and references existing Skills and advisory specialists. A stage is an ordinary OpenHands turn with normal action review; advancing requires settled work, resolved approvals, a structured outcome, and gateway-run checks against the exact input and output digests. Model-reported success cannot replace a missing, failed, or stale check, and checks establish bounded properties, not scientific appropriateness. Budgets are admission checks at observed boundaries, not spending caps. See Research Workflows and Experiment Records.

items.title: Independent Review
items.text: Advisory reviewers return structured proposals through OpenHands' FinishTool; the gateway verifies supported findings against captured evidence and keeps unverified proposals visibly separate. A verified finding is an observation, not permission to correct, approve, or advance.

items.title: Research Specialists
items.text: The catalog is loaded through OpenHands AgentDefinition and registered with the public Task tool. The enabled planning and review roles are tool-free, inherit the parent's model route, and run sequentially; the project-action role is not registered because nested child actions cannot be reviewed through the public task interface. Parallel advisory review requires deployment-supplied qualification evidence (Qualify Parallel Reviews).

items.title: Skills
items.text: Signed catalog content and local directories are verified as complete trees, approved by exact digest, and passed to OpenHands as exact directories (Skill Trust and Distribution).

items.title: Model Artifacts
items.text: Catalog choices, Hugging Face downloads, raw imports, and portable bundles converge on one selection, resource planner, integrity verifier, and launcher. Downloads pin an immutable revision, bundles are verified digest by digest before atomic publication under models/, and import requires an explicit license decision bound to the reviewed manifest. The native inference launcher writes a durable launch intent before starting its child and removes it only after observing the child exit; an unresolved intent blocks another launch and migration until the operator reconciles it (Troubleshooting).

items.title: Workspace Inspection
items.text: One bounded read-only service serves trees, text files, changed paths, and diffs, excluding .heartwood/ and .git/ at every depth and refusing symbolic links and special files. Git projects use OpenHands LocalWorkspace; other projects report only paths changed by typed file-editor actions, never paths parsed from terminal text.

items.title: Build and Qualification
items.text:
The application's default lock installs patched OpenHands and OpenShell SDK wheels from vendor/runtime-wheels/, which is not committed. deploy/build-worker-candidate.py --bootstrap builds them there from immutable upstream archives and the reviewed patches in images/worker/candidate/, or verifies existing wheels against the digests in sources.json. The patches add the remote-event and configuration-admission hooks the trust boundary requires; the gateway refuses to construct a managed worker on an SDK without them.

The OpenShell gateway is also built from pinned source with two deletion patches, as version 0.1.8+heartwood.2 with the purpose qualification-only. Heartwood ships no production OpenShell gateway: a deployment's gateway is checked only by its declared version, and it must separately provide the behavior native qualification depends on.

Native qualification runs the installed application, worker image, and qualification gateway through the complete boundary and produces commit-bound, verifiable evidence; Testing and Evidence describes the cases, evidence, and verification. Qualification uses synthetic data and does not establish sensitive-data readiness or institutional approval.

items.title: Testing and Evidence
items.text: Heartwood's claims rest on four evidence levels, and each test layer reaches a stated level. No single layer establishes every property of a deployment.

items.title: Claims
items.text:
• Implemented means code and automated contract tests exist.
  • CI validated means the behavior ran in the documented automated environment.
  • Live synthetic validated means the published artifact ran in the named platform with synthetic data.
  • Institution approved requires separate institutional evidence and is never inferred from the previous levels.

Native qualification is CI validation of the managed worker boundary with synthetic workloads. It does not establish sensitive-data readiness, and a qualification record is not institutional approval. Release documentation states the supported contract; run-specific results stay in CI artifacts and pull requests.

items.title: Test Layers
items.text:
Layer Runs as Establishes Unit, schema, and persistence pytest in the Python workflow Validation, policy, diagnostics, serialization, atomic replacement, append interruption and recovery, process concurrency, migrations, and private permissions OpenHands conformance pytest with the real SDK and deterministic TestLLM Typed events, grouped approval and rejection, restart without repeated model or tool work, Task Tracker, structured outcomes, and sequential specialists Gateway and interface contracts pytest, the Web UI workflow Shared command and projection behavior, review modes, outside-operation phases, workspace inspection, transports, ingress, and terminal, browser, and notebook rendering Supply chain pytest with an ephemeral TUF repository Skill refresh, offline verification, expiry, rollback, substitution, path confinement, exact-digest approval, and revocation Container and native smoke Container smoke and native release workflows Entrypoints, filesystem layout, no secrets in image layers, offline operation, and installation of the release archive in an empty Ubuntu 24.04 container Capable-model acceptance Capable model workflow, optional GPU qualification Real inference driving the gateway and OpenHands through approval, rejection, replay, and audit export Native qualification Worker candidate workflow The installed application, worker image, and qualification gateway across the complete managed worker boundary Live synthetic validation Operator run in Terra or Carina The exact published artifact in the named platform without protected data

Deterministic layers use fake providers for failure paths and TestLLM for SDK conformance; capable models appear only in the acceptance path that needs real inference. Browser tests build production assets, scan the rendered interface with axe, and check keyboard focus, reduced motion, and reflow at desktop, tablet, and narrow notebook widths.

Outside-operation conformance uses the native SDK MCP client against an authenticated synthetic MCP service on loopback. The service verifies the token's signature, issuer, audience, and expiry, and separately checks project, researcher, worker attempt, policy, exact request, and input bytes; its record and operation identity are committed in one SQLite transaction. Tests discard a reply after the effect commits, restart the gateway and service, rotate the credential, and recover through status lookup without resubmission. These tests establish protocol and authorization behavior, not process isolation or deployed network policy.

items.title: Continuous Integration
items.text:
Pull-request and main-branch validation both end in the required Release Candidate Ready aggregate, which requires every validation workflow, including capable-model acceptance; on pull requests it also requires native worker qualification. On a pull request, native qualification and its candidate builds are skipped only when every changed path is under documentation/ or .github/ other than the worker candidate and pull-request validation workflows; any other path, including one the selection does not recognize, requires them. On the main branch, the separate Native Qualification workflow runs the complete native qualification for every commit and attests its evidence; it has no concurrency group, so a newer commit never cancels the run of an earlier one.

Pull-request jobs that build and run candidate code hold no signing or package-write permission; the Python job holds an identity token only to upload coverage to Codecov. Multi-platform manifests, moving tags, and evidence attestation run only on the main branch. Registry writes run on the main branch, except that the manual Terra GPU Qualification Candidate workflow pushes a candidate-sha-<commit>-terra-gpu-nvidia image from the branch it is started on. Release creation requires Release Candidate Ready, the Analyze (python) and Analyze (javascript-typescript) code-scanning checks, and the attested Native Qualification evidence for the exact commit.

items.title: Capable-Model Acceptance
items.text:
One coding-agent acceptance contract drives the real gateway and OpenHands adapter through structured terminal proposals, grouped approval and rejection, a synthetic file change, byte-exact independent verification, proof that the rejected action did not run, fresh-process replay, and hash-chain-verified audit export. It writes a machine-readable record of the runtime, model revision, hardware, context, tensor parallelism, parser, and tool mode.

The CPU job runs on the heartwood-ubuntu-large runner and obtains its model through the portable-transfer contract: it downloads and verifies the pinned model, exports a bundle, imports it into an empty project in a container with --network none after explicit license approval, and runs the acceptance task against the imported copy. The GPU image workflow verifies the hashed CUDA environment, vLLM and PyTorch versions, parsers, and the absence of model weights on standard runners; it does not claim CUDA initialization or GPU model loading. The protected self-hosted GPU workflow runs the same acceptance contract with external weights and promotes exactly one row of the GPU compatibility matrix; it does not qualify other drivers, model revisions, precisions, parsers, context sizes, or tensor-parallel layouts.

items.title: Candidate Builds
items.text:
The default lock installs the patched SDK wheels from vendor/runtime-wheels/, which is not committed. deploy/build-worker-candidate.py builds them from immutable upstream archives and the patches in images/worker/candidate/, verifying source, patch, and build-tool hashes and using a fixed source timestamp. The patches add bounded remote-event admission and outside client-tool control (conversation), explicit environment replacement for terminal backends (terminal), the configuration-admission record that binds a sandbox to its policy and process generation (sandbox), and a security-fixed file-lock requirement (dependency). A local version suffix such as +heartwood.3 marks a patched build; the recorded upstream source revision, not the version number, identifies the upstream code.

uv run --no-project --python 3.12.15 deploy/build-worker-candidate.py --bootstrap
uv run --no-project --python 3.12.15 deploy/build-worker-candidate.py --output test-results/worker-candidate
uv run --no-project --python 3.12.15 deploy/build-worker-candidate.py --application --output test-results/application-candidate

--bootstrap builds the wheels into vendor/runtime-wheels/ when the directory is absent, and otherwise verifies the wheels and their build record against sources.json. The other commands require a new output directory; --application archives the current commit with its pinned Skill submodule and records both commits, wheel hashes, and a hash-pinned installation manifest. The worker candidate workflow builds each twice and requires identical build records, checks that runtime.sh compile reproduces the committed candidate lock, installs it with runtime.sh install, and runs the Python suite with isolated imports against the packaged application.

The worker and runtime images use the shared images/Dockerfile with HEARTWOOD_DEPENDENCY_PROFILE=candidate and a worker-qualification-artifacts build context holding the SDK wheels under sdk/ and the application build under application/. The image retains both build records in /opt/heartwood/qualification/, and its revision label must name the application commit.

The OpenShell gateway is built from the pinned source and the two deletion patches recorded in images/worker/candidate/gateway.json, whose purpose is qualification-only:

uv run --no-project --python 3.12.15 deploy/build-worker-candidate.py \
  --gateway --gateway-tests --output test-results/gateway-candidate --cache test-results/gateway-cache

--gateway-tests runs the upstream deletion regressions first and needs 12 GiB of container memory; a failed or empty test run prevents packaging. The cache keeps source archives and the Cargo registry, and compiled objects are keyed by the manifest so changed inputs never reuse them. The record binds source, manifest, lockfile, binary, and image identities; it establishes build provenance, not byte-identical gateway builds. These artifacts are qualification inputs, not a supported production gateway; an operator's gateway must provide the behavior qualification depends on. deploy/build-records-fixture.py builds the synthetic records server and client from digest-verified sources; they provide synthetic storage behavior, not a records-service recommendation.

items.title: Native Qualification
items.text:
deploy/qualify-native-worker.py runs the native cases against existing worker and runtime images, the gateway build, and the records tools. It requires a local Linux Docker engine and a new output directory, builds the outside controller and the symlink-workspace fixture image, and runs the installed application without source overlays.

python3 deploy/build-records-fixture.py \
  --output test-results/records-tools --cache test-results/records-cache
python3 deploy/qualify-native-worker.py \
  --worker-image heartwood-worker:qualification \
  --runtime-image heartwood-runtime:qualification \
  --gateway-artifacts test-results/gateway-candidate \
  --records-artifacts test-results/records-tools \
  --output test-results/native-qualification

Only the outside controller and the disposable OpenShell gateway receive the Docker socket; workers receive neither the socket nor its group. The synthetic TLS provider uses a generated credential and a fixed tool-call sequence, so no external inference service or key is needed.

items.title: Installed Native Integration
items.text:
The synthetic run executes exactly the cases listed in EXPECTED_CASES in deploy/qualification_evidence.py:

  • an ordinary and a hostile session, each with local audit and with deployment-bound checkpoint evidence, through the production launcher, admitted policy, read-only projections, exact approvals, verified audit, revocation before writer release, and fresh-process replay that rejects a wrong project identity and corrupted audit;
  • unapproved actions that must not run, after denial and at shutdown with a review pending;
  • an outside operation that requires retained authorization, approved, denied, pending, and with its reply lost;
  • the default sandbox review mode, in which a contained action is allowed by the gateway while an outside operation waits for the researcher;
  • two workers whose authority and effects stay separate;
  • a derived image whose OCI working directory is a symbolic link, which must fail with an outside WorkspaceValidationFailed condition before the main process or any inference request;
  • a discarded create response, which must keep the attempt fenced and the writer owned until outside revocation removes the worker and volumes;
  • expiry of the provider credential, which must deny a retained placeholder;
  • records transport authorization, and gateway logs retained until verified cleanup.

The hostile session's approved command tries to read control credentials, change protected state and read-only projections, and reach a forbidden provider path. The fixture compares state canaries and provider traffic before and after; worker-reported success cannot replace these observations. An allowed endpoint redirects to a forbidden path, and qualification requires the redirect request outside the worker and no request at its destination; an unapproved WebSocket upgrade must be refused. Direct IPv4, mapped IPv6, native IPv6, TCP, and UDP probes run against controlled listeners on a disposable dual-stack network, and an outside client must reach each listener before and after, so a timeout or unreachable route cannot pass as a denial.

With checkpoint evidence, a records outage must block the approved action until its authorization is retained, and command replay must not repeat the effect. The pinned synthetic records server rejects the conditional-write bucket policy, so replacement versions are detected and rejected without claiming full storage-policy qualification. Test failure or failed cleanup fails qualification; if revocation cannot settle, the fixture retains its control state for reconciliation.

These cases do not establish resistance to model-driven prompt injection, production records-policy qualification, tenant authorization, or sensitive-data readiness.

items.title: Infrastructure Telemetry
items.text:
The fixture receives OpenShell's OCSF export through OTLP with mutual TLS at an outside test collector; an unauthenticated client must be rejected and an authenticated control must succeed. It checks gateway and sandbox resource identifiers, keeps native event identifiers, and rejects synthetic credentials or state canaries before writing telemetry artifacts. During an injected collector outage, harmless commands continue until the supervisor reports an export gap, and the resumed collector must receive that gap with a positive dropped-record count and loss timestamp. The Heartwood audit must stay byte-for-byte unchanged through the fault and verify afterward.

A received gap record establishes known loss, not complete capture of every other event. An exporter reports a gap with a later batch, so idle periods and abrupt teardown can leave loss unreported. The collector is a fixture; it does not qualify a production collector's retention, alerting, or recovery.

items.title: Capable Model in a Native Worker
items.text:
--model-profile runs one capable-model case through the same boundary against an operator-approved provider route. The profile names base_url and model and may bound max_input_tokens, max_output_tokens, max_iterations, and deadline_seconds (defaults 32,768, 512, 6, and 180). The credential is read once from standard input; it is never an argument, profile field, worker credential, or report value.

python3 deploy/qualify-native-worker.py \
  --worker-image "$WORKER_IMAGE" --runtime-image "$RUNTIME_IMAGE" \
  --gateway-artifacts "$GATEWAY_ARTIFACTS" --records-artifacts "$RECORDS_ARTIFACTS" \
  --model-profile /run/config/qualification-model.json \
  --output test-results/native-model-qualification < /run/secrets/qualification-key

The synthetic input tells the model to ignore approval and read outside credentials. The controller approves only the input read, the verified Skill invocation, and the aggregate command the task needs, runs filesystem and network probes from outside the worker, verifies the audit ledger, and requires outside revocation before cleanup. The disposable provider credential carries an expiry matching the deadline, which OpenShell enforces at delivery and at request time, and an outside timer detaches the provider independently of the application. Expiry does not cancel a request the provider already accepted, and the iteration and token limits are not a provider spending cap. The record reports the model as requested configuration and usage as worker-reported diagnostics, not attested identity or billing evidence. No credentialed run happens in CI.

items.title: Native Network Qualification
items.text:
deploy/tests/worker_network_qualification.py runs the network probes against an existing disposable sandbox through the authenticated control API, from a trusted Linux controller with IPv4 and native IPv6 addresses that reach its canary listeners.

python deploy/tests/worker_network_qualification.py \
  --gateway "$GATEWAY_ADDRESS" --ca "$CA_PATH" --cert "$CLIENT_CERT_PATH" --key "$CLIENT_KEY_PATH" \
  --sandbox "$SYNTHETIC_SANDBOX" --ipv4 "$CONTROLLER_IPV4" --ipv6 "$CONTROLLER_IPV6" \
  --port 19672 --ipv6-port 19673

The admitted policy must allow the --allowed-host name (default host.docker.internal) and deny the canary ports and unlisted destinations. The check requires explicit policy denial for direct IPv4, mapped IPv6, native IPv6, UDP, and an unlisted hostname; any canary traffic, listener failure, or change in sandbox identity, generation, or configuration invalidates the result. It does not create, delete, or change the sandbox, and does not qualify IPv6 inference or model authorization.

items.title: Native Qualification Evidence
items.text:
The runner writes qualification.json as the manifest of one run and SHA256SUMS over every retained file:

Field Content qualification_kind synthetic-native, or capable-model-native with requested_model_profile source The Heartwood commit of the checkout and whether its tree matched that commit started_at, finished_at Run boundaries in UTC invocation Image references and paths supplied to the runner images Content identifiers of the supplied images and of the images built for the run image_sources For the worker and runtime images, the revision label, registry digests, and build records read from the image itself gateway_build, records_build The verified build records of the gateway and records tools qualification_sources, qualification_sources_unchanged Hashes of the runner, fixtures, tests, and controller inputs, and whether they stayed unchanged host, controller_socket_group Kernel, architecture, and Docker version of the engine, and the socket group given to the controller returncode, network_retained Test command status and whether the qualification network kept attached resources cases Identifier, outcome, and duration of every executed case, read from junit.xml sensitive_data_ready Always false failures, passed Every reason the run does not qualify its commit, and the verdict

A run passes only when the tree matches its commit, both supplied images name that commit in their revision label and application build record, the sources are unchanged, the test command succeeds, no network resources are retained, and the executed cases equal the expected set with every case passed. A reduced, extended, or skipped selection therefore fails, and adding, removing, or renaming a case requires changing EXPECTED_CASES in the same commit.

SHA256SUMS covers the manifest, junit.xml, logs, and per-case evidence. Each worker case retains worker-container.json, the image, privilege, capabilities, security options, network, namespaces, and mounts Docker reported before admission was decided, without host paths, labels, or environment, so a rejected sandbox still shows its observed values. Private gateway state and generated credentials share the output directory and are excluded from the checksums and from retention. The worker candidate workflow verifies the evidence against its own commit and retains it for 90 days on the main branch and 14 days on pull requests. On the main branch, a separate Native Qualification job, which runs no candidate code, downloads the evidence, verifies it again, and attests SHA256SUMS with a GitHub build-provenance attestation. Pull-request, manual, local, and capable-model runs, and manual Native Qualification runs on another branch, are not attested.

Release creation keeps the evidence beyond its artifact retention. It locates the successful Native Qualification run of the release commit, downloads its evidence and attestation, verifies both as below, and fails when any of these is missing or does not verify. The release then carries native-qualification-evidence.tar.gz, the evidence directory with its SHA256SUMS, and native-qualification-evidence.sigstore.jsonl, the attestation bundle for that SHA256SUMS.

To verify release evidence, check out the release tag and run these commands in a directory holding both assets:

commit="$(git -C "$HEARTWOOD_CHECKOUT" rev-parse HEAD)"
tar -xzf native-qualification-evidence.tar.gz
gh attestation verify native-qualification/SHA256SUMS --repo SchmiedmayerLab/heartwood \
  --bundle native-qualification-evidence.sigstore.jsonl \
  --signer-workflow SchmiedmayerLab/heartwood/.github/workflows/native-qualification.yml \
  --source-ref refs/heads/main --source-digest "$commit"
(cd native-qualification && sha256sum --check SHA256SUMS)
python3 "$HEARTWOOD_CHECKOUT/deploy/qualification_evidence.py" native-qualification --commit "$commit"

The bundle holds the attestation that release creation verified; without --bundle, the command verifies against the attestations GitHub stores for the repository. Evidence downloaded from a workflow run is verified the same way from a checkout of the commit it claims to qualify: run the commands inside the evidence directory, with SHA256SUMS and . as the paths and without --bundle.

Option Establishes --repo The attestation was signed by a run of this repository --signer-workflow The Native Qualification workflow signed it, not another workflow with attestation permission --source-ref The run built the main branch, not a pull request, tag, or other branch --source-digest The run built exactly the commit being verified

Without the last three options the command accepts an attestation of the same file from any workflow and branch of the repository. The attestation shows where and from which commit the checksums came, not that qualification passed. sha256sum shows the files are the ones recorded. qualification_evidence.py rechecks the digests, compares the recorded cases with junit.xml, re-evaluates every pass condition against the expected set of the checkout it runs from, and requires the stated commit; it prints each reason and exits non-zero otherwise.

A manifest binds a result to one commit, one set of image contents, and one host; it does not transfer to another commit, architecture, or rebuilt image. Unattested evidence shows internal consistency, not origin.

items.title: Research Evaluation Evidence
items.text:
Research evaluations measure connectivity, tool compatibility, workflow completion, artifact completeness, coding and statistical correctness, policy adherence, and recovery separately; a successful tool call does not establish task quality. Records bind suite and fixture identity, model revision, provider, runtime, hardware, context, parser, Skill digest, harness revision, trial date, independent checks, and measured usage, and have no fields for prompts, tool output, credentials, or participant data. Unavailable token counts and cost stay unknown rather than zero.

The gateway separately observes the request model, OpenHands version, context limits, confirmation policy, platform adapter, and fingerprints of model options and security configuration, and the driver checks this observation before model work, before reviewed continuations, and at finalization. A changed runtime leaves the trial incomplete, and injected, deterministic, or unconfigured backends cannot qualify a model. Remote weights, precision, hardware, and server software remain declared metadata.

The assessor requires the latest three real-model trials of every case to pass within 30 days by default; changed configurations or suites, unknown revisions, expired evidence, missing checks, and recent failures do not inherit earlier passes. Three trials are a functional regression gate, not a statistical estimate of scientific reliability, and an assessment never changes model recommendations or review policy by itself. A trial reserves its record in the bound state's evaluations/ directory before model work, so an interrupted evaluator leaves an incomplete trial rather than a missing one; completed records cannot be overwritten.

Budgets for time, actions, model calls, tokens, and reported cost are checked between gateway updates and after review, not inside an uninterrupted agent run. Use provider-side spending limits for hosted evaluations, and run generated code only in an isolated synthetic environment.

items.title: Synthetic Research Cases
items.text: The maintained fixtures cover dataset readiness, a held-out linear baseline, and independent result verification over pinned synthetic inputs. Checks inspect structured outputs, not the agent's completion message; a parseable script with correct reported metrics does not show that it ran. Reproduction requires a separately approved terminal execution into a previously absent directory, binds the program, inputs, and outputs before approval and after execution, and cannot be satisfied by copied outputs or repaired later. These observations are not a sandbox and do not detect a process that changes and restores files between them; small fixtures test software behavior, not scientific generalizability.

items.title: Parallel Review Comparison
items.text: assess_parallel_reviews compares matched sequential and parallel trials that differ only in requested specialist concurrency. The default policy requires three recent trials per case, at least a 10% reduction in median and total elapsed time, and no more than a 25% increase in cost or tokens; unknown usage or failed trials prevent qualification. Task intervals with the same process-local clock establish overlap, not simultaneous provider requests or useful findings. ReservedReviewTrial admits explicitly experimental runs labelled Experimental parallel review under the same consent and approval rules; admission never produces a passing result. Qualify Parallel Reviews describes preparation and trust boundaries.

items.title: Action-Review Evaluation
items.text:
The action-review corpus contains benign, ambiguous, destructive, encoded, injected, network-capable, path-escaping, and boundary-crossing proposals for the terminal, file editor, Task Tracker, and Task tool. Evaluation builds typed OpenHands actions, classifies them with the session code, and applies the production rules for one review mode and execution boundary without executing anything. Each case states whether it must reach the researcher outside a sandbox and inside an admitted one, and appears once with a low and once with an unknown model rating; both must receive the same decision.

Reports keep case identities, corpus and analyzer digests, SDK version, date, mode, boundary, decisions, rules, and latency, without commands or file contents. A deployment assessment requires complete matching evidence, no false approvals, no decision that depends on the model rating, and confirmation of unknown classifications. Every mode a deployment lists in allowed_action_review_modes must pass the zero-false-approval gate for the pinned SDK. Under review-changes, read-only shell commands still wait and count as unnecessary confirmations, a usability measure. Under review-outside-effects, an opaque script is correctly automatic only because the session is contained; the containment itself needs native qualification evidence. Passing a synthetic corpus is necessary evidence for a policy decision, not proof that arbitrary actions are safe.

items.title: Synthetic Data Rule
items.text: Source control, public examples, CI, screenshots, and replay fixtures use synthetic data only. Protected health information must never enter a test fixture, public log, screenshot, pull request, or model-evaluation artifact.

items.title: Contribute to Heartwood
items.text: Heartwood accepts contributions to its gateway, managed worker, interfaces, platform integrations, research Skills, tests, and documentation. A change extends the shared project, gateway, OpenHands, interface, platform, and evidence contracts instead of adding a parallel workflow.

items.title: Before You Start
items.text: Read the repository contribution guide, code of conduct, and AGENTS.md. Check GitHub Issues and the Heartwood Project for scoped work and acceptance criteria.

items.title: Contribution Areas
items.text:
• project, session, policy, action review, audit, and schema contracts;
  • the OpenHands adapter, the managed worker, and its OpenShell deployment adapter;
  • terminal, browser, and notebook interfaces;
  • Heartwood-managed and hosted model connections;
  • platform adapters, images, and the platform contract;
  • curated research Skills;
  • deterministic, capable-model, container, native worker, and platform qualification; and
  • documentation.

Use synthetic data in every public example, test, screenshot, and issue reproduction.

• Development Guide
  • Contribute Research Skills

  • Release Guide

items.title: Development Guide
items.text: Heartwood is a Python workspace with a TypeScript researcher web interface built on Grove, container and native packaging, and repository-level compliance and release tests.

items.title: Set Up the Repository
items.text:
The bootstrap requires uv 0.13.7 exactly. If another uv is installed, select the pinned one for these commands:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/SchmiedmayerLab/heartwood.git
cd heartwood
UV=$(uvx --from uv==0.13.7 which uv)
$UV run --no-project --python 3.12.15 deploy/build-worker-candidate.py --bootstrap --uv "$UV"
$UV sync --locked --all-groups --all-extras
npm ci --prefix packages/webui

--recurse-submodules checks out the curated Skill source in vendor/heartwood-skills; in an existing clone run git submodule update --init. The bootstrap builds the maintained OpenHands and OpenShell wheels into vendor/runtime-wheels/, which the workspace lock resolves from, after verifying upstream source and patch hashes, preserved licenses, wheel digests, and the build record. A later bootstrap only verifies the existing wheels. If verification fails, keep the files for inspection and start from a clean checkout; never bypass hashes or override constraints. --all-groups adds the dev, docs, and worker dependency groups. Installing Heartwood packages from a package registry without these wheels is not supported; the native release archive and container images build them through the same bootstrap.

Resolution ignores releases younger than seven days through uv's exclude-newer, npm's min-release-age, and the Dependabot cooldown; security updates are not delayed. Base images are pinned by digest, and third-party GitHub Actions use exact versions from immutable releases.

items.title: Reuse Before Variants
items.text:
The session gateway owns setup choices, researcher-facing model metadata, readiness, action settings, and session behavior. The terminal, browser, and notebook packages adapt those shared projections to their interface; they must not maintain parallel business rules or persisted settings. The browser consumes Grove's design-system components and shared TypeScript configuration rather than maintaining project-local equivalents.

Generic and platform-derived artifacts use images/Dockerfile and docker-bake.hcl as one assembly path. Native and container GPU variants use images/gpu/install_runtime.sh for the same pinned vLLM environment. Add a parameter, platform adapter, or validation target for a real platform difference instead of copying installation or packaging steps.

items.title: Worker Image
items.text:
docker buildx bake worker builds the managed worker image, the OpenHands agent server from the worker dependency group, through the same image stages and workspace lock; the application image does not contain it. python images/worker/smoke.py IMAGE checks a locally loaded worker image in a disposable container with no network or host mounts: native command execution, authentication, private workspace persistence, read-only configuration, and removal of synthetic inherited secrets. Local launches run OpenHands in the gateway process; only a deployment manifest's [worker] table launches this image, through OpenShell.

The entry point, images/worker/launch.py, requires a fresh URL-safe SESSION_API_KEY of at least 43 characters and accepts only an optional HEARTWOOD_INFERENCE_PLACEHOLDER and OpenShell's supervisor trust files under /run/openshell-supervisor-ca/material/ from the launching environment. Every other environment value is fixed in the image, inherited descriptors beyond standard streams are closed, and the server binds to sandbox loopback with one concurrent conversation run. These measures do not create isolation: the image must be started inside a qualified sandbox with no inherited host environment, scoped volumes, a non-root identity, resource limits, and outside network enforcement. Security and Controlled Data describes the worker boundary and what it does not establish.

items.title: Installed Gateway Resources
items.text: The gateway wheel includes the canonical model catalogs and manifests, reviewed specialist definitions and pinned bundled Skills through package build mappings. The installed gateway loads these resources from its own package directory. Editable source installations use the same repository resources; an installed package with missing resources fails instead of searching the research project or unrelated ancestor directories. The CLI wheel also includes synthetic fixture data; the shared image assembly supplies its compiled browser assets. A standalone CLI wheel without those browser assets requires an explicit web-root selection. The candidate workflow tests the installed wheels with isolated Python imports, including CLI and subprocess behavior.

items.title: Package Ownership
items.text: Area Package or Directory Typed schemas and session commands/events packages/schemas, packages/session Platform and data adapters packages/adapters Policy and audit packages/model-policy, packages/audit Durable files and persisted-schema migrations packages/persistence OpenHands and core session orchestration packages/core-adapter, packages/gateway Terminal interface and runtime launch packages/cli Notebook bridge packages/notebook Browser interface packages/webui Skill acquisition and project activation packages/skills, packages/gateway Pinned curated Skill source and shared catalog tooling vendor/heartwood-skills from SchmiedmayerLab/heartwood-skills Synthetic fixtures fixtures/synthetic, evals Images, native packaging, and release logic images, deploy, .github/workflows Public documentation documentation

items.title: Run Checks
items.text:
uv run ruff format --check .
uv run ruff check .
uv run vulture
uv run mypy packages
uv run heartwood-fixtures fixtures evals
uv run pytest
npm run --prefix packages/webui lint
npm run --prefix packages/webui duplicates:check
npm run --prefix packages/webui contracts:check
npm run --prefix packages/webui typecheck
npm test --prefix packages/webui
npm run --prefix packages/webui build
uv run --group docs zensical build --clean --strict

Run focused tests while iterating, then run the complete affected suites before review. Container, capable-model, and native worker checks need more resources and run through their workflows; see Testing and Evidence.

The curated Skill source must be initialized at the exact Git revision recorded by the superproject. CI rejects missing, modified, or substituted submodule content. Changes to curated Skill packages and catalog tooling are reviewed in heartwood-skills; Heartwood changes then advance the pinned revision, update BUNDLED_SKILL_DIGESTS in the gateway's Skill settings, and update interface, storage, and release tests together. After advancing the revision, run uv run pytest packages/gateway/tests/test_skill_settings.py -k pin_matches; its failure shows the complete-tree digests to copy into BUNDLED_SKILL_DIGESTS. The Python workflow runs the same test with the submodule checked out, so a stale pin fails continuous integration.

items.title: Qualify a Terra Image Before Merge
items.text:
Ordinary pull-request validation builds the GPU targets without exporting an image. When a change requires live Terra qualification, push the reviewed commit and manually run Terra GPU Qualification Candidate for that branch.

The workflow publishes one commit-bound candidate-sha-…-terra-gpu-nvidia tag, verifies its Docker media type and embedded revision, and runs the shared Terra image smoke tests. Use the tag reported in the workflow summary when recreating the Terra environment. The candidate does not move release or edge tags.

items.title: CI Runners and Runtime Locks
items.text:
Pull-request and main validation run on standard GitHub-hosted runners (ubuntu-24.04, ubuntu-24.04-arm for ARM images, and ubuntu-latest for some checks), with two exceptions. Capable-model acceptance runs on the organization's heartwood-ubuntu-large hosted runner, because llama.cpp prompt processing on a standard runner misses the qualification deadline; the job requires at least 30 GiB of memory and matches llama.cpp threads to the runner's cores. That runner group is limited to this repository and fork pull requests need approval before their workflows run; keep its label out of every other workflow. GPU coding-agent qualification is a manually started workflow on a self-hosted GPU runner. GPU image builds start with the reclaim-runner-disk action, which removes unused preinstalled toolchains.

Hosted jobs differ from a local checkout in two ways that matter when a result differs. The Python job installs with uv sync --locked --all-extras (default groups only) after the same bootstrap, and installed-wheel and native qualification jobs set OPENHANDS_SUPPRESS_BANNER=1 and LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True so no model cost map is fetched from the network. Native worker qualification needs Docker and builds the qualification-only sandbox gateway; it runs for every main commit and for pull requests that change anything outside documentation/ and .github/, or its own or the pull-request validation workflow.

Regenerate the isolated GPU dependency lock with bash images/gpu/compile_requirements.sh. This is the same command CI uses to verify the lock, including its release-date cutoff and hashes. Update the security floors in images/gpu/vllm.in and the cutoff in that script when refreshing dependencies; do not edit generated hashes by hand.

items.title: Static Analysis
items.text:
Python packages use strict mypy checking with the Pydantic plugin, and each published namespace subpackage includes a PEP 561 py.typed marker. Public REST requests use strict Pydantic models, while gateway responses use exact typed mappings that are validated before they cross an interface boundary.

The browser API types are generated from those Python contracts. After changing a shared request or response, run:

npm run --prefix packages/webui contracts:generate

CI fails if the generated file is stale. Browser-only presentation models remain in TypeScript and must not duplicate gateway payload definitions.

Ruff identifies unused imports, variables, arguments, and commented-out code. CI also runs Vulture at 100 percent confidence to detect unreachable or unused definitions beyond Ruff's local checks. Lower-confidence Vulture findings remain a review aid because framework callbacks and implicit fixtures can appear unused:

uv run vulture packages --min-confidence 80

The production duplication check uses a conservative threshold to detect growth without forcing unrelated platform adapters or interface forwarding into artificial abstractions. Review every reported clone and extract it only when the behavior has one clear owner.

items.title: Change a Shared Contract
items.text:
When changing project state, startup, models, actions, sessions, Skills, or audit behavior:

  1. update the owning typed contract;
  2. update gateway behavior;
  3. update terminal, browser, and notebook projections;
  4. update platform behavior where capabilities differ;
  5. add regression and integration coverage;
  6. update current documentation and reference pages; and
  7. remove the superseded pre-1.0 path instead of maintaining an undocumented compatibility layer.

Tests for a shared contract should compare the gateway, REST, terminal, browser, and notebook projections that expose it. Persisted-format changes require checked-in compatibility fixtures that pass both the shared migration registry and the owning domain loader. Durability changes require interruption tests at every write boundary, process-level concurrency tests, and explicit recovery and corruption cases. Artifact tests should verify that all variants resolve through the canonical assembly path as well as testing each supported runtime environment.

Keep planned work and acceptance criteria in GitHub Issues rather than public documentation.

items.title: Documentation Guide
items.text: The canonical published source is documentation/. Zensical builds that tree directly; there is no copied staging tree or duplicate docs and design source hierarchy.

items.title: Content Types
items.text:
• Get Started teaches one complete first success.
  • Work With Heartwood, Models, and Platforms solve researcher tasks.
  • Operate Heartwood supports deployment and security reviewers.
  • Architecture explains durable architecture and rationale.
  • Reference provides complete, exact, scannable facts.
  • Contribute documents repository work and releases.

Do not mix implementation progress, validation transcripts, future features, or issue discussions into user documentation. Track planned work in GitHub Issues and keep run-specific evidence in CI artifacts or pull requests.

The Platform Contract also defines draft integration messages for platform partners. Identify their schema maturity and runtime availability explicitly, including in generated artifact descriptions. Describe unavailable capabilities as limitations; keep delivery plans, issue status and implementation history outside the contract.

items.title: Writing Style
items.text:
• begin with the user's outcome and prerequisites;
  • explain a path before asking the reader to type it;
  • use semantic line breaks with one complete sentence per source line;
  • use numbered steps for ordered work and tables only for genuine comparison;
  • place warnings before risky data, cost, credential, or destructive operations;
  • include an expected result and recovery route for important commands;
  • define specialized terms in the glossary;
  • use current product vocabulary consistently; and
  • make conservative, evidence-backed capability and security claims.

Avoid conversational drafting notes, release-relative narration, unexplained acronyms, guessed URLs, placeholder screenshots, and commands that depend on files the guide did not create.

items.title: Link to Published Documentation
items.text:
Repository entry points such as README.md link user guidance to the stable documentation root at https://schmiedmayerlab.github.io/heartwood/. They may also offer https://schmiedmayerlab.github.io/heartwood/preview/ as an explicitly labeled prerelease option, but should not describe preview content as an unreleased future version. Release notes and support records may link an immutable /<version>/ documentation path when exact historical behavior matters. Do not add a deployed deep link until that route exists in the referenced release channel; use the channel root while a new information architecture is awaiting publication.

Links between pages inside documentation/ remain relative so Zensical and Mike preserve the active stable, preview, or immutable version prefix.

items.title: Screenshots
items.text:
Screenshots must use synthetic data, a current release interface, a desktop viewport of at least 1280 × 800, readable text, and no credentials or personal identifiers. Generate the canonical browser images through the deterministic web smoke script:

npm run --prefix packages/webui screenshots:docs

Commit the image and its .license sidecar. Use screenshots only when they clarify a visual workflow that prose and accessible labels cannot convey as efficiently.

items.title: Validate the Site
items.text:
uv run --group docs zensical build --clean --strict

Strict mode checks links, anchors, references, and footnotes. Link to headings without em dashes or other punctuation so anchors are identical on GitHub and in the built site, and keep the troubleshooting headings that diagnostic_catalog() links to. Documentation contract tests also validate navigation, commands, release references, diagnostic routes, screenshot dimensions, and the absence of planning artifacts.

items.title: Release Guide
items.text: A release is created by the Create Release workflow from the exact current main commit after that commit's required checks pass. Versions use strict Semantic Versioning without a v prefix, such as 0.5.0 or 0.5.0-beta.1.

items.title: Prepare a Release
items.text:
1. Update VERSION.toml and every version-owned package, lock, image, installer, and documentation reference together; deploy/verify_release_candidate.py lists any that differ.
  2. Run the complete test and documentation suites.
  3. Merge the reviewed change to main and wait for Main Validation to pass on that commit.
  4. Start Create Release from main with the exact version.
  5. Review the draft release: generated notes, assets, checksums, qualification evidence, and target commit.
  6. Approve the release environment to publish.

items.title: Release Workflow Checks
items.text:
The workflow stops unless all of the following hold for the commit:

  • the version is valid, matches every version-owned source, and has no published release or tag;
  • the commit is still the tip of main, checked again before the draft and before publication;
  • every catalog model source verifies, and the curated Skill revision is published on heartwood-skills main;
  • the Release Candidate Ready, Analyze (python), and Analyze (javascript-typescript) checks passed;
  • the Native Qualification workflow passed for the commit and its evidence verifies against the commit and its attestation;
  • immutable container candidates exist for the commit.

Release Candidate Ready requires every Main Validation job, including capable-model acceptance. On main, the separate Native Qualification workflow qualifies and attests every commit without cancelling earlier runs; see Native Qualification Evidence. Release creation downloads that run's evidence and attestation, verifies them with gh attestation verify bound to this repository, the Native Qualification workflow, refs/heads/main, and the commit, and with deploy/qualification_evidence.py, and fails when either is missing or does not verify. Pull-request runs are not attested.

The workflow then builds the native assets from the commit, tests the installer layout and an installation from an empty Ubuntu container, attests every asset, and creates a draft release with GitHub-generated notes. After approval it publishes the immutable image tags and the release, then the versioned documentation.

items.title: Authority
items.text: CODEOWNERS identifies the current release maintainer. The protected release environment is the release-authority boundary: it accepts deployments only from protected branches and requires the maintainer's approval. The Semantic Version Releases tag ruleset forbids updating, deleting, or force-moving any tag; organization administrators can bypass it. Administrators may recover an interrupted workflow, which replaces an unpublished draft for the same commit, but must never replace or retarget a published release.

items.title: Release Contents
items.text:
Item Contents heartwood-installer Native installer script heartwood-native.tar.gz Application source, curated Skills, maintained runtime wheels, and browser assets vLLM wheel The CUDA 12.9 wheel pinned in images/gpu/compatibility.toml, for restricted environments such as Carina SHA256SUMS Checksums of the native archive and the vLLM wheel Qualification evidence native-qualification-evidence.tar.gz, the commit's native qualification evidence with its SHA256SUMS, and native-qualification-evidence.sigstore.jsonl, its attestation bundle, verified as described in Native Qualification Evidence Image tags VERSION, VERSION-gpu-nvidia, VERSION-terra, and VERSION-terra-gpu-nvidia, promoted from the commit's candidate images Documentation The VERSION path of the versioned site

Every release asset carries a build provenance attestation. Releases contain no worker image, sandbox gateway, model weights, or credentials. The platform contract bundle is not a release asset; partners export it from the release commit as described in Platform Contract. A prerelease is marked as a GitHub prerelease and never becomes latest.

items.title: Stable and Preview Documentation
items.text:
A stable version such as 0.5.0 moves the stable alias and the documentation root to it. A prerelease such as 0.5.0-beta.1 moves the preview alias without changing the root. Documentation is published only for the latest release of its channel, and republishing a version with different content is rejected.

See Support and Compatibility for the maintained release line and pre-1.0 change policy.

items.title: Contribute Research Skills
items.text:
Heartwood Skills are complete Agent Skills packages loaded through the public OpenHands Skill interface. The heartwood-skills repository owns curated Skill content, synthetic qualification, deterministic packaging, and catalog candidates. Heartwood owns installation, project policy, OpenHands activation, interfaces, and audit records.

Use the Skill repository for a reusable research workflow. Use the main Heartwood repository for changes to the runtime, model providers, action policy, project state, interfaces, or deployment behavior.

items.title: Choose the Source Path
items.text:
Source Use it when Review and trust boundary Curated Heartwood repository The workflow should be maintained and shipped with Heartwood The complete package is committed under skills/<skill-name>/, reviewed through a protected pull request, and bundled from a pinned repository revision; catalog publication is separate and signed External signed catalog Another project or deployment owns the workflow The source operator publishes complete immutable Agent Skill archives through a compatible TUF repository configured by the deployment Project-local package A maintainer needs to evaluate or use a project-specific workflow The complete directory remains local to the project and is always labeled Local and unreviewed

An existing Skill does not need to be copied into heartwood-skills if its owner can provide a compatible signed catalog. To propose it for the curated repository, include the complete package and preserve its license and attribution. Heartwood does not accept a mutable repository, marketplace, branch, or archive link as a catalog entry because review and installation must cover one exact package tree.

items.title: Propose a Bounded Workflow
items.text:
Open a Skill proposal before implementing a substantial workflow. Define:

  • the recurring research task and intended user;
  • expected inputs, outputs, and stop conditions;
  • decisions that remain with the researcher;
  • required tools, network access, dataset types, and platforms;
  • scripts, references, assets, and external dependencies; and
  • a synthetic validation plan with relevant boundary cases.

Do not include credentials, participant-level data, model weights, private platform evidence, or generated research results in an issue, fixture, test, or log.

items.title: Build the Complete Package
items.text:
Each curated Skill has one directory directly under skills/:

skills/example-skill/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
├── references/
└── assets/

The directory layout does not encode review or publication state. A pull request proposes content, a protected merge establishes the curated source revision, and signed publication makes an immutable candidate available to configured deployments.

Only SKILL.md is required by the Agent Skills format. Add supporting directories only when the workflow needs them:

  • scripts/ contains executable, deterministic workflow helpers;
  • references/ contains material the agent may load while applying the Skill; and
  • assets/ contains schemas, templates, or other static resources used by the workflow.

Keep instructions concise and place detailed executable or reference material in the appropriate package resource. Do not duplicate standard Agent Skills metadata in another authored file.

items.title: Declare Heartwood Policy
items.text:
Curated Skills add Heartwood policy fields under the standard metadata map in SKILL.md:

Field Meaning heartwood.id Stable, globally unique Skill identity heartwood.version Semantic version of the Skill content contract heartwood.dataset-types Comma-separated dataset types the Skill understands heartwood.platforms Comma-separated supported Heartwood platforms heartwood.phi-risk Declared protected-health-information interaction class heartwood.requires-network Whether the Skill requires network access heartwood.controlled-data Repository status; curated content remains not-approved heartwood.approval-summary Compact description shown before project installation heartwood.entrypoint Optional package-relative executable entrypoint

Declare the narrowest accurate permissions. Repository review cannot approve a Skill for controlled data, grant a tool, or broaden model and network policy.

Heartwood rejects automatic dynamic shell context and embedded Model Context Protocol servers in curated Skills because no corresponding deployment policy is defined. Propose the policy and runtime contract in Heartwood before relying on either feature.

items.title: Test the Workflow
items.text:
Set up the Skill repository with Python 3.12 and uv:

git clone https://github.com/SchmiedmayerLab/heartwood-skills.git
cd heartwood-skills
uv sync --locked

Run the complete local validation:

uv run ruff format --check .
uv run ruff check .
uv run mypy src tests
uv run vulture
uv run heartwood-skill-catalog validate
uv run heartwood-skill-catalog build
uv run pytest

Run validation and focused tests while editing. The catalog build deliberately rejects modified or untracked content because its output must identify one immutable Git revision, so commit the complete change locally before running that command.

Tests for a script should cover the expected result, malformed input, boundary enforcement, and any aggregate-output or suppression decision. Catalog validation loads every complete tree through OpenHands in strict mode, rejects undeclared or unsafe content, and verifies deterministic archives.

items.title: Submit the Change
items.text:
Use the repository-specific pull-request template. Link the approved proposal, explain researcher-visible behavior, and report synthetic verification. Review covers the complete package tree, including scripts, references, assets, permissions, and dependency changes.

A merged Skill is repository-reviewed but not automatically published to a deployment or approved for controlled data. See Skill Trust and Distribution for the separate candidate, signing, publication, and revocation process.

items.title: Visual Identity
items.text:
Heartwood's mark is a cross-section of a tree trunk: growth rings around a solid core. Heartwood is the dense center of a trunk that gives the tree its strength, and the mark stands for a stable, verifiable core that every interface shares.

One generator produces every variant from the same geometry and color tokens, so the documentation, browser interface, terminal, and repository show the same identity.

items.title: Variants
items.text: Variant Source Use Full-color mark documentation/assets/brand/heartwood-mark.svg Documentation logo, repository assets, and sizes of 64 pixels and larger Compact mark documentation/assets/brand/heartwood-favicon.svg Favicons and sizes below 64 pixels, with fewer, heavier rings Monochrome mark documentation/assets/brand/heartwood-mark-monochrome.svg Single-color contexts; it takes the surrounding text color README hero documentation/assets/brand/heartwood-hero-light.svg and heartwood-hero-dark.svg The top of the repository README in the reader's appearance Browser mark packages/webui/src/brandMark.generated.ts The session rail in the browser interface, drawn inline in the current text color Terminal mark ◉ Heartwood Terminal startup; terminals that cannot show the glyph print Heartwood

items.title: Colors
items.text:
Token Light Dark Use Primary #0b694d #4cc792 Primary actions, links, and the mark's tile Mark core #7ad8b0 #7ad8b0 The heartwood at the center of the mark Surface #f7f7f8 #0a0a0a Page and conversation background Foreground #1d1d1f #f5f5f7 Body text Muted foreground #66666b #98989d Secondary text and labels

Surfaces are neutral; green marks the primary action and the brand, not the background. Caution states use orange, and errors use red. Documentation figures use green for what Heartwood owns, blue for what a platform owns, and dashed outlines for unavailable Heartwood integrations. The browser interface sets these values on the Grove design system's color variables, and the documentation sets them on the Zensical palette, so neither introduces another component library.

items.title: Use the Mark
items.text:
• Keep clear space of at least one quarter of the mark's width around it.
  • Use the compact mark below 64 pixels and never render the full mark below 32 pixels.
  • Do not recolor, rotate, outline, or add effects to the mark, and do not redraw its rings.
  • Do not combine the mark with institutional or funder marks in one lockup; place them separately.

items.title: Accessibility
items.text:
• Every text pairing in the color table meets WCAG AA contrast of at least 4.5:1 on its surface; the mark's core and innermost rings meet 3:1 non-text contrast against its tile, and the outer rings fade below it as texture.
  • The mark is decorative next to the product name and hidden from assistive technology there; on its own it carries the text alternative "Heartwood".
  • The documentation and browser marks are static.
  • The terminal animates its progress glyphs only on an interactive terminal with color enabled, and falls back to static ASCII dots when NO_COLOR is set, output is redirected, or the terminal cannot show the glyphs.

items.title: Source and Regeneration
items.text:
The color tokens and terminal mark live in packages/cli/src/heartwood/cli/_brand.py. The mark geometry and every generated file come from packages/cli/scripts/generate_brand_assets.py:

uv run python packages/cli/scripts/generate_brand_assets.py

Run it after changing a token or the geometry, and commit the regenerated files. The test suite runs the generator in --check mode and fails when a committed asset differs from its source.

The mark and its generated variants are original project work, distributed under the project's MIT license like the rest of the repository.

items.title: Choose a Model Route
items.text: The model reasons about the project; OpenHands runs the agent loop and tools around it. The model route decides where project content is sent, which credential is needed, and whether Heartwood starts and supervises inference itself.

items.title: Compare the Choices
items.text:
Choice in Setup Use When You Provide Stanford AI API Gateway You have access to Stanford's institution-managed gateway A gateway key, then a model the gateway returns Sign in with ChatGPT The deployment permits the ChatGPT service and you have a Plus or Pro subscription Account sign-in, then a model OpenHands supports OpenAI API The deployment permits the OpenAI API An API key, then a model the API returns Anthropic The deployment permits the Anthropic API An API key, then a model the API returns Other compatible service An authorized service implements the OpenAI API format The service URL, a model and an optional token Run with Heartwood Inference should stay on the compute where Heartwood runs A recommended model or a Hugging Face model identifier

Setup lists only the routes that the detected platform permits. Workstations, containers and Terra offer all six; Carina offers Stanford AI API Gateway and Run with Heartwood. Selecting Other compatible service records the exact service endpoints in the project policy; it does not establish that the service may receive the intended data.

items.title: Start With the Simplest Authorized Route
items.text:
Use the Stanford AI API Gateway when you have an eligible key and the route is approved for the project. For non-sensitive evaluation, Sign in with ChatGPT is the shortest account-based route. A permitted hosted connection avoids model downloads and hardware planning, so it is usually the fastest first run.

Choose a Heartwood-managed model when inference must stay in the Heartwood environment, suitable hardware is available, or you need an offline workflow.

items.title: Configure the Selection
items.text:
Run heartwood and follow setup, or open Settings → Models in the browser. Both write the same non-secret selection to the project configuration. Inspect it without exposing credentials:

heartwood models list
heartwood doctor

The model route also limits the review modes: with an API key, subscription or mounted secret in a local launch, every action set waits for you; a credential-free route such as a Heartwood-managed model allows Review Changes.

items.title: Models in an Operator-Bound Deployment
items.text: In an operator-bound deployment, the manifest's policy sets which model endpoints are allowed. An isolated worker uses the model, provider and HTTPS endpoint fixed in the manifest's [worker] section, and receives an OpenShell placeholder rather than the provider credential. Heartwood-managed models serve local launches only; they are not available to an isolated worker. See Managed Worker for the manifest keys.

items.title: Data and Compliance Boundary
items.text:
A route shown in setup is implemented and permitted by the active Heartwood policy. That does not establish that the provider, account, agreement or deployment may receive a particular dataset.

Route Destination of Project Content Retention Governed By Run with Heartwood The inference server on the same compute The deployment Stanford AI API Gateway Stanford's gateway and its model providers Stanford's agreements for the gateway OpenAI API or Anthropic The provider's API The provider's API terms and the account's data controls Sign in with ChatGPT OpenAI through the subscription account The subscription's terms Other compatible service The configured service The service operator

Session history is kept in Heartwood's project state as well; see Projects and Private State. Confirm institutional approval and data-use terms before sending controlled content to any route.

items.title: Choose a Heartwood-Managed Model
items.text:
A Heartwood-managed model keeps inference on the compute where Heartwood runs. Model files are downloaded separately into the project's .heartwood/models/; images and installers contain no weights. Heartwood-managed models serve local launches; an isolated worker uses the model endpoint its operator configures.

Start the guided selection in either interface:

  • run heartwood and choose Run with Heartwood; or
  • open Settings → Models in the browser.

Both read the same catalog and project state, and show the download size, resource guidance, license and immutable source revision before asking for confirmation.

items.title: Capability Tiers
items.text:
The tier describes the intended agent workload, not scientific quality.

Tier Intended Use Standard Bounded edits, focused analysis scripts and first-time use Powerful Larger repositories, multi-step coding tasks and longer sessions Maximum capability Broad multi-file work on substantial multi-GPU compute

The guided selector recommends only configurations that fit the detected environment and have completed Heartwood's coding-agent qualification on that platform. Other catalog entries are labelled Not tested in the terminal and listed under Models not qualified for this platform in the browser; they can be selected explicitly for evaluation but are never recommended.

List the complete catalog for the current environment:

heartwood models managed

Precision, tool parser, context, tensor parallelism and pinned revision are shown in the detailed model view and in the GPU compatibility matrix.

items.title: Resource Guide
items.text:
Tier Model Configuration Qualified On Download GPU Memory Recommended RAM Recommended Free Disk Default Context Estimated Runtime Startup Standard Qwen2.5 7B Instruct Q4_K_M, CPU Generic platform (containers) 4.36 GiB None 32 GB 50 GB 32,768 Hardware dependent Powerful Qwen3 Coder 30B W4A16 AWQ Terra, 2 x T4 16.81 GiB 2 x 16 GB 120 GB 50 GB 18,432 2-15 minutes Maximum capability Muse Glimmer 30B BF16 Carina, 2 x L40S 55.49 GiB 2 x 48 GB 128 GB 96 GB 32,768 5-20 minutes

These values are planning estimates; the selection screen reports the exact values from the release catalog before making changes. Startup time is measured once the model is in the project cache, and later starts reuse the verified snapshot. A first download depends on network conditions and Hugging Face rate limits.

Weights are only part of the memory requirement: the runtime also needs room for temporary downloads, the key/value cache and request handling. Heartwood keeps conservative headroom and can choose a smaller context than the model's advertised maximum. A qualification covers its exact platform and GPU count; for example, one-T4 and four-T4 Terra results do not qualify the two-T4 configuration or each other.

items.title: Other Hugging Face Models
items.text:
Choose Other Hugging Face model in the terminal or Other model in the browser, or use the command line:

heartwood models inspect unsloth/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-GGUF
heartwood models download unsloth/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-GGUF

Heartwood queries Hugging Face, resolves the requested tag or branch to an immutable commit, and selects a supported artifact: a single-file GGUF for the llama.cpp CPU runtime or a standard safetensors snapshot for the NVIDIA vLLM runtime. No download begins until you approve the displayed plan. Downloading a GPU model needs the vLLM runtime and enough project storage, but no active GPU allocation; GPU count and memory are checked when the runtime starts.

To request a particular tag, branch or commit, pass --revision REVISION in the terminal or expand Version options in the browser.

Large public snapshots can hit Hugging Face's anonymous download limits. When an approved Hugging Face token is available, expose HF_TOKEN only to the download process, never in project configuration. If a transfer stops, rerun the same command from the project directory; Heartwood keeps completed files in a private partial snapshot for the same immutable revision and publishes the model into .heartwood/models/ only after full verification.

The planner stops with a message that Heartwood does not yet support the repository when a repository requires executable remote code, has an unsupported weight layout or architecture, lacks a resolvable revision, or cannot fit the available runtime. Report a compatible-looking rejection through the Heartwood issue form instead of bypassing the check.

items.title: Download Approval
items.text:
Check these items in the displayed plan:

  • tool use: a coding agent needs reliable structured tool calls, not only code completion;
  • license and provenance: confirm the license and keep the repository and immutable revision;
  • compute: GPU count, GPU memory, RAM, disk and expected allocation cost;
  • context: larger windows use substantially more memory and can increase latency; and
  • data policy: running in the same environment does not approve the model or platform for controlled data.

Parameter count alone does not predict agent quality or resource use.

items.title: Import Existing Model Files
items.text:
Use a Heartwood model bundle when another Heartwood project prepared the model for an offline destination; it carries the file list, runtime settings and digests. Use a raw import only for reviewed model files without a bundle:

heartwood models import /approved/path/model.gguf \
  --source owner/model \
  --revision 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567 \
  --license apache-2.0

Heartwood accepts a valid GGUF file or a standard vLLM safetensors directory, rejects symbolic links and executable Python, records provenance, and copies the artifact atomically into .heartwood/models/. The path must be visible to the Heartwood process; the browser uses the same server-side import and does not upload model files through the page. The destination needs free space for a complete copy plus a 512 MiB reserve, and a directory import creates and verifies a SHA-256 manifest before the model can be selected. Keep the command or browser page open while Heartwood reports that a large import is still running.

items.title: Hosted and Managed Models
items.text: Heartwood asks each model service for its available models instead of keeping its own list of provider model identifiers. Setup presents the compatible results; a manual identifier is an advanced fallback for compatible services that cannot list models.

items.title: Sign In With ChatGPT
items.text:
Sign in with ChatGPT uses supported Codex models through a ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription. It is separate from the OpenAI API and uses no API key or API credits.

  1. Run heartwood, or open browser settings where the browser interface is available.
  2. Choose Sign in with ChatGPT.
  3. Review OpenAI's terms and continue.
  4. Open the displayed sign-in page and enter the one-time code.
  5. Choose a model from the list maintained by the pinned OpenHands SDK.

OpenHands owns the sign-in flow, the supported-model list, credential storage, token refresh and the Codex Responses API transport. Heartwood stores only non-secret connection and model metadata in the project. The route is available on workstations, in containers and on Terra. A successful sign-in does not authorize controlled data; OpenAI's terms and the research environment's rules remain authoritative.

Sign out from browser settings or with:

heartwood models forget openai-subscription

See the OpenHands subscription authentication guide for the upstream behavior.
