  • Published versions are immutable.
  • An added field is not compatible with a consumer that rejects unknown fields.
  • Draft integrations pin the exact bundle version and reassess each change.
  • Document identifiers such as heartwood.platform-estimate.v1 name format families, not independent releases; the bundle version and artifact digest identify a revision.
  • Upstream specifications keep their own versions, such as the date-based MCP Tasks revision.

Each artifact in contract.json carries a maturity of current, draft or upstream.

The shared data-class vocabulary is public, internal, confidential and restricted. The classes are not an ordered permission hierarchy, an allowance for one class on one route does not extend to other classes or purposes, and unknown eligibility stays unknown.

Class Handling meaning public Approved by its owner for public release internal Nonpublic, for ordinary use within an authorized organization or project confidential Sensitive, restricted to authorized recipients and purposes restricted Requires additional legal, contractual, institutional or owner controls

items.title: Contract Artifacts
items.text:
Artifact Defines Maturity contract.json Bundle version, compatibility rules, artifact digests, pinned design sources Index gateway.openapi.json Gateway routes, bodies, streams and the capability security scheme Current capabilities.schema.json The platform capability manifest served at GET /project/capabilities Current policy-profile.schema.json heartwood.policy-profile.v1, the policy in the deployment manifest Current model-connections.schema.json heartwood.model-connections.v1; startup does not load it Current model-metadata.schema.json Model protocol, capability and eligibility declarations Draft data-classification.schema.json The data-class vocabulary Draft mcp-service.schema.json, mcp-tool-annotations.schema.json Deployment service references and required tool annotations Draft mcp-tasks.schema.json MCP Tasks revision 2026-07-28, with mcp-tasks.LICENSE.txt and mcp-tasks.SOURCE.txt Upstream launch-context.schema.json, budget-observation.schema.json Platform project binding and budget observations Draft workload-prediction.schema.json, platform-estimate.schema.json Predictions and platform estimates with coverage, units and validity Draft operation-set.schema.json, researcher-decision.schema.json, platform-authorization.schema.json, operation-observation.schema.json, planning-overview.schema.json Reviewed proposals, decisions, platform authorization and observed operations Draft

The bundle does not export the deployment manifest or the worker profile; Configuration and State specifies them.

items.title: Generate and Review the Current Artifacts
items.text:
From a development checkout of the release commit, export the bundle into a new directory:

uv run python packages/gateway/scripts/export_platform_contract.py /tmp/heartwood-contract

The exporter refuses an existing directory. Review contract.json first: it lists each artifact's path, media type, maturity and SHA-256. Request schemas use validation mode and response schemas use serialization mode, so their fields match the owning parser or serializer. JSON Schema validation alone does not perform the cross-field checks of the owning parsers, such as endpoint normalization and duplicate identities. Distribute the complete directory with the exact source revision or release digest.

items.title: Check Platform Service Responses
items.text:
Capture a response with an independently authenticated platform client, then check it offline:

uv run python packages/adapters/scripts/check_platform_response.py model-catalog models-page.json
uv run python packages/adapters/scripts/check_platform_response.py mcp-tools tools-result.json
uv run python packages/adapters/scripts/check_platform_response.py mcp-tasks fixtures/synthetic/platform-contract/mcp-tasks.json
uv run python packages/adapters/scripts/check_platform_response.py planning-overview.schema.json fixtures/synthetic/platform-contract/batch.overview.json

The first argument is model-catalog, mcp-tools, mcp-tasks or a draft schema filename. The checker never contacts a service. It prints a JSON report with its checks and limitations and exits with status 0, or prints "Response could not be read or failed contract validation." and exits with status 1.

Check Validates Does not validate model-catalog Page structure and unique, nonempty model identifiers Model metadata, eligibility, protocol behavior, other pages mcp-tools Descriptions, unique names, four explicit boolean annotations, object input and output schema syntax Schema references, tool calls, other pages, safety claims mcp-tasks Each exchange in a transcript of server_capabilities and request/response pairs against the pinned Tasks definitions Transition history, input lineage, the complete core protocol Draft schema Structure and the owning parser's cross-field consistency Issuer identity, referenced document bytes, current validity

Annotations and output schemas are optional upstream but required by this profile. An empty catalog or tool list is valid for an identity with nothing available. The same checks are available in Python as validate_model_catalog, validate_mcp_tools_list and validate_platform_message(schema_filename, response) in heartwood.adapters.service_conformance, and validate_mcp_task_exchange(request, response, server_capabilities=..., result_schema="platform-estimate.schema.json") in heartwood.adapters.mcp_tasks_conformance. A passing check never makes a parsed authorized field, tool hint or decision record an authorization token.

items.title: Runtime Conformance
items.text:
Offline checks do not establish runtime controls. An integration must also demonstrate, in a synthetic environment:

  • project settings cannot widen the deployment ceiling;
  • approvals bind the complete reviewed action contents and reject changed arguments or groups;
  • worker tools cannot reach credentials, launch capabilities, canonical state or management authority;
  • inference and platform services remain independent optional capabilities; and
  • outside operations are reauthorized by the destination and uncertain outcomes are reconciled before any retry.

For the isolated worker, deploy/qualify-native-worker.py runs the native qualification and deploy/qualification_evidence.py verifies its evidence; see Native Qualification Evidence. Platform API and Access Requirements lists the positive and rejected controls to return for each capability.

items.title: Validate a Platform
items.text:
Heartwood advertises a platform capability only at the evidence level it has reached, as defined in Testing and Evidence:

  1. Implemented: an adapter reports capabilities, detection and policy, with contract tests.
  2. CI validated: conformance, ingress, credential-boundary, persistence and interface tests pass in a production-derived image.
  3. Live synthetic validated: the published artifact completes a synthetic task on the platform, including approval, file verification, replay and audit export.
  4. Institution approved: separate institutional evidence covers the deployment; it is never inferred from the levels above.

The built-in generic, Terra and Carina adapters are CI validated. Follow Validate Conformance and Validate the Deployment, then confirm the deployment security checklist before a wider rollout.

items.title: Add a Platform
items.text: A platform adapter adapts storage, identity, scheduling, browser routing, model connections and policy to one environment while the project, gateway, OpenHands, session and interface contracts stay shared. Do not add a platform-specific agent loop or separate terminal or browser state. The adapter implements the PlatformAdapter protocol in heartwood.adapters; start from the Platform Contract for what the platform itself must provide.

items.title: Define Capabilities
items.text:
PlatformAdapter.capabilities() returns a PlatformCapabilities record with:

  • platform_id and display_name;
  • supported interfaces and the browser_route;
  • supported ingress_modes and one default_ingress_mode;
  • managed_runtimes for Heartwood-managed inference;
  • scheduler and persistent_storage guidance;
  • credential_backends;
  • permitted model_sources and any platform_isolated_model_sources;
  • managed_model_connections; and
  • validation_level, either ci or ci-and-live-synthetic.

The gateway serves this record at GET /project/capabilities, and every interface uses it to hide unsupported choices.

items.title: Detect the Environment
items.text: PlatformAdapter.detect() must use deterministic, content-safe evidence such as explicit deployment markers, scheduler identity or Jupyter platform variables. Do not inspect research data or infer institutional authorization. The generic adapter is the fallback when no other adapter matches.

items.title: Define Policy and Connections
items.text: PlatformAdapter.default_policy_profile() returns a deny-by-default PolicyProfile with exact model catalog and completion endpoints, capability tiers, action-review modes and credential reference names. It applies when no deployment manifest is supplied; a manifest's [policy] table replaces it. The built-in generic, Terra and Carina adapters permit review-all and review-changes. Expose managed connection metadata without secret values, and never let a user-entered compatible endpoint widen managed-platform policy.

items.title: Gateway Ingress
items.text:
Choose one of the shared ingress modes instead of adding platform-specific request parsing:

  • direct-loopback for a client that connects directly to a loopback gateway;
  • jupyter-proxy for an authenticated local Jupyter proxy that strips one exact external prefix and supplies only validated Jupyter route metadata; or
  • trusted-proxy for a non-loopback deployment with exact proxy source ranges, external origin, base path and forwarded metadata.

The deployment supplies route values to heartwood gateway serve, which validates them once for the REST API, server-sent events, WebSockets, browser assets and the generated browser base path. Interface clients do not read Terra, Carina, Jupyter or proxy environment variables. A trusted proxy removes inbound forwarding and identity headers before setting its own, and its upstream route reaches only the configured gateway bind.

Every request also needs the launch capability. Either let the researcher open the launch link that heartwood gateway serve prints and forward the browser's header and WebSocket authentication frame unchanged, or supply the capability through --capability-fd and inject X-Heartwood-Capability from the proxy for callers it has authenticated. Keep the descriptor source and the capability away from the worker and from other users.

items.title: Model Credential Isolation
items.text:
Leave platform_isolated_model_sources empty unless an exact model source uses a transport separated from the operating-system identity that runs OpenHands tools. Listing a source lets review-changes apply in local execution for that source, and the gateway does not check the claim, so add a source only after live synthetic validation on the platform shows that terminal, file-editor and Task tools cannot read its credential. Qualification is per source: isolating an institutional gateway does not qualify a subscription, hosted-provider or custom endpoint on the same platform. The selected profile must use the exact model-source identifier and a managed-identity binding; an environment variable or mounted credential file stays application-scrubbed. Cover restart, every advertised interface, research files, state, inherited process resources, logs, events, browser and notebook outputs and audit exports, and keep model authorization and tool execution independently revocable.

An OpenHands remote workspace isolates the agent environment from its caller, but its agent server holds both the model client and the tools, so it is not a model-only credential boundary. Prefer a platform-native model proxy or a separately authorized service identity to a Heartwood-managed secret store.

items.title: Protected State and Worker Execution
items.text:
Managed launch binds the research directory, project UUID, state directory and policy ceiling through the deployment manifest. Platform detection and project files cannot establish deployment authority.

A worker adapter confines the complete agent server, model client, tools and subprocesses, and reuses native infrastructure for sandbox creation, mandatory filesystem and network controls, resource limits and credential delivery. The reference adapter uses OpenShell on a local Docker engine and the native OpenHands remote contracts; its control objects are not portable platform schemas. Keep the gateway, canonical records, approvals, signing authority and management sockets outside the worker, and supply only selected read-only inputs and verified Skills with separate writable storage. Bind each attempt to project, session, image, effective policy and input manifest before admitting events; observe admission and revocation through the outside control plane; and keep ownership fenced while creation or deletion is uncertain. The worker ownership contract and native integration checks define the expected behavior.

items.title: Package the Shared Application
items.text: Extend the platform's supported base image with the shared Heartwood payload, preserving its entrypoint, user, Jupyter paths, proxy behavior and required libraries unless the platform requires a change. Declare image targets in images/platforms.toml, parameterize the shared images/Dockerfile assembly in docker-bake.hcl, and add platform validation scripts only where the inherited environment requires them. Keep model weights and credentials out of image layers, and publish the manifest media type and architectures the platform accepts.

items.title: Configure Checkpoint Signing
items.text: When the platform retains authoritative checkpoints, install one deployment-owned signer registry at /etc/heartwood/checkpoint-signers.toml, or set HEARTWOOD_CHECKPOINT_SIGNER_REGISTRY to an absolute operator-controlled path. In containers, mount the registry and public keys read-only and inject any bearer token as a separate secret file. Publish a production profile as the registry default, keep KMS or HSM credentials and private keys in the signer service, and never bake tokens, keys or project-specific signer choices into an image. See Audit Checkpoints and Retention.

items.title: Validate Conformance
items.text: Add adapter protocol, capability serialization, ingress adversarial, read-only startup, project persistence, model-policy, credential-boundary and interface tests for every advertised surface. Use a production-derived CI image where the real base cannot run in pull-request CI, then validate the published artifact in a synthetic live environment before setting validation_level to ci-and-live-synthetic.

items.title: Platform API and Access Requirements
items.text: These are the APIs, access and deployment controls a platform team such as Terra or Seven Bridges provides to integrate Heartwood. The Platform Contract defines the message semantics, versioning and conformance checks behind each request.

items.title: Select the Integration Scope
items.text:
Hosting, isolated workers, inference and research services are independent capabilities; select only what the integration needs and start with a synthetic project.

Capability Requested from the platform Heartwood status Run the application A release artifact, durable storage and an authenticated researcher route Current; interfaces depend on the platform adapter Isolate complete workers A Docker engine and sandbox gateway under operator control, protected state, selected read-only inputs, bounded writable storage and enforced egress Current for the OpenShell Docker reference adapter; qualified only against the qualification-only gateway build Use approved inference Authorized model discovery and an inference endpoint with streaming and native tool calls Current through built-in and configured routes; connection-manifest startup unavailable Inspect research metadata Authorized project, dataset, file and workflow descriptions Draft profile and offline checks; no built-in connector Execute research workflows Native submission, status, results and cancellation with independent authorization Draft profile; the trusted Python outside operation interface requires a platform-specific adapter Estimate work and inspect budgets Platform-owned estimates, observed spend and allocation constraints Draft schemas only

The service requests below describe an integration target; no Terra workflow or Seven Bridges connector is installed. The Terra image supports the documented terminal and notebook paths.

items.title: Hosting and Researcher Access
items.text:
Provide one authorized research directory and persistent canonical state on storage with native advisory locks that preserves the project UUID across restart and restore; an object-store mount is not sufficient because it exposes files. For a managed project, bind state outside the research directory with an operator-owned deployment manifest and keep it inaccessible to workers. The manifest is read only by heartwood gateway serve --deployment, heartwood project migrate and heartwood project recover-migration; qualify each interface against the gateway it binds.

Provide, without secret values:

  • the artifact digest, architecture and execution shape;
  • the research directory, state location and the operator responsible for their binding;
  • the authenticated public origin, exact base path, proxy source ranges and TLS termination;
  • the secret-manager reference or protected descriptor source for the gateway capability;
  • gateway lifecycle, session expiry, backup and restoration arrangements; and
  • the available interfaces and the synthetic environment used to qualify them.

The proxy authenticates and authorizes the researcher, strips client-supplied forwarding and identity headers, supports unbuffered streaming and WebSocket upgrades, and prevents direct access to the gateway. Use one gateway per researcher and project, and separate authenticated origins for mutually untrusted projects. Heartwood does not verify OpenID Connect identities or exchange platform tokens. The Gateway API reference and the generated gateway.openapi.json define every route.

items.title: Inference Access
items.text:
For a compatible inference service, provide the API base URL, the authenticated model-list endpoint and the approved model identifiers. The model list returns only the caller's authorized models. The minimum profile is Chat Completions with streaming and native tool calls; declare Responses support separately. State context and output limits, tool support, rate limits, quota behavior, permitted data classes, retention terms and region restrictions where known; missing declarations stay unknown.

For isolated workers, the outside inference transport holds the real credential and gives the worker only a placeholder. The reference adapter uses the OpenShell inference transport; an institutional gateway can remain the provider endpoint behind it. Enforce model and tenant restrictions at the provider or an authorized inference gateway, because a hostname allowlist does not constrain which account, model or request a compromised worker sends there. State whether the credential authorizes one model or an approved set, and demonstrate revocation separately from rotation, including existing connections. A Heartwood-managed local model server is not reachable from an isolated worker; local compute for a worker needs a separately authenticated outside route.

items.title: Research Service APIs and Permissions
items.text:
Select each capability individually; inspection does not imply permission to execute, export or change membership. Credentials belong to the trusted outside adapter, and the platform checks the caller's permission on every request. Never give raw platform credentials or unrestricted API tools to a worker.

Capability Required API behavior Minimum access to request Project discovery Resolve an authorized project and its stable identifier Read selected project metadata Dataset and file discovery Return identifiers, metadata, versions or checksums, and access restrictions Read metadata for selected resources Input access Resolve authorized content or scoped retrieval references Read only the selected data Workflow discovery Retrieve the immutable workflow or app revision, input schema and resources Read approved workflow definitions Submission Submit the exact reviewed native request and return an operation identifier Execute only in the selected project and billing context Monitoring Read status, outputs and permitted logs by operation identifier Observe the authorized operation Cancellation Request cancellation and observe the terminal outcome Cancel the authorized operation only Output publication Write reviewed outputs to an authorized destination Destination-scoped write or export permission Budget observation Return timestamped allocation and spending, including unknown or delayed values Read the relevant allocation; no billing-administrator role

State which APIs accept idempotency keys or support lookup after a lost response; a native POST is not assumed safe to retry. Cancellation acknowledgement does not prove that work or charges stopped, and data retrieval, logging and export can incur cost under read-only permissions. An MCP service for these capabilities follows the service discovery profile.

items.title: Terra
items.text:
These requirements apply to the Google Cloud Terra workspace integration; confirm the deployment and cloud first. Terra workflows use WDL and Cromwell; provide the approved workflow revision and configured inputs. See Terra workflow execution.

Request a synthetic workspace, an authorized principal and a declared permission set. Request Reader for inspection, and Writer with Can-compute for workflow or interactive-compute launch. Writer also permits changes to workspace tables and method configurations; use a dedicated integration workspace when that authority is unacceptable. Owner and sharing permissions are not required. Workspace charges use its Terra billing project, and some read or copy operations incur transfer costs. See Terra workspace access controls.

The Terra API specification defines these routes relative to /api/workspaces/{workspaceNamespace}/{workspaceName}:

Operation Native method and path Requested access Inspect data-table types GET /entities Selected workspace metadata Inspect workflow configurations GET /methodconfigs Approved configuration metadata Inspect submission history GET /submissions Authorized workflow history Submit the reviewed configuration POST /submissions Writer with Can-compute Monitor the submission GET /submissions/{submissionId} Authorized submission state Read workflow execution metadata GET /submissions/{submissionId}/workflows/{workflowId} Authorized metadata; outputs may need storage access Request abort DELETE /submissions/{submissionId} Abort permission; observe terminal status afterward

Use the native specification for request bodies and validation. Confirm bucket and object access and controlled-data entitlements separately from workspace metadata access. Include the Terra Data Repository API only when the selected datasets require it. Use a least-privilege user or service identity following Terra's service-account guidance, and never mount a researcher's cloud credential directory into a worker.

items.title: Seven Bridges
items.text:
Confirm the deployment and regional API base: the public Platform documents https://api.sbgenomics.com/v2 (AWS US) and https://eu-api.sbgenomics.com/v2 (AWS EU). The API authenticates with X-SBG-Auth-Token; keep the token in the outside adapter. See the Seven Bridges API overview.

Request a synthetic project, its identifier and an approved app revision. Use the native project, file and app APIs for discovery; file identifiers select inputs. The task lifecycle is:

Operation Native API relative to /v2 Reference Create a draft task POST /tasks Create a draft task Start the reviewed task POST /tasks/{task_id}/actions/run API task workflow Read status and outputs GET /tasks/{task_id} Get task details Request cancellation POST /tasks/{task_id}/actions/abort Abort a task

Read covers names, metadata and workflows; Copy covers content access and downloads; Execute covers running and aborting tasks; Write covers changes to files and workflows. Admin, membership and funding-source permissions are not required. See Seven Bridges project permissions. These permissions apply per project, so use a dedicated project when the required authority must be narrower than a platform role. The platform keeps the project billing binding, and a download URL or copied file is not approval to export controlled data.

items.title: Audit and Records Access
items.text:
Provide the signer endpoint, its authentication mechanism, the approved deployment identifier, public verification keys with key versions, and the retention policy. The signer implements POST /v1/checkpoints/sign as described in Audit and Records; it is an outside service, not a gateway route.

For managed evidence, also provide the records service origin, versioning and Object Lock retention, authorized publishers and readers, and the restore procedure, with these principals:

Principal Authority Boundary Gateway Stage candidate audit and experiment records, read retained history, request signing for its scope No checkpoint publication, signing key or policy administration Signing service Authorize the fixed scope, read candidates and retained history, sign and conditionally publish checkpoints Private key stays in the service or its KMS or HSM; no retention bypass or deletion Independent verifier Read retained versions, signatures and retention metadata No write, signing or key administration Worker None No credentials for or network route to these services

Records Permissions and Retention maps these roles to S3 actions. A signing endpoint that returns a valid signature without retaining the checkpoint first does not satisfy managed evidence. Define how loss of signing, retention or telemetry is detected and which work stops.

items.title: Worker and Sensitive-Data Controls
items.text: The complete worker, including its model client, tools and subprocesses, belongs inside the externally enforced boundary; the gateway keeps policy, approvals and canonical records outside it. Request mandatory filesystem and process controls, resource limits and default-deny networking with exact approved routes. Qualification must cover private and metadata addresses, alternate routes, redirects, peer workers, management endpoints and process inheritance on the selected infrastructure. No Docker socket, infrastructure credential, research-directory mount or state mount belongs in the worker. The reference adapter needs an operator-controlled Docker engine; it does not hand Docker administration to the researcher or agent.

items.title: Gateway Behavior Behind Native Qualification
items.text:
Heartwood does not distribute a production sandbox gateway. Native qualification runs against a gateway built only for qualification from the upstream OpenShell revision and the two patches recorded in images/worker/candidate/gateway.json. Its revocation and cleanup evidence depends on two behaviors of that build that the unmodified upstream release at the same revision lacks:

  • The Docker driver rejects deletion of a sandbox whose provisioning has not settled, instead of abandoning the provisioning task; without it, a container request already sent to Docker can produce a worker after the gateway reported the sandbox deleted and Heartwood recorded its absence.
  • An explicit delete of a sandbox already marked as deleting calls the driver again; without it, a failed deletion stays marked as deleting, later requests are acknowledged without cleanup, and revocation times out without evidence of absence.

A deployment's gateway must provide both behaviors before qualification results for revocation or cleanup apply to it. Declare each gateway version covered by such evidence in the manifest's gateway_versions; Heartwood stops with HW-WORKER-001 when the gateway's Health API reports any other version. That check detects a replaced or misregistered gateway; it is not proof of behavior, because it compares a declaration with the gateway's own report. The qualification build reports 0.1.8+heartwood.2 from openshell-gateway --version and its Health API, and the gateway_build entry of the qualification evidence records its source revision and binary digests. Compare the deployed gateway with that record, or repeat native qualification against it and retain the evidence; a gateway that reports another version needs its own evidence for both behaviors.

items.title: Sensitive Data
items.text: Sensitive-data use requires institution-approved data eligibility, provider agreements, residency, retention, monitoring and output-release controls for the exact deployment. Heartwood provides selected-input staging and read-only mounts, not quarantine or steward-approved release. Managed evidence in required mode blocks a reviewed action while signing or retained-history verification is unavailable; buffered mode lets ordinary work continue with a visible gap, but outside operations and result releases still wait for retained evidence. A successful synthetic sandbox run is not sensitive-data approval.

items.title: Information to Return
items.text:
Item Requested information Scope Hosting, isolation, inference, metadata, workflow execution, output publication and budget capabilities, each selected independently Environment Deployment, cloud, region, synthetic project identifier and technical contact Identity Principal type, audience and scopes, project permissions, token lifetime, secret reference and revocation mechanism APIs Base URLs, specification versions, selected operations, request limits, pagination, retry and error semantics Inference Model identifiers and protocols, permitted model set, data eligibility, quota and retention terms Storage Research and state locations, project identity binding, locking, backup and restore, input and output controls Network Proxy origin and base path, gateway access restrictions, approved egress and its enforcement Compute Worker architecture, isolation mechanism, sandbox gateway version, image policy and resource limits Operations Workflow or app revisions, billing binding, status and cancellation behavior, lost-response reconciliation Records Signer endpoint and identity, verification keys, retention destination and policy, publisher and verifier permissions, restore procedure Evidence Synthetic test procedure, audit correlation, revocation checks, known limitations and the institutional approval owner

Send identifiers and secret-manager references through the integration documentation and credentials through the approved secret channel. Never include real research data or credentials in examples, tickets or qualification artifacts.

items.title: Contract Bundle and Acceptance
items.text:
Export the contract bundle and distribute the complete directory with these requirements, the Platform Contract, the Gateway API reference and the exact source revision or release digest. The bundle supports integration and access review; it does not assert that draft services are deployed.

Check captured model and service responses with the offline conformance checks, then qualify the artifact in the synthetic environment. For each selected capability, return an authorized control and its rejected alternative; a failed request alone can indicate a broken service rather than effective policy.

Capability Authorized control Rejected or interrupted control Gateway access The owning researcher reaches the declared route and reconnects to the event stream Another principal, an invalid capability, a wrong origin or a direct upstream connection is refused Inference The approved model and identity complete a bounded synthetic tool call A disallowed model or tenant, direct credential access and a revoked worker route fail Data access A selected synthetic input is readable through its staging route Unselected resources, writes to read-only inputs and unauthorized export fail Workflow execution The exact reviewed request yields a correlated native operation Changed inputs or project, expired approval and conflicting replay fail; a lost reply reconciles without resubmission Retained evidence An authorized checkpoint is readable and verifies after restore Wrong-scope signing, unauthorized publication, replacement and deletion fail; a required-mode outage prevents dispatch Worker lifecycle The outside controller admits and then revokes the exact attempt The worker cannot reach protected state or management authority; uncertain deletion does not release ownership

For capabilities without a Heartwood runtime integration, platform-side evidence establishes only the native service behavior. Record the result against the deployment following Validate a Platform.

items.title: Security and Controlled Data
items.text: Heartwood controls what an agent may do inside a research environment; the environment's identity, network, storage and data-governance controls remain the authoritative boundary. No Heartwood configuration establishes institutional approval, HIPAA compliance, or readiness to process protected health information or other sensitive data.

items.title: Threat Model
items.text:
Heartwood treats the following as untrusted input: model output, tool output, research files, Skill content, external service responses, and, in an isolated deployment, everything the worker reports. It trusts the operator who writes the deployment manifest, the platform proxy that authenticates researchers, the gateway process and the host it runs on. The threats it addresses are an agent that proposes harmful actions, content that injects instructions, other operating-system users and network clients reaching the gateway, and a worker that tries to claim authority it was not given. A compromised host, platform proxy, model provider or sandbox control plane is outside what Heartwood can detect.

There are two execution shapes. State placement is a separate choice: a deployment manifest without a [worker] table moves canonical state outside the research directory but keeps local execution.

items.title: Local Execution
items.text:
OpenHands tools run in the gateway process, as the operating-system user who started Heartwood. The file editor rejects paths outside the project and inside .heartwood/. Terminal commands are not confined: an approved command can read anything that user can read, including .heartwood/ settings, installed Skills, session records, audit files and browser profiles, and can inspect same-user processes.

Local execution protects against other operating-system users and against callers without the launch capability. It does not protect against the agent's own approved commands, other processes running as the same user, or a privileged administrator. For that reason no review mode allows a terminal command automatically in local execution, and every reduced mode also requires the credential gate.

items.title: Isolated Worker
items.text:
A deployment manifest with a [worker] table runs the complete OpenHands agent server, model client, tools and subprocesses as a worker inside an OpenShell sandbox on a local Docker engine. The gateway, canonical state, deployment authority, provider credentials, signer material and management sockets stay outside the worker's mounts and process identity. The worker receives only the inputs selected in the manifest and verified Skills, both read-only, plus a private writable workspace, home and temporary directory.

The isolated worker passes native qualification against a patched OpenShell gateway that exists only in the qualification build; see Testing and Evidence. Heartwood distributes no production sandbox gateway, and checks a deployment's sandbox gateway only by its declared version, as described in Gateway Behavior Behind Native Qualification.

items.title: Sandbox Enforcement
items.text:
The sandbox and the surrounding infrastructure enforce everything that constrains code running inside the worker:

  • filesystem access limited to the projected volumes, with inputs and Skills mounted read-only;
  • a non-root process identity with no-new-privileges and no added Linux capabilities;
  • Docker network=none for the worker container, with network access only through the sandbox's deny-by-default policy and inference transport;
  • CPU and memory limits from the manifest;
  • substitution of the real provider credential outside the worker, which holds only an openshell:resolve:env: placeholder; and
  • deletion of the sandbox when the gateway revokes the attempt.

Heartwood sets no expiry on the provider credential behind that placeholder. Credential lifetime, rotation and detachment are the operator's OpenShell provider configuration; native qualification checks only that its own fixture's expired credential is refused.

Heartwood does not inspect commands the worker runs. In review-outside-effects, these controls are the only limit on what an automatically allowed command can do inside the worker.

items.title: Gateway Enforcement
items.text:
The gateway enforces everything that decides authority, independently of anything the worker reports:

  • the deployment manifest's paths, ownership, policy ceiling and qualified gateway versions, before any store opens;
  • the sandbox's reported version against gateway_versions, and stops with HW-WORKER-001 otherwise;
  • outside inspection of the worker container, which rejects an unexpected image, a network other than none, privileged mode, added capabilities, a shared host or container namespace, mounts that expose withheld host paths, and any security option other than no-new-privileges, AppArmor docker-default, or an SELinux container_t or svirt_lxc_net_t type with individual categories;
  • admission of the sandbox's accepted policy hash and process generation against sandbox_policy_sha256;
  • worker attempts bound to project, session, image, policy and input-manifest identity, journaled and fenced so that only one attempt can write a session;
  • worker responses admitted only when every conversation setting equals what the gateway sent, so a worker cannot select the agent, model client, security analyzer or secret source the gateway constructs;
  • a 120-second deadline per worker request and fixed size limits per response, with a fenced attempt on violation;
  • action review, outside authorization and audit records, which a worker message cannot create or settle; and
  • revocation of a fenced attempt and removal of its volumes, and of attempts left by an earlier gateway process at the next gateway serve --deployment start.

An uncertain revocation keeps the attempt fenced and the session's writer ownership retained until outside reconciliation observes that its resources are gone. After a recorded revocation, the next task can start a replacement worker in a new sandbox; it shares no credential, placeholder, conversation memory or workspace file with the revoked worker. The system architecture describes attempt ownership and the response limits.

items.title: Action Review
items.text:
The agent loop pauses before every registered action set. The gateway then either waits for the researcher or records its own decision under the actor gateway and one named rule. Model risk ratings and model-written summaries are not inputs to that decision.

Mode Allowed automatically Applies when Residual exposure review-all Nothing Always None beyond the researcher's own decisions review-changes A set containing only file views of paths the gateway resolved inside the project (rule read.file-view), or only task-tracker updates (rule plan.task-tracker) The model route is credential-free or platform-isolated, or the session runs in an isolated worker Viewed file content reaches the model route without a per-file decision review-outside-effects A set containing only file views, task-tracker updates, file edits and terminal commands (rule sandbox.contained) The session runs in an admitted, active worker attempt with a live lease Code runs unreviewed on mounted inputs, can alter or delete the worker workspace, and can send content to the admitted model endpoint

An action set with any other tool, or with an action that the deterministic OpenHands policy-rail and pattern analyzers rate high or cannot assess, waits for the researcher in every mode. Outside operations and result releases are never allowed automatically; see Outside Authorization. Actions and Audit History describes how researchers select a mode and read automatic decisions.

items.title: Deployment Ceiling
items.text:
allowed_action_review_modes in the manifest's [policy] table lists every mode the deployment permits and must include review-all. When it is omitted, all three modes are permitted. A session in an isolated worker with no selection then uses review-outside-effects, so in-worker commands run without a researcher decision. List the modes explicitly, and list only review-all until a mode has passed the action-review evaluation for the deployment.

The gateway reads the ceiling from the manifest each time it loads the project. A project policy can list fewer modes; the modes in force are those both lists permit. A stored selection that the ceiling no longer permits stops the project from loading until the selection is reset or the manifest permits it. At decision time the ceiling is applied again, and any mode outside it, unknown, or not applicable to the session resolves to review-all.

Without a deployment manifest, the built-in workstation and container, Terra and Carina policies permit review-all and review-changes. State is then inside the research directory, so the gateway keeps the researcher's selection in process memory and ignores any review mode in .heartwood/config.toml. --review-mode on heartwood or heartwood gateway serve makes the same selection at start and stops with the reason when the ceiling, worker or credential gate refuses it.

items.title: Failure Behavior
items.text: The gateway asks the researcher whenever it cannot establish that a rule applies: the session is paused or the researcher's last command paused, denied or was refused; the selection, ceiling or credential boundary cannot be read; the worker attempt is missing, fenced, revoked or being replaced; the action set is not fully journaled; or the session has an unresolved outcome. A decision is computed once, when the review request is journaled, and bound to the pending set's identity. A set whose request was journaled before a restart or a mode change waits for the researcher. An automatic decision that cannot be completed, for example because required checkpoint evidence is unavailable, is withdrawn: the journal records that it was not applied, and the set waits for the researcher.

items.title: Outside Authorization
items.text:
An outside operation is a request to a platform service prepared through a trusted embedding's adapter; a result release discloses that operation's result to the worker and its model route. No outside-service adapter ships with Heartwood, and heartwood gateway serve installs none, so a deployment offers outside operations only through an embedding launcher that supplies one, as the native qualification fixture does. Each needs its own researcher decision bound to the exact proposal digest, including the request, input digests, destination, worker identity, policy revision and a five-minute validity interval. No review mode decides either one.

Before submission or delivery, the gateway rechecks the live worker attempt, current policy, validity interval and input contents. The decision and dispatch intent are journaled before the service is contacted, and with managed evidence, retained outside the gateway first. An approved operation is sent only by an exact retry of its own approval command; reads, reconciliation and restarts never send it. A Heartwood approval is necessary, never sufficient: the destination service authenticates the caller and enforces its own authorization. The Platform Contract defines the embedding interface.

items.title: Credentials
items.text: Provider credentials are excluded from project configuration, browser storage, command arguments, durable session events, logs and audit exports. Heartwood resolves process values, operator bindings, optional system-keyring entries or platform identity only for named provider calls. Provider failures are reduced to a typed category before persistence, so raw provider exception text is not retained. Custom compatible-service tokens remain process-only; project-scoped keyring persistence is explicit and requires a working system credential store. For Sign in with ChatGPT, OpenHands owns the user-level OAuth credential and transport, and Heartwood stores only a non-secret subscription reference.

items.title: Model Credential Isolation
items.text:
The credential gate reports one boundary for the active model route:

Boundary Meaning Reduced review outside an isolated worker Credential-free No model credential is placed in the Heartwood process, as with an unauthenticated local model server Permitted Application-scrubbed The credential is in the Heartwood process but excluded from tool inputs, project state, terminal environments, interfaces, events, logs and audits Refused; review-all applies Platform-isolated A separately authorized transport keeps the credential outside the identity that runs agent tools, with live synthetic qualification for that platform and model source Permitted

Application scrubbing is not process isolation: the local model client and tools share one operating-system identity. No built-in adapter claims a platform-isolated model source. An isolated worker never holds the provider credential, so review-outside-effects does not depend on this gate.

Local terminals receive an explicit environment instead of the gateway's: executable and virtual-environment paths, locale and terminal settings, temporary directories, selected CUDA and Slurm variables, thread limits and public certificate paths. TERMINAL_ENVIRONMENT_NAMES in the gateway defines the exact names, and HEARTWOOD_TERMINAL_ENV_ALLOWLIST in the trusted launch environment adds comma-separated names. Configured provider credential names and the gateway capability stay excluded even when listed; proxy variables are excluded unless explicitly listed. The allowlist does not stop a local command from reading same-user process memory, credential files, keyrings or cloud metadata services.

A Heartwood-managed local model server listens on an owner-only Unix socket in an owner-only directory outside the project, with no TCP fallback. That protects it from other operating-system users, not from same-user processes; an isolated worker cannot reach it.

Removing a credential from Heartwood settings does not revoke it at its issuer or in running processes. Rotating a sandbox provider credential is not revocation: confirm acknowledged detachment or worker revocation, neither of which recalls requests already forwarded. OpenShell's stable_placeholder provider capability allows value-only rotation without replacing the worker; qualify it against the deployed gateway before relying on it.

items.title: Gateway Ingress
items.text:
The gateway accepts traffic through one configured ingress mode:

  • direct-loopback binds to loopback and rejects forwarding headers;
  • jupyter-proxy binds to loopback, requires the exact external origin and stripped prefix, and validates the route metadata of jupyter-server-proxy; and
  • trusted-proxy accepts only configured source ranges with one complete forwarded client, host, protocol and prefix set, and can require an exact non-secret identity assertion header.

Every mode validates host, origin, WebSocket origin, path, query encoding and base path, and rejects duplicated security headers, undeclared forwarding metadata, encoded or traversing paths and wildcard origins. Request bodies are limited to 1 MiB of UTF-8. Browser responses set a restrictive content security policy, same-origin framing, no referrer, MIME-sniffing protection, and a permissions policy that disables camera, geolocation and microphone. Heartwood does not authenticate end users or terminate public TLS; the platform proxy must do both and strip client-supplied forwarding and identity headers.

items.title: Launch Capability
items.text:
Every API request, server-sent event stream and WebSocket requires a process-lifetime capability. heartwood gateway serve prints one launch link after it owns a listening socket; the browser removes the fragment token and exchanges it once through POST /launch for a capability kept in tab-scoped sessionStorage under the gateway base path. The browser sends it in X-Heartwood-Capability, or in the first WebSocket frame within five seconds and 8192 bytes; no cookie is set and redirects are rejected. Automation supplies the capability through --capability-fd, at most 4096 bytes, which the gateway reads and closes; environment delivery is rejected. Access logging is disabled, and a request without the capability receives HW-INGRESS-003.

The capability separates the researcher's browser from other operating-system users and from requests that lack it. It does not separate the researcher from same-user processes, from scripts on the same origin, or from another person sharing the account. Every accepted command records the launching principal as its actor; a command cannot claim another actor, and the actor gateway is reserved for automatic review decisions. Use separate authenticated origins for mutually untrusted projects; in Jupyter proxy mode, notebook content on the same origin is trusted.

items.title: Model Content
items.text:
Prompts, selected project content, tool results and summaries go to the active model route. Policy denies unlisted endpoints, but infrastructure egress controls and provider agreements are authoritative; confirm data eligibility for the exact endpoint, account, model and deployment.

The browser renders agent responses as untrusted GitHub-Flavored Markdown: it removes raw HTML and unsafe link protocols, does not fetch model-provided images, shows invisible control characters, and opens external links only on explicit action without a referrer.

The GPU runtime's optional outlines cache is disabled by default and does not use diskcache. Do not enable unbounded runtime caches, share them between users, or place them inside an agent-writable project.

items.title: Skills and Instructions
items.text: Reviewed external Skill packages install only from deployment-approved TUF roots, after verification of signatures, expiry, rollback state, target hashes, the complete file manifest, declared policy and OpenHands compatibility. Approval binds the exact tree digest, installation is atomic, and a signed revocation prevents later activation. Only the deployment-owned system Skill registry can approve a digest for controlled data. The agent receives each verified active Skill directory individually, never a parent directory that OpenHands would scan for more Skills. Content placed beside an installed Skill in the project store, including another Skill directory or an interrupted installation, is not loaded; Heartwood names it in the Skill list, in heartwood doctor and in the gateway log. Release-bundled Skills must match the complete-tree digests pinned in the Heartwood release; an edited or missing bundled Skill stops Skill use, and unpinned entries beside them are reported and never loaded. Container and worker images install that directory and the pin root-owned. Source checkouts and native installations leave both writable by the runtime user, so the pin detects drift there but cannot stop that account, or a terminal command it approves, from rewriting the installation. Verification establishes source and integrity, not that instructions are safe for a dataset; see Skill Trust and Distribution.

items.title: Audit Data
items.text: The audit log is hash-chained and its export is scrubbed, but operational metadata can still be sensitive; store and delete it under the project's records policy. A signed checkpoint authenticates one export against a key obtained through a separate channel. It does not enforce retention or prove that no events were removed before it was created. Managed evidence additionally verifies each checkpoint against independently retained history, and the signer, not the gateway, publishes checkpoint ordinals. See Audit Checkpoints and Retention.

items.title: Security Limits
items.text: Native qualification runs synthetic and benign workloads, and no deployment of Heartwood is qualified for sensitive or regulated data. Synthetic qualification, CI validation and a running sandbox are evidence for an institutional review, not institutional approval. Review modes do not constrain a compromised isolated worker, which can act inside its sandbox without an approval. A released outside result reaches the model as a user-role message; the envelope that labels it is not an instruction boundary. Heartwood does not verify individual identities, attribute commands to individual people behind one gateway, or replace platform authorization. Heartwood provides no quarantine, steward-approved output release, encrypted execution storage or records-system retention enforcement.

items.title: Deployment Security Checklist
items.text:
Confirm each control before researchers add project data, and again after each update:

  • authenticate every user before they reach the execution environment, and isolate projects and users with platform permissions;
  • keep the gateway on loopback or behind one configured authenticated proxy, and keep the launch link and capability private to the researcher;
  • deny network egress except reviewed model and package endpoints;
  • keep provider secrets in a keyring, mounted secret or managed identity, and production checkpoint keys in an independently authorized signer;
  • list allowed_action_review_modes explicitly, with only the modes evaluated for the deployment;
  • for an isolated worker, confirm that the sandbox gateway provides the behavior native qualification depends on before declaring its version;
  • pin release artifacts, images, model revisions and Skill versions;
  • collect content-minimized operational logs outside project outputs;
  • validate backup, retention, deletion and incident-response procedures; and
  • complete synthetic end-to-end validation before any controlled-data decision.

Describe a deployment as suitable for a data class only when the institution can point to the platform controls, agreements, security review and validation evidence for it.

items.title: Support and Compatibility
items.text: Heartwood uses Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 and has not reached 1.0.0. This policy describes project maintenance; it is not a service-level agreement or an institutional support commitment.

items.title: Supported Releases
items.text:
The latest stable release is the maintained release line. A patch for that line is issued when a confirmed security, data-integrity, installation or release defect affects a supported configuration. Older stable releases, prereleases, development branches and the moving edge image tags receive no maintenance.

A release is published only from a protected main commit whose Release Candidate Ready check passed, which includes the native worker qualification and the attestation of its evidence. Published release contents are immutable, and the release notes and versioned documentation describe the supported behavior of each version.

items.title: Versioning Rules
items.text:
• Before 1.0.0, a minor release may change commands, configuration, persisted state, interfaces, platform requirements and deployment artifacts.
  • A patch release preserves compatibility, including validation rules and documented behavior.
  • From 1.0.0, incompatible public-contract changes increment the major version, compatible additions the minor version, and compatible fixes the patch version.
  • The platform contract bundle has its own SemVer version, independent of the application; upstream protocols keep their own versions.

items.title: Compatibility
items.text:
A configuration is supported only when the versioned documentation of the selected release describes it. GPU deployments must also match that release's GPU compatibility matrix, including platform, driver, CUDA runtime, model revision, precision, context size, tensor parallelism and tool parser.

Support levels follow Testing and Evidence, and each claim names its level:

Configuration Support level Workstation, container and native installation with local execution CI validated Terra terminal and notebook, Stanford Carina terminal CI validated Isolated worker on a dedicated Linux Docker engine with OpenShell Native qualification against the qualification-only sandbox gateway build, with synthetic and benign workloads Sensitive or regulated data Not supported in any configuration

Releases do not include a worker image or a production sandbox gateway. Native qualification evidence binds one commit, one set of image contents and one host, and does not transfer to a rebuilt image, another architecture or another sandbox gateway; see Gateway Behavior Behind Native Qualification. Live-platform qualification is stated separately from CI validation and expires when a material platform, driver, runtime, model, sandbox or policy component changes.

items.title: Update Cadence
items.text:
Review the latest stable release at least once per quarter and apply a published security patch promptly. Before each update, read the release notes, back up the research files with their matching state, and record the new artifact digest in the standard environment record. After the update, review the deployment manifest against the release's manifest reference and repeat Validate the Deployment.

Project state migrates forward only: an older release does not open state that a newer release has migrated.

items.title: Changes and Deprecation
items.text: Before 1.0.0, the project favors one coherent interface over preserving superseded behavior, and removes superseded commands, settings and schemas without a deprecation period. A user-visible breaking change updates the implementation, tests, release notes and versioned documentation together. A security or data-integrity concern can require immediate removal at any version. After 1.0.0, any change to the support window or deprecation policy requires a documented release decision before the affected release is published.

items.title: Ownership and Reporting
items.text:
Repository CODEOWNERS identifies the current maintainer responsible for code, bundled Skill and release review. The configured release environment requires explicit maintainer approval to publish, and repository administrators retain recovery authority for interrupted workflows, compromised credentials and protected tags.

Report security concerns through the repository security policy. Use GitHub Issues for reproducible defects and compatibility requests that contain no sensitive information.

items.title: Choose a Platform
items.text: Run Heartwood where the project files are already stored and governed. The platform determines installation, durable storage, available interfaces, credentials, Heartwood-managed inference and which model connections are allowed. Each path on this page is a local launch with .heartwood/ state in the project folder.

items.title: Supported Paths
items.text:
Platform Installation Terminal Browser Notebook Models Run by Heartwood Workstation Standard container Yes Yes Not in the image CPU inference NVIDIA workstation or server GPU container Yes Yes Not in the image NVIDIA GPU inference Linux without containers Native installer Yes Yes Yes, through heartwood-jupyter CPU inference Terra Terra or Terra GPU image Yes No Yes CPU or NVIDIA GPU inference Stanford Carina Native installer Yes No No NVIDIA GPU inference through Slurm

The standard image is a multi-platform Linux image for AMD64 and ARM64. GPU images are AMD64 because the pinned NVIDIA and vLLM stack is built for that architecture. Terra images are AMD64 single-platform Docker manifests because Terra image auto-detection requires that shape.

items.title: Qualification
items.text:
Platform What the release establishes Containers Images built and smoke-tested in CI on AMD64 and ARM64, including offline and no-network checks; the CPU model qwen25-7b-instruct-q4_k_m is qualified for coding-agent use on this platform Native Linux Installer built and installed from an empty Ubuntu 24.04 AMD64 container in CI Terra Images built from the Terra base and tested in CI for Jupyter inheritance, proxy routing and persistence; one GPU model configuration was qualified live in a Terra workspace Stanford Carina Installer layout tested in CI; one GPU model configuration was qualified live on Carina

Each platform adapter reports its validation level as ci. The live model qualifications are listed with their dates and drivers in GPU Compatibility; they qualify that model configuration, not a deployment for research data.

items.title: Choose the Simplest Route
items.text:
• Use the standard container for the shortest workstation setup.
  • Use the native Linux installer when Docker is unavailable but uv and a compatible host are.
  • Use the Terra image when the project is in a Terra workspace.
  • Use the Carina installer on Stanford Carina, where containers are not the interactive path.
  • Follow Add a Platform to deploy into another managed environment.

items.title: Isolated Worker Deployments
items.text: The isolated worker is an operator-bound deployment, not a platform image. It runs on a Linux host with an operator-controlled Docker engine and a registered OpenShell gateway, and is qualified in CI with synthetic workloads only. None of the platforms above runs it by installing an image; Terra and Carina launches use local state and the Heartwood process identity. See Security and Controlled Data for what the worker boundary covers and what it does not establish.

items.title: Use Heartwood on Stanford Carina
items.text:
Carina is a Stanford research-computing platform with project storage and Slurm-managed compute. Heartwood runs there from a native installation in project storage, with the terminal interface, an optional Stanford AI API Gateway connection, and vLLM on requested GPU compute for Heartwood-managed models.

Do not access protected health information while evaluating Heartwood unless the complete deployment, model route, project and task are approved for that data.

items.title: Qualification
items.text: The Carina installer and its installation layout are tested in CI with a simulated Slurm environment; the Carina adapter reports validation level ci. The two-L40S Muse Glimmer 30B BF16 configuration completed Heartwood's coding-agent qualification on Carina on 2026-08-14 with the pinned vLLM runtime listed in GPU Compatibility. A Carina launch is a local launch: .heartwood/ state lives in the project directory and agent tools run with your account's permissions. The isolated worker deployment is not qualified on Carina.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
You need Carina access, the Stanford full-tunnel VPN, an authorized project directory, and enough project storage for the installation and any Heartwood-managed model. Follow Carina's connection guide. Login nodes are resource-limited and meant for setup, file management and job submission, not inference.

The guide uses two sibling directories: heartwood-installation/ for the release and its Python and vLLM environments, and heartwood-project/ for research files and .heartwood/ state.

items.title: Enter Approved Project Storage
items.text:
Ask the project owner for the approved writable directory below /projects; its structure varies by allocation.

cd /projects/APPROVED_PATH
test -w "$PWD" && echo "Project storage is writable"
df -h .
mkdir -m 700 heartwood-installation heartwood-project

Replace APPROVED_PATH with your group's path, and do not use a shared project root itself as the Heartwood project.

items.title: Install the Release
items.text:
cd heartwood-installation
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 --fail --location --remote-name \
  https://github.com/SchmiedmayerLab/heartwood/releases/download/0.5.0/heartwood-installer
chmod 700 heartwood-installer
./heartwood-installer --platform carina
export PATH="$PWD/bin:$PATH"

Where the GitHub CLI is available, gh attestation verify heartwood-installer --repo SchmiedmayerLab/heartwood confirms that the release workflow built the installer. The installer downloads the matching native archive, the GPU runtime and their checksums, verifies them, checks storage, and assembles a private installation before making it current. The GPU runtime is mirrored as a release asset because Carina blocks the upstream vLLM wheel host; its digest is pinned to the upstream artifact. On a login node, the installer moves dependency installation into a CPU-only Slurm allocation on the dev partition; no GPU is requested. It reports the allocation, seven named stages and elapsed time, and can take several minutes.

Add the printed bin path to your shell configuration, or export it again in each new shell.

items.title: Open the Project
items.text:
cd ../heartwood-project
heartwood doctor
heartwood

Heartwood detects Carina, uses this directory as the project, and creates .heartwood/ only after you confirm. The first command after installation can take tens of seconds while Python dependencies load; later commands start faster. Carina offers the terminal interface only.

items.title: Choose a Model Route
items.text: Carina's policy permits two routes: Stanford AI API Gateway and Run with Heartwood.

items.title: Stanford AI API Gateway
items.text: Choose Stanford AI API Gateway when your project has an eligible key and the route is approved for the intended data. Heartwood lists the models the gateway enables for that key and keeps an entered key only for the running process unless the deployment supplies a mounted secret. Stanford's AI API Gateway service page states the current access, data-security status and rates; those terms, not Heartwood's platform detection, decide data eligibility.

items.title: Heartwood-Managed GPU Model
items.text:
Start managed-model setup from the project directory:

heartwood setup --model-source heartwood

On a login node, the installed command moves download and verification into a CPU Slurm allocation with 8 CPUs, 64 GiB RAM and a two-hour limit on dev; set HEARTWOOD_MODEL_PREPARATION_PARTITION to use another CPU partition. Select a catalog model or another public Hugging Face repository and review the download and resource plan. Model files are stored in .heartwood/models/ in the project, not in the installation, and every file is verified before the selection is saved; on project storage, verifying a large existing cache can take several minutes. An approved HF_TOKEN can raise Hugging Face rate limits during the first download and is used only by the download.

Tier Model Configuration GPUs Recommended RAM Free Project Storage Default Context Estimated Runtime Startup Maximum capability, qualified Muse Glimmer 30B BF16 2 x L40S 128 GB 96 GB 32,768 5-20 minutes

The model download is about 55.5 GiB, and the startup estimate applies once it is in .heartwood/models/. Complex agent turns can take several minutes after startup. See Choose a Heartwood-Managed Model for the catalog.

items.title: Start GPU Compute
items.text:
When you run heartwood with a managed model selected, Heartwood inspects the GPU-capable Slurm partitions, available L40S GPUs, memory limits and model cache. It prints the strongest compatible qualified configuration, the expected startup range and the complete srun request, and asks before downloading weights and again before allocating GPUs. Without a partition, Heartwood uses Slurm's default compatible GPU partition, usually dev on Carina.

If no default GPU partition can be selected, name one:

heartwood runtime start --partition dev --time 01:00:00

Preview a capability tier without downloading or allocating:

heartwood runtime start --task-profile maximum --dry-run

The preview neither selects nor downloads a model; complete setup before running heartwood runtime start without --dry-run. --task-profile accepts auto, standard, powerful or maximum, and --gpus must match a GPU count at which a catalog configuration was qualified. For scripted deployment, --yes-download and --yes-request-allocation are separate approvals; interactive use should keep both prompts.

Heartwood waits up to ten minutes for the runtime (--startup-timeout, in seconds) and reports the elapsed time every 15 seconds. For multi-GPU allocations, Heartwood's vLLM launcher applies the NCCL communication fallback itself; do not set NCCL or custom all-reduce options manually. The Carina 2.0 nodes, partitions and their time limits are described in Carina's Slurm guide and Carina Facts.

items.title: Review, Exit, and Return
items.text: Use the terminal workflow; action sets wait for Allow Once or Reject, or /allow and /reject in the plain terminal. Exit with /exit. The interactive Slurm allocation and the supervised vLLM process end with Heartwood; the project, model files, sessions and audit records remain in project storage.

items.title: Troubleshooting Carina
items.text:
• If a command disappears or is killed on a login node, stop and use Slurm for the compute work; Carina enforces strict login-node limits.
  • If the installer's dev partition is unavailable, inspect sinfo --noheader --format='%P|%G|%a' and retry with another CPU partition, for example HEARTWOOD_INSTALL_PARTITION=normal ./heartwood-installer --platform carina.
  • If a GPU partition is unavailable, run the same sinfo command and choose one of the GPU-capable partitions Heartwood reports.
  • If Slurm reports QOSMaxGRESPerUser or QOSMaxMemoryPerUser, the account cannot request the planned GPUs or RAM; ask the Carina project owner to review the account limits.
  • If the model does not fit the available GPUs or memory, do not change tensor parallelism or precision manually.
  • If startup reports a driver or CUDA incompatibility, keep the released CUDA 12.9 environment and report the detected driver; do not install CUDA 13 into the Heartwood runtime.
  • If a Hugging Face transfer is interrupted, rerun the same command from the project directory; completed files are reused.
  • If model startup fails, inspect .heartwood/logs/ and the HW-COMPUTE-* checks from heartwood doctor without sharing project content or secrets.
  • If an interactive allocation disconnects, the process ends with the terminal; use tmux, screen or a batch job for work that must survive a connection loss.
  • For platform and Slurm failures, use Carina's troubleshooting guide.

items.title: Run Heartwood in a Container
items.text: The Heartwood container is the recommended first installation on a macOS or Linux workstation. It packages the heartwood command, the browser interface, OpenHands, repository-verified Skills and managed inference software. It contains no model weights and no credentials, and it is not set up for notebooks; use the terminal or browser, or a Terra image for notebooks.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text: Install Docker Desktop or Docker Engine and confirm that docker version succeeds. Create a dedicated host folder for the project; the bind mount makes it /workspace inside the container.

items.title: Start the Terminal
items.text:
mkdir heartwood-project
cd heartwood-project

docker run --rm -it \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  --env HOME=/tmp \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace" \
  ghcr.io/schmiedmayerlab/heartwood:0.5.0 \
  heartwood

The user mapping keeps files created in the project owned by your host user. The container is temporary; the mounted folder and its .heartwood/ state persist on the host. After a Heartwood-managed model finishes downloading, the terminal continues into the session. If the container stops during setup, repeat the same command; project state and verified downloads are reused.

items.title: Keep a ChatGPT Sign-In
items.text:
With HOME=/tmp, a ChatGPT sign-in lasts only until the container stops. To reuse it without placing credentials in the project, mount a private host directory as OpenHands' credential directory:

mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/share/heartwood/openhands-auth"
chmod 700 "$HOME/.local/share/heartwood/openhands-auth"

docker run --rm -it \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  --env HOME=/tmp \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace" \
  -v "$HOME/.local/share/heartwood/openhands-auth:/tmp/.openhands/auth" \
  ghcr.io/schmiedmayerlab/heartwood:0.5.0 \
  heartwood

Treat that directory as a secret: keep it out of repositories, shared project folders and images.

items.title: Start the Browser
items.text:
docker run --rm -it \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  --env HOME=/tmp \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8767:8767 \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace" \
  ghcr.io/schmiedmayerlab/heartwood:0.5.0 \
  heartwood --interface web --host 0.0.0.0 --host-loopback-publication

Open the launch link the container prints and keep the container running; the page continues at http://127.0.0.1:8767/. The process listens on the container interface, but -p 127.0.0.1:8767:8767 publishes it only on host loopback. --host-loopback-publication is your assertion that this is the case; Heartwood refuses a wildcard bind without it and still accepts only loopback or private bridge sources. Do not publish the port on a shared network address or put an unauthenticated proxy in front of it. When the setup page reports that a managed model is downloaded, stop the container with Ctrl-C and run the command again to load the model.

items.title: Use an NVIDIA GPU
items.text:
Install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and confirm that Docker can expose the GPU, then use the GPU image:

docker run --rm -it \
  --gpus all \
  --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  --env HOME=/tmp \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace" \
  ghcr.io/schmiedmayerlab/heartwood:0.5.0-gpu-nvidia \
  heartwood

Choose Run with Heartwood and a vLLM-compatible model. Heartwood inspects the GPU model, memory and driver, selects a conservative context size, and starts the CUDA 12.9 vLLM runtime once the model is ready. No GPU model configuration is qualified for a generic workstation; the GPU compatibility matrix lists the qualified Terra and Carina configurations.

items.title: Image Tags
items.text:
Use immutable release tags for research work:

Tag Image Architectures ghcr.io/schmiedmayerlab/heartwood:0.5.0 Standard AMD64, ARM64 ghcr.io/schmiedmayerlab/heartwood:0.5.0-gpu-nvidia NVIDIA GPU AMD64 ghcr.io/schmiedmayerlab/heartwood:0.5.0-terra Terra AMD64 ghcr.io/schmiedmayerlab/heartwood:0.5.0-terra-gpu-nvidia Terra NVIDIA GPU AMD64

The moving edge tags follow main and are for development, not reproducible analyses. Release publication promotes only the candidate digests it verified for the release commit.

items.title: Isolation Limits
items.text: A container launch is a local launch. Agent tools run as the container user with full access to the mounted folder, including .heartwood/, and to the container's network. The container is packaging, not an authorization boundary: add read-only mounts, network controls and resource limits according to the deployment's threat model, and use platform secrets or mounted credential files rather than tokens in an image or command. The isolated worker is a separate operator-bound deployment.

items.title: Install Natively on Linux
items.text: Use the native installer on a Linux host when containers are unavailable or conflict with the platform's normal execution model. The container is the simpler workstation route because the image fixes the operating-system dependencies.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
You need a 64-bit Linux system on an AMD64 or ARM64 processor and a writable installation directory outside the research project, so that the application and project state have independent lifecycles. Release CI installs the release assets in an empty Ubuntu 24.04 AMD64 container and exercises the installed command. Other glibc-based distributions with compatible system libraries can work but are not release-tested.

On Debian or Ubuntu, install the prerequisites:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install ca-certificates coreutils curl git libgomp1 tar tmux

Omit sudo when the shell already runs as root. On another distribution, install packages that provide the same commands and libraries. Then install uv by following its official instructions, and confirm the commands:

curl --version
git --version
tar --version
sha256sum --version
tmux -V
uv --version

Open a new terminal if the uv installer asks you to, then rerun uv --version.

items.title: Install a Release
items.text:
mkdir -m 700 heartwood-installation
cd heartwood-installation

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 --fail --location --remote-name \
  https://github.com/SchmiedmayerLab/heartwood/releases/download/0.5.0/heartwood-installer
chmod 700 heartwood-installer
./heartwood-installer --platform generic
export PATH="$PWD/bin:$PATH"

Where the GitHub CLI is available, gh attestation verify heartwood-installer --repo SchmiedmayerLab/heartwood confirms that the release workflow built the installer. The installer downloads the matching native archive and checksums, verifies them, checks available storage, installs the locked Heartwood environment and the llama.cpp CPU runtime, and publishes the heartwood and heartwood-jupyter commands. It reports seven named stages; dependency installation can take several minutes. No model weights are included.

items.title: Open a Project
items.text:
mkdir ../heartwood-project
cd ../heartwood-project
heartwood doctor
heartwood

The current directory is the project, and .heartwood/ inside it holds configuration, sessions, downloaded models and audit records. Run heartwood --interface web for the browser interface on http://127.0.0.1:8767/. Setup can download a recommended model or another compatible Hugging Face model and run it on the CPU runtime. For GPU inference, use the NVIDIA container image or the Carina installer; the generic native package has no GPU runtime.

The installation also provides a Jupyter launcher in the same locked environment:

heartwood-jupyter

Start it from the project directory, open the URL it prints, and select the Python 3 (ipykernel) kernel. In a disposable container that runs only as root, add --allow-root; do not use it for a normal user installation. Then follow Use Heartwood From a Notebook.

A native launch is a local launch: agent tools run with your user's permissions, as described in Projects and Private State.

items.title: Update
items.text: Download the installer from the new release and run it in the same installation directory.
