Area Conditions PROJECT Project boundary, storage, and private project state SETUP Non-secret Heartwood configuration and policy agreement MODEL Model selection, compatibility, and managed model files CREDENTIAL Provider API key, subscription credential, or managed-identity availability INGRESS Gateway binding, proxy trust, origins, forwarding metadata, and paths AGENT OpenHands agent runtime availability WORKSPACE Read-only project file and change inspection COMPUTE Scheduler allocation, GPU, memory, and scratch storage TERRA Terra-specific project and compute requirements WORKER Managed worker sandbox gateway ENV Readiness checks without a more specific code

Numbers 001 to 899 are assigned in sequence within an area and never reused; 900 to 999 are generic fallbacks. A gap is a retired code. Warning or failure status is reported separately, so the number does not imply urgency.

items.title: HW-PROJECT-001: Project Storage Is Unavailable
items.text:
Enter an existing writable directory dedicated to the analysis. Check the path and permissions:

pwd
ls -ld .

On Terra, use a child directory below /home/jupyter. On Carina, use an approved writable project directory below /projects.

items.title: HW-PROJECT-002: Project Setup Needs Attention
items.text: Run heartwood from the intended project and confirm Use this project. If local .heartwood/ already exists but has no valid state marker, preserve it and investigate its contents before any migration or replacement. For a managed deployment, have the operator verify the manifest, project UUID and external state path; do not delete markers or fall back to project-local state.

items.title: HW-PROJECT-003: Choose a Dedicated Project Directory
items.text: Heartwood refuses a filesystem root or home directory because that boundary is too broad. Create and enter a child folder, then run heartwood doctor again.

items.title: HW-SETUP-001: Project Configuration Needs Attention
items.text: Run heartwood setup or open browser settings and choose a model connection. Do not repair config.toml by inserting a token or copying a profile from another platform.

items.title: HW-SETUP-002: Model and Policy Settings Do Not Agree
items.text: Open setup and select the intended model connection again. This regenerates the non-secret model profile and matching platform policy as one update.

items.title: HW-MODEL-001: No Model Is Selected
items.text: Run heartwood and choose a model returned by an available connection. For Heartwood-managed inference, download or import the model before starting the agent.

items.title: HW-CREDENTIAL-001: Model Credential Is Unavailable
items.text: Reopen setup and enter the provider API key, or ask the platform operator how its secret binding is supplied. An operating-system keyring entry is project-scoped, so another project may correctly ask again. For Sign in with ChatGPT, repeat the one-time-code flow. If the account should no longer be used, run heartwood models forget openai-subscription before signing in with another account.

items.title: HW-CREDENTIAL-002: Model Credential Isolation Is Unavailable
items.text:
The selected model uses a credential, but the active platform provides application scrubbing rather than a separate model-only credential boundary. Outside an isolated worker the session then reviews every action, and Review Changes is listed as unavailable with this reason. Choose a credential-free or platform-isolated model route to select it.

Application scrubbing still keeps the credential out of supported tool inputs, project state, browser and notebook output, session events, logs, and audit exports. It does not isolate same-identity process memory or every operating-system resource. See Security and Controlled Data.

items.title: HW-MODEL-002: Heartwood-Managed Model Files Are Unavailable
items.text:
Run:

heartwood models managed
heartwood models inspect OWNER/MODEL

Choose a Qualified configuration, confirm enough free disk, and download again. For a Heartwood bundle, run heartwood models inspect-bundle PATH and then heartwood models import PATH. For raw GGUF or safetensors files, use heartwood models import with the immutable source revision and license record.

items.title: A Model Bundle Cannot Be Imported
items.text:
Run heartwood models inspect-bundle PATH from the destination project and keep the complete error message. Do not edit the archive or its manifest.

For a checksum, size, or file-list mismatch, obtain a new bundle from the connected source project. For an interrupted import, rerun the unchanged command; Heartwood discards incomplete private staging before retrying. For an existing model mismatch, investigate changes to models/ under the bound state directory before attempting recovery. For a runtime warning, install a compatible Heartwood release or choose a model supported by the destination compute.

items.title: HW-AGENT-001: Agent Runtime Is Unavailable
items.text: The installed OpenHands dependency set cannot be loaded. Run heartwood --version, reinstall the same Heartwood release through its documented installation route, and rerun heartwood doctor. Model download, import, and inspection commands remain available so a broken agent runtime does not block project recovery.

items.title: HW-AGENT-002: An Agent Action Failed
items.text: Heartwood received a failed action from the OpenHands runtime. Review the proposed action set and model connection in Activity & audit, then try the task again. Heartwood deliberately omits provider and project content from this diagnostic.

items.title: HW-AGENT-003: The Agent Conversation Stopped
items.text: OpenHands stopped the conversation before the task completed. Review Activity & audit, verify the model connection, and start the task again.

items.title: HW-AGENT-004: The Agent Worker Stopped
items.text: The background OpenHands worker stopped unexpectedly. Run heartwood doctor, review Activity & audit, and try the task again.

items.title: HW-AGENT-005: The Agent Cannot Perform That Operation
items.text: The requested operation does not match the conversation's current state. Review the active task or pending action set before trying the operation again.

items.title: HW-AGENT-006: An Approved Action Has an Unknown Outcome
items.text: Heartwood stopped after an action was approved but before OpenHands recorded whether it completed. Do not approve or repeat the action blindly. Inspect the project files and Activity & audit, then continue in a new session once you understand the project state.

items.title: HW-AGENT-007: An Agent Turn Has an Unknown Outcome
items.text: Heartwood stopped during a model turn before OpenHands recorded a stable completion boundary. Do not repeat the task blindly because the provider may already have processed the request. Inspect the session replay and Activity & audit, then continue in a new session.

items.title: HW-AGENT-008: Model Provider Authentication Failed
items.text: The model provider rejected the credential configured for the active connection. Open model settings, update the credential through the supported secret mechanism, and validate the connection before retrying.

items.title: HW-AGENT-009: Model Provider Quota Exhausted
items.text: The provider reported that the configured quota, credit, or budget is exhausted. Review the approved provider account or select another approved model connection before continuing.

items.title: HW-AGENT-010: Model Provider Rate Limited
items.text: The provider temporarily limited requests. Wait briefly and retry the task without repeating any action whose outcome is unknown.

items.title: HW-AGENT-011: Model Configuration Is Invalid
items.text: The selected model, endpoint, or provider configuration cannot serve the requested task. Open model settings, correct the connection, and validate it before retrying.

items.title: HW-AGENT-012: Model Provider Is Unavailable
items.text: The configured model service could not be reached or returned a temporary availability failure. Check the connection and provider status, then retry the task.

items.title: HW-AGENT-013: Session Runtime Is Incompatible
items.text: The session was saved by a different OpenHands SDK version and cannot be resumed without a supported migration. Keep its history and start a new session in the same project to continue working with the updated runtime. To resume the original conversation, use the Heartwood version that created it. Do not edit or delete the persistence marker to bypass this check; pending actions must not be replayed against an unqualified runtime.

items.title: HW-AGENT-999: The Agent Runtime Reported an Error
items.text: An execution backend returned an error without a more specific stable code. Review Activity & audit, run heartwood doctor, and try the task again.

items.title: HW-WORKSPACE-001: Project Path Is Invalid
items.text: Use a normalized path relative to the current project. Do not use an absolute path, .., backslashes, repeated separators, control characters, or a trailing separator.

items.title: HW-WORKSPACE-002: Private Project State Is Not Available
items.text: The Files and Changes interfaces never expose .heartwood/ or .git/, including nested directories with either name. Use the documented audit export or Git commands from a trusted terminal when you are authorized to inspect that state.

items.title: HW-WORKSPACE-003: Symbolic Link Inspection Is Not Available
items.text: Heartwood does not follow symbolic links through its read-only project API. Inspect the intended regular file through its project-relative path.

items.title: HW-WORKSPACE-004: Expected a Directory
items.text: Use heartwood files show FILE for a file or choose a directory for heartwood files list.

items.title: HW-WORKSPACE-005: Project Entry Is Unavailable
items.text: The path does not exist or its metadata cannot be read. Confirm the spelling and project permissions, then retry from the same project directory.

items.title: HW-WORKSPACE-006: Requested Tree Depth Is Unsupported
items.text: Choose a positive depth no greater than the limit reported by the workspace response. Omit --depth to use the default bounded depth.

items.title: HW-WORKSPACE-007: File Fingerprint Is Unavailable
items.text: Use a regular project file, not a symbolic link, and wait for any process writing it to finish. The file must fit within the capture operation's byte limit. Retry capture before relying on its digest as execution evidence.

items.title: HW-SKILL-001: Installed Skill Storage Needs Attention
items.text: Each installed Skill is stored alone in its content-addressed directory under the project's Skill store. Something else in that directory, such as a directory written beside the Skill or a staging directory left by an interrupted installation, has no verified digest or activation record. Heartwood never loads it, and the verified Skill stays active. Remove each path named in the check summary, or under Unverified content in the Skill list, with an account that owns the Skill store. The same check fails when the installation index cannot be read or locked, because no conversation can select Skills until the project state is repaired or restored.

items.title: HW-SKILL-002: Bundled Skills Do Not Match This Release
items.text: Heartwood pins the complete-tree digest of every Skill bundled with the release. A failing check names a bundled Skill that is missing or has changed; Skills and specialists stay unavailable until it is restored. In a source checkout, run git submodule update --init and discard local changes under vendor/heartwood-skills. Restoring tracked files does not remove git-ignored files inside a Skill folder, such as __pycache__/ or .DS_Store, and any extra file changes the Skill's digest; list them with git -C vendor/heartwood-skills status --ignored skills and delete them. In a native installation, reinstall the same release; in a container, use the published image unchanged. A warning names entries in the bundled Skill directory that are not part of the release, such as .DS_Store; Heartwood never loads them, and you can delete them.

items.title: HW-WORKER-001: Sandbox Gateway Version Is Not Declared as Qualified
items.text: heartwood gateway serve --deployment could not read the version the registered sandbox gateway reports, or that version is not in the manifest's gateway_versions. Confirm that the gateway named in the manifest is running, reachable with its registered mutual TLS identity, and the one your qualification evidence covers. After an upgrade or replacement, obtain evidence for the behavior native qualification depends on before adding the reported version. Never add a version only to pass the check: it compares your declaration with the gateway's own report and proves nothing about its behavior. The same condition after start stops that worker launch or reconciliation and leaves the attempt fenced.

items.title: Managed Worker Control Is Unavailable
items.text: gateway serve prints Managed worker control is unavailable: with the reason when the native tools, gateway registration, or protected state named by [worker] cannot be used. deployment manifest is unavailable or invalid and the other deployment … messages name the manifest requirement that failed, such as ownership, write protection, a symbolic link, a path inside the project, or a changed policy file digest. Correct the operator files; do not loosen their permissions or move them into the project.

items.title: Worker Revocation Was Not Observed
items.text: At start, gateway serve reports Worker revocation was not observed for session ID; its attempt remains fenced until the next gateway start. The earlier worker may still be running. Confirm through OpenShell and Docker that its sandbox is gone or stop it there, then restart the gateway so reconciliation records the revocation. Do not delete the session's records or writer files to release it.

items.title: A Replacement Worker Started
items.text: A session whose earlier worker was revoked shows "A new worker replaced the earlier one" when its next task starts a replacement. The replacement does not remember the earlier conversation and starts with an empty sandbox workspace; restate the context it needs. A session is refused instead while its earlier worker left an unsettled run, an unended pause, an action awaiting review, an unrecoverable outcome, or a non-terminal outside operation or result release; inspect its record and continue in a new session.

items.title: Action Review Mode
items.text:
--review-mode, /permissions, browser settings, and PUT /settings/actions/review refuse a mode for one of these reasons, shown with the mode:

Cause Resolution The mode is outside the deployment's allowed_action_review_modes Only the operator can change the ceiling; in a local launch the built-in policy lists only review-all and review-changes, so review-outside-effects is reported as not permitted by the deployment's policy review-outside-effects without an admitted sandbox worker Available only under a deployment manifest with a [worker] table; a local launch never runs one, so the mode is always unavailable there Reduced review outside a sandbox worker with a credential-backed model route See HW-CREDENTIAL-002 A session is active and the selection asks less often than the current mode Finish or resolve the active session work; a stricter mode is always accepted

items.title: HW-COMPUTE-001: A Compute Allocation May Be Required
items.text: On Carina, start heartwood, inspect the full Slurm request, and approve it only when the resources and duration are appropriate. Use heartwood runtime start --dry-run to inspect without allocating.

items.title: HW-COMPUTE-002: Allocation Scratch Storage Is Unavailable
items.text: Request an allocation that provides writable job scratch or use the platform's supported runtime path. Keep durable project and model state in approved project storage.

items.title: HW-COMPUTE-003: A Compatible GPU Is Unavailable
items.text: Choose a hosted model, a GGUF CPU model, or GPU-enabled compute. For containers, verify the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and --gpus all; for Terra, select the GPU image and attach an NVIDIA GPU. The CUDA 12.9 runtime requires compute capability 7.5 or newer, so P4, P100, and V100 GPUs are rejected before model startup. Compare the detected environment with GPU Compatibility.

items.title: Managed Inference Outcome Is Unresolved
items.text:
Heartwood reports managed inference outcome is unresolved when an earlier Heartwood-managed launch did not observe its inference process exit. The launcher stops the process and clears its record on normal exit, Ctrl+C, SIGTERM, and SIGHUP. A launcher that was killed outright, lost its host, or could not start or stop the process leaves runtime/managed-inference.pending.json in the project state directory, .heartwood/ for a local project. New managed launches, project migration, and migration recovery stay blocked while that record exists, because an absent launcher does not prove that inference stopped.

  1. Read the record for the launcher process identifier and research directory, and confirm on the host or allocation that started it that the launcher is no longer running.
  2. Confirm with the platform supervisor, for example squeue and nvidia-smi or the process list, that no vLLM or llama.cpp process started for this project remains, and stop any that does.
  3. Remove runtime/managed-inference.pending.json and start Heartwood again.

Do not remove the record while the process outcome is unknown; a surviving runtime can keep reading model files that a migration or a second launch is about to change.

items.title: HW-TERRA-001: Choose a Dedicated Terra Project Directory
items.text:
mkdir -p /home/jupyter/heartwood-project
cd /home/jupyter/heartwood-project
heartwood doctor

Do not use /home/jupyter itself as the agent boundary.

items.title: HW-TERRA-002: Terra GPU Support Is Unavailable
items.text: Use the -terra-gpu-nvidia image and attach supported GPU compute, or choose hosted inference. Delete and recreate the Cloud Environment with a T4 while retaining the persistent disk; Terra does not apply a changed image or GPU selection to an existing environment.

items.title: HW-ENV-999: Environment Check Needs Attention
items.text: Heartwood encountered a readiness check that has no more specific public diagnostic. Run heartwood doctor, inspect the failed check and its next action, and include the structured heartwood doctor --json output in a synthetic issue report if the condition persists.

items.title: HW-INGRESS-001: Gateway Ingress Configuration Is Unsafe
items.text:
The requested bind, origin, prefix, or proxy trust values do not form one safe route. Use the default loopback gateway for direct access. For a Jupyter or trusted platform proxy, configure the exact browser-visible origin and base path, the expected prefix behavior, and the trusted proxy source boundary.

Do not solve this diagnostic by widening the bind or using a wildcard origin. See Add a Platform.

items.title: HW-INGRESS-002: Gateway Request Does Not Match the Configured Route
items.text:
Use the exact URL supplied by the deployment. If the route is operator-managed, verify the upstream source address, external host and protocol, stripped or preserved prefix, HTTP and WebSocket origins, and complete forwarded-header set.

The proxy must remove forwarding and identity headers supplied by the client before adding its own values. Do not disable host, origin, or path validation to make the request pass.

items.title: HW-INGRESS-003: Gateway Request Is Missing the Launch Capability
items.text:
The request reached the gateway route but did not carry the capability that heartwood gateway serve issued at startup. Open the launch link printed by the terminal that started Heartwood; it works once and authorizes that browser tab. Reload the same tab to retain access; after restarting the gateway, use its new launch link. If the link was already used or the gateway was restarted, stop Heartwood, start it again, and open the new link.

Automation must send the capability supplied through --capability-fd in the X-Heartwood-Capability header. Do not share the link or the secret with other users or processes.

items.title: Browser Access
items.text:
If the browser page does not open:

  1. Keep the launching terminal running.
  2. Confirm that heartwood --interface web reported ready.
  3. Use the printed launch link; when it was already used, start Heartwood again.
  4. Check whether port 8767 is in use, or start with another --port.
  5. Run heartwood doctor from the same directory.

The browser interface is not supported on Terra or Stanford Carina. Use the terminal or the Terra notebook interface instead of constructing a proxy path.

Do not work around a proxy failure by binding the gateway publicly without authentication.

items.title: Session Ownership and Interrupted Commands
items.text:
If Heartwood reports that a session is active in another process, stop the terminal, browser server, or notebook kernel that owns it and try again. Do not remove .writer.lock or .writer.json; the operating-system lock determines ownership, and Heartwood reclaims stale metadata after the prior process has exited. If Heartwood reports that state storage does not support required process locks, preserve the research files and matching state before migrating to a native local, attached persistent or qualified filesystem. A managed migration must also preserve the project identity and update the operator binding explicitly. Do not substitute a state directory from another project or use an object-store mount as session storage.

A completed request can be retried with the same command identifier and content without repeating model or tool work. If Heartwood reports that a command was interrupted after acceptance, replay the session and verify the project files and audit records before continuing. Then continue in a new session; the interrupted session remains read-only so an uncertain action cannot be repeated. Do not edit or remove files below the session's .commands/ directory or its recovery journal.

items.title: Audit Verification and Checkpoints
items.text:
Run the full session check before transferring evidence:

heartwood --session-id session-main audit verify

If verification fails, stop mutating that session and preserve the complete project state for authorized review. Do not edit an audit line, remove a recovery journal, or recreate a missing hash.

A checkpoint output, signer registry, trusted public key, signer credential, and local fallback key must be outside the Heartwood project. Run heartwood audit signer list to confirm that a deployment registry is available and that the expected profile is active. For the explicit offline fallback, keep heartwood signer serve-local running and confirm that its Unix socket endpoint, profile, key fingerprint, and owner-only token still agree. The socket and its immediate directory must be owner-only, owned by the current user, and outside the project; directory symlinks are rejected. If startup reports an existing socket, confirm that no signer is using it before removing a stale socket and restarting the service. Use a new output directory, a valid retention date on or after checkpoint creation, and storage that supports native process-shared locks. Verify a restored bundle with the active deployment profile or an independently retained public key before relying on it.

See Audit Checkpoints and Retention for the complete workflow and the limits of the signed retention declaration.

items.title: Collect Safe Diagnostics
items.text: Share the Heartwood version, heartwood doctor --json, platform, image tag or digest, failing HW-* code, and a minimal synthetic reproduction. Remove project content, credentials, protected data, signed URLs, user identifiers, and unrestricted logs before attaching anything to a public issue.

items.title: Your First Heartwood Project
items.text: This guide goes from an empty folder to a conversation in which you review and allow an agent action. It uses a local launch, so Heartwood keeps its state in .heartwood/ inside the folder. Use synthetic or non-sensitive files.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
You need:

  • a Heartwood installation;
  • a terminal, the application for entering text commands;
  • a new folder that Heartwood may read and modify; and
  • access to one model connection, or enough disk and memory for a model that Heartwood runs in the current environment.

On Terra or Stanford Carina, follow the platform guide first; installation and storage differ there. If an operator runs Heartwood for you in a managed deployment, use the launch link and setup the operator provides; the installation and setup steps below apply to a local launch.

items.title: Create a Project Folder
items.text:
mkdir heartwood-first-project
cd heartwood-first-project

mkdir creates the folder and cd enters it. The current directory is the Heartwood project.

Choose the boundary carefully

Heartwood works with files in this folder and its subfolders. Do not start it from your home directory, a shared storage root, or a folder that contains unrelated files.

items.title: Check the Environment
items.text:
heartwood doctor

The command reports the project path, the detected platform and the next setup step without creating .heartwood/ or changing project files. On a new project it reports Readiness: setup-required.

items.title: Start Heartwood
items.text:
heartwood

Heartwood shows the resolved project path before it creates any state. In an empty folder, choose Add the synthetic first example to add two small synthetic CSV files under data/, or Use this project to keep the folder unchanged.

items.title: Choose a Model Connection
items.text:
Heartwood lists the model connections that the detected platform permits. Choose one, select a model returned by that service, and enter a credential only when the route requires one. Sign in with ChatGPT uses a Plus or Pro account and a one-time browser code; OpenAI API, Anthropic and Stanford AI API Gateway use API keys.

For Run with Heartwood, Heartwood shows its recommendations and an Other Hugging Face model option, with the model format, license, download size, runtime and resource guidance, before anything is downloaded. See Models for the differences between routes.

items.title: Ask for a Bounded Task
items.text:
If you added the synthetic example, enter:

Inspect the CSV files under data. Summarize their columns and row counts in a new file named summary.md. Do not access files outside this project.

Heartwood shows activity while the model works. When the agent proposes one or more related actions, Heartwood presents them as one action set, with the tool, risk and relevant arguments of each member.

items.title: Review the Action Set
items.text: A local launch starts in Review Every Action, so every action set waits for you. Inspect each proposed command and file operation, then choose Reject or Allow Once for the complete set. In the plain terminal (heartwood --plain), enter /allow or /reject.

items.title: Verify and Resume
items.text:
After allowing the expected action, inspect the result:

ls
cat summary.md

Exit Heartwood with /exit, then run heartwood again from the same folder. The project configuration and session history are still in .heartwood/. Use /replay to review the durable session events and /audit-export to write a scrubbed JSON Lines export.

items.title: Next Steps
items.text:
• Read Projects and Private State before adding real project files.
  • Learn the core workflow and the terminal, browser and notebook interfaces.
  • Read Actions and Audit History for review modes and what each one allows.

items.title: Install Heartwood
items.text: Install Heartwood where your project files already reside. Each route below produces a local launch: the heartwood command, with project state in .heartwood/ inside the folder where you run it. An isolated-worker deployment is set up by an operator; see Deploy Heartwood.

items.title: Choose an Installation
items.text:
Situation Use What You Install You have Docker Desktop or Docker Engine Container One versioned Heartwood image You use Terra Terra image A versioned image selected in Terra You use Stanford Carina Native installer for Carina A release-scoped installation in project storage You use Linux without Docker Native installer for Linux A release-scoped installation using uv You change Heartwood itself Development installation The repository and locked development dependencies

Images and installers contain inference software but no model weights and no credentials.

items.title: Confirm the Installation
items.text:
heartwood --version
heartwood doctor

The first command prints the installed release. The second inspects the current directory and environment without changing either.

items.title: Development Installation
items.text:
Use this route only to change Heartwood. It requires Git, uv 0.13.7, and Node.js for browser-interface work.

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/SchmiedmayerLab/heartwood.git
cd heartwood
uv run --no-project --python 3.12.15 deploy/build-worker-candidate.py --bootstrap
uv sync --locked --all-groups --all-extras
uv run heartwood --version

The bootstrap builds the patched OpenHands and OpenShell wheels that the lock references under vendor/runtime-wheels/; a registry-only installation cannot resolve those local versions. See the Development Guide for tests and repository structure.

items.title: Update or Remove Heartwood
items.text:
Container users select a new versioned image tag and remove old images through normal Docker maintenance. Native installations are release-scoped: run the new release's installer in the same installation directory, and it switches the current link only after the new installation passes its startup checks.

.heartwood/ belongs to each project, not to the installation. Do not copy it into an installation directory.

items.title: Projects and Private State
items.text: A Heartwood project is the directory from which you run heartwood. The agent works with files in that directory and its descendants; Heartwood does not search for a Git root or read a separately configured workspace path.

items.title: Choose the Project Boundary
items.text:
Create a dedicated folder that contains only the code, permitted inputs and outputs the task needs. Starting Heartwood from a nested analysis folder limits the project to that folder, even when a parent directory is a Git repository.

Heartwood refuses obviously broad roots such as a home directory or the Terra persistent-storage root. Operating-system permissions and the surrounding platform remain the authoritative filesystem boundary.

items.title: Heartwood Project State
items.text:
In a local launch, confirming the project creates .heartwood/:

project/
├── analysis files and folders
└── .heartwood/
    ├── config.toml
    ├── state.json
    ├── sessions/
    ├── models/
    ├── skills/
    ├── audit/
    ├── runtime/
    ├── logs/
    └── cache/

The directory and its contents are owner-only, and an internal .gitignore ignores everything below it. It holds non-secret configuration, sessions, downloaded or imported model files, installed Skills, runtime records, logs, caches and audit records.

Provider API keys and subscription tokens are not written to config.toml, session events, logs, browser storage or audit exports. On workstations with a system credential store, Heartwood can save an API key there after explicit confirmation; otherwise an entered key lasts only for the running process, or the deployment supplies a secret binding. ChatGPT sign-in credentials stay in OpenHands' user-level credential store, outside the project.

Local state is not protected from the agent

In a local launch, agent tools run with your permissions. An allowed terminal command can read and change .heartwood/, including settings, installed Skills, and session and audit files. Review any command that touches .heartwood/ as a change to Heartwood's own controls.

items.title: Operator-Bound External State
items.text:
An operator can bind a project to protected state outside the research directory:

heartwood gateway serve --deployment /etc/heartwood/projects/research.toml

The deployment manifest binds the exact canonical research directory, a project identifier, an external state directory, a deny-by-default model policy and the review-mode ceiling. Configuration, sessions, audit records, Skills, models, runtime records, logs and caches then live in the external state directory, and no .heartwood/ is created in the research directory. Project content is never read as deployment authority, and a copied research directory needs its own binding.

The launch stops instead of falling back to local state when the manifest or state directory is missing, malformed, mismatched, writable by others or a symbolic link. The project identifier is a canonical UUID and is the final path component of the state directory. Manifest and state directory both stay outside the research tree, under operator-owned parents that other users cannot replace; the state parent must already exist. An existing .heartwood/state.json stops the launch until its records are migrated as described below.

Only heartwood gateway serve and the heartwood project migration commands accept --deployment. Standalone terminal, notebook and maintenance commands do not discover the binding, so researchers use the bound gateway or the operator's integration. External placement alone does not stop a process with the same operating-system identity from reaching the state; the isolated worker is the deployment that keeps agent code away from it. Configuration and State lists the manifest keys, including the [worker] table.

items.title: Moving Existing Local State
items.text:
Stop the project's gateways, model runtimes and recorded experiments, then run the migration from the research directory with the operator manifest and a new backup path:

heartwood project migrate --deployment /etc/heartwood/project.toml --backup /srv/heartwood/backups/project-original

The backup must be on the research directory's filesystem so that the original state can be retired atomically; the destination can be on another filesystem. Allocate space for a complete copy of the state, including model files. Migration verifies the session and audit chains, command receipts, preferences, experiment journal and installed Skill content before it activates the protected state, and stops on symbolic links, multiply linked files and special files. The complete original directory is retained as the backup, and relocation does not change the assurance of historical records.

After retirement, a .heartwood-migration.json file in the research directory prevents local startup; do not delete it to reinitialize the project. If retirement or activation is interrupted, both startup paths stay closed until an operator inspects the retained evidence and resumes:

heartwood project recover-migration --deployment /etc/heartwood/project.toml

Add --rollback to restore the original local state, which is refused once the protected project has changed or when local state already exists. Backups and failed staging directories are removed only by explicit operator cleanup.

items.title: Persistence by Environment
items.text:
Environment Durable Project Location Workstation The folder used as the project Container The host folder mounted at /workspace Terra A dedicated directory below /home/jupyter on the persistent disk Stanford Carina A dedicated writable directory in approved project storage Operator-bound deployment The research directory, plus the manifest's external state directory

Job scratch space, temporary container filesystems and /tmp are not durable project locations. Project state requires native process-shared advisory file locks, so use a persistent disk or native project filesystem rather than an object-store mount.

items.title: Back Up and Share Carefully
items.text: Back up research files according to institutional policy, together with the matching state: .heartwood/ or the operator-bound state directory. That state can contain prompts, paths, model metadata, tool summaries and session history even though credentials are excluded. Do not commit it to source control or copy it into a public artifact; use an audit export when a reviewed, content-minimized record is needed.

items.title: Work With Heartwood
items.text: Heartwood runs an OpenHands coding agent on your project. The gateway decides which proposed actions need your review and records every request, decision, and result.

items.title: The Core Workflow
items.text:
1. Open the folder that contains only the files Heartwood may use.
  2. Run heartwood for the terminal or heartwood --interface web for the browser.
  3. Describe the outcome: what should change, what must stay untouched, and how to check the result.
  4. Review each proposed action set and allow or reject it; see Actions and Audit History.
  5. Ask the agent to run bounded checks, then inspect the resulting files or diff yourself.
  6. Resume the session later, replay its history, or export the scrubbed audit record.

Started this way, Heartwood runs on your machine without an isolated worker: allowed commands run as your user, with that user's file and network access unless the platform restricts it. In an operator-managed deployment, the agent can run in an isolated worker and protected state lives outside the project; see Security and Controlled Data. Heartwood is qualified with synthetic data only and does not claim readiness for sensitive data; that decision belongs to your institution and deployment.

items.title: Write Effective Requests
items.text:
Name the artifact you want, the input paths, the constraints, and how to verify the result:

Read analysis/cohort.py and tests/test_cohort.py. Correct the date-window logic without changing the public function signature. Run only the cohort tests and summarize the diff and test result.

For a staged tabular analysis with fixed inputs and completion checks, use a research workflow. To get a focused second opinion on a plan or result, ask the agent to involve a research specialist.

A request is not a security control. If a task must not use the network, parent directories, or particular files, say so and use a deployment that enforces it.

items.title: Choose an Interface
items.text:
Interface Use For Start With Full-screen terminal Daily work and SSH sessions heartwood Plain terminal Logs, basic terminals, and accessibility tools heartwood --plain Browser Visual history, setup, review, Skills, and audit export heartwood --interface web Notebook bridge Driving a session beside exploratory analysis NotebookSession()

Every interface uses the project in the process's current directory and the same sessions. Only one process writes a session at a time: close one interface before continuing the same session in another, or use separate session identifiers for simultaneous work.

items.title: Verify Before Trusting the Result
items.text: An agent response is not evidence that an analysis is correct. Inspect code and outputs, run appropriate tests, keep the original data, and apply the same scientific and statistical review as for work you wrote yourself. Heartwood records actions and route decisions; it does not validate a scientific conclusion.

items.title: Actions and Audit History
items.text: The agent proposes commands and file operations; the gateway decides whether each proposal needs your decision, and the session records every decision and result.

items.title: Review an Action Set
items.text:
OpenHands groups related tool calls into one action set and pauses before running it. When a set needs you, every interface lists all of its members: the exact command or file operation, the arguments, a risk label, and a summary.

  1. Read the exact command or file operation first. The summary below it is labelled Model-provided summary because the model wrote it.
  2. Allow or reject the whole set. Allowing runs every member once; rejecting runs none of them.
  3. Terminal: arrow keys and Enter, or /allow and /reject in the plain interface.
  4. Browser: Allow All Once or Reject All in the review panel.
  5. Notebook: session.approve(group_id=pending.group_id) or session.deny(group_id=pending.group_id).
  6. Check the outcome under Agent actions, which shows each action's state, exit status, bounded output, and the project paths a typed file operation changed.

Each interface applies your decision to the set it displayed, so a set you have not seen is never decided. The risk label comes from fixed threat checks on the action itself, not from the model. An interrupted action whose result cannot be established is marked Outcome Unknown rather than treated as safe to repeat.

items.title: Review Modes
items.text:
The review mode decides which action sets the gateway allows on your behalf. The gateway decides from the typed action alone: the tool, its validated arguments, and whether the session runs in an isolated worker. Model-written summaries and risk ratings never cause an action to run without you.

Mode Heartwood allows without asking Heartwood asks you about Review Every Action (review-all) Nothing Every action set Review Changes (review-changes) Viewing a file inside the project, and plan updates in the task tracker Every terminal command, every file change, specialist tasks, and anything else Review Outside Effects (review-outside-effects) Terminal commands, file operations, and plan updates inside the isolated worker Specialist tasks, anything bound to an outside service, and anything else

A lone thinking note with no effect is the only proposal OpenHands runs without pausing.

items.title: Default and Available Modes
items.text:
When you run heartwood, heartwood --interface web, or a notebook, the session runs on your own machine without an isolated worker:

  • Review Every Action is the default.
  • Review Changes can be selected when the selected model route needs no credential, such as a Heartwood-managed model; a platform-isolated route would also qualify, but no built-in platform declares one. With an API key or a sign-in token, the mode is listed as unavailable with that reason, because the credential is not isolated from commands the agent runs.
  • Review Outside Effects is never available.

When an operator starts the gateway with a deployment manifest that defines an isolated worker, Review Outside Effects is the default if the manifest permits it, and Review Every Action otherwise. A manifest without an isolated worker follows the rules above. The operator's manifest sets which modes a deployment permits, as described in Security; a project can narrow that list, never widen it.

Each interface shows the mode in use, the default, and every unavailable mode with its reason.

items.title: Actions That Always Require Review
items.text:
No review mode decides these on your behalf:

  • an action that the fixed threat checks rate as high risk or cannot classify;
  • an action set that mixes members under different rules, or contains any member no rule covers;
  • a file view of the project root, of .heartwood/ or .git/, of a path the gateway cannot resolve inside the project, or whose reviewed arguments differ from the typed action;
  • every terminal command outside an isolated worker, because a persistent shell can change what the same command text does;
  • outside operations and outside result releases;
  • Skill installation, model changes, and workflow stage review.

Automatic decisions also stop when you pause the session, reject an action set, or send a message that Heartwood refuses: whatever the agent proposes next waits for you.

items.title: Change the Mode
items.text:
=== "Terminal"

Enter `/permissions` to see the modes, or `/permissions review-changes` to select one.
In the full-screen interface, `Ctrl-P` and **Action Review** open the same choice.

=== "Browser"

Select the current mode in the session header, or open **Settings** and then **Action Review**.

=== "Notebook"

```python
session.action_settings()
session.select_action_review_mode("review-changes")
```

To start with a mode selected, pass it when you launch:

heartwood --review-mode review-changes

The same permission checks apply as for a selection made later; when they do not allow the mode, Heartwood stops with the reason instead of starting in another mode. heartwood actions prints the modes the current project offers without starting a session.

Without a deployment manifest, project state lives inside the research directory, so Heartwood does not store a review mode there. A selection lasts until that Heartwood process or notebook gateway exits, and the next launch starts at the default. With a deployment manifest, the selection is stored in protected project state and shared by every browser session of that project.

A stricter mode applies to the next action set at any time. A less strict mode can be selected only while no session is running, paused, or waiting for review. Changing the mode never decides a set that is already waiting for you.

items.title: Exposure Under Reduced Review
items.text:
Under Review Changes, file content the agent views goes to the selected model route without a per-file decision. The first step that could change a file or send data anywhere else is a command or a file change, and it waits for you.

Under Review Outside Effects, the sandbox confines commands, not review: they can change or delete files in the worker workspace and send content to the admitted model endpoint without asking. Review applies to proposed tool calls; it does not intercept every operation of code already running inside the sandbox.

items.title: Automatic Decisions in the Record
items.text:
The gateway records an automatic decision exactly like yours, under the actor gateway. The session journal holds a command.received event and an approval.recorded event with actor_id gateway, the decision, the content-bound action-set identifier, and review naming the mode and the rule:

Rule Applies when read.file-view The file editor views a project file under Review Changes plan.task-tracker The task tracker reads or updates the plan under Review Changes sandbox.contained A terminal, file-editor, or task-tracker action runs in an admitted, active worker under Review Outside Effects

The audit export keeps the actor, mode, rule, action-set identifier, and action count. The decision binds the exact set: if the pending set differs when the decision is applied, nothing runs. Checkpoint evidence, model-route authorization, and workflow limits apply as they do to your decisions. If Heartwood cannot apply an automatic decision, for example because required audit evidence is unavailable, the set returns to you with a note that automatic review was not applied.

Every interface shows these actions as allowed automatically, with the rule, and never as approved by you. No interface command can record a decision as gateway.

items.title: Outside Operations and Result Releases
items.text:
An outside operation sends a request from the worker to a deployment service; an outside result release passes that service's result to the worker and its model. Heartwood ships no outside-service adapter, and heartwood gateway serve installs none; outside operations exist only where a trusted launcher that embeds the gateway supplies one. See the Platform Contract.

Where a deployment provides outside operations, each one is reviewed separately from the tool call that proposed it, under the title Outside Operation or Outside Result Release. Without expanding anything, the review shows:

  • that the content leaves the sandbox, or leaves Heartwood for the model route;
  • the service, destination, and operation, or the model route;
  • the size and SHA-256 digest of the canonical JSON that would be sent;
  • each submitted input by reference, size, and digest, without its bytes;
  • the time until which the review is valid.

The browser shows the request or result content directly. When it is longer than the 2,000-character preview, the browser marks the preview as truncated and offers all of it under Complete reviewed proposal; the terminal and notebook print the complete proposal. The summary of these reviews comes from the outside-service adapter or the gateway and is labelled Gateway-provided summary. A released result reaches the model as message content; it is data from the service, not instructions Heartwood has checked.

If an approval is recorded but cannot be sent, for example while the records service is unavailable, nothing is sent until you choose. In the browser, Retry request resends that same approval; a new approval from any interface is refused while it waits, so in the terminal and notebook you can only reject it or let it expire. Opening or refreshing the session, other commands, and automatic decisions never send it. An approval not sent before the review's validity ends is recorded as expired.

items.title: Session History
items.text:
The session records your requests, model-route decisions, final responses, proposed tools, decisions, tool outcomes, task status, model usage, specialist lineage, and stable errors. Every interface reads the same gateway projection of that history. Response tokens are shown while the model works but are not persisted.

Each proposed tool has one action record with its OpenHands identifiers, decision, typed arguments, state, bounded outcome, and affected paths where a typed file operation reported them. States are proposed, awaiting review, approved, rejected, running, succeeded, failed, and outcome unknown. Heartwood does not infer file changes from shell command text.

Use /replay in the terminal or Activity & audit in the browser to inspect the history. Replay verifies the audit chain and its hash binding to each session event before returning anything.

items.title: Audit Export
items.text:
Use /audit-export, Export audit in the browser, or session.audit_export() in a notebook to create a JSON Lines file for review. The export is scrubbed and content-minimized: task counts instead of task text, usage totals instead of completions, and stable error codes instead of provider messages. Commands, arguments, paths, file content, diffs, tool output, and specialist instructions and results stay in private session state. Identifiers, decisions, counts, and timestamps remain and may still be sensitive in context.

From the command line, heartwood audit verify fully verifies the session and audit history, and heartwood audit export --output PATH writes an export.

An audit record supports review and reproducibility; it does not show that a scientific result is correct or that a deployment meets a regulatory requirement. A normal export is not an authoritative record, because the project owner can replace or delete it. Operators can create an externally retained, signed record by following Audit Checkpoints and Retention.

items.title: Use the Browser
items.text: The browser interface is available on workstations and in the generic container. Terra and Stanford Carina do not expose a supported browser route; use the terminal or notebook on Terra and the terminal on Stanford Carina.

items.title: Open the Interface
items.text:
From the project directory, run:

heartwood --interface web

Keep the terminal process running and open the launch link Heartwood prints. The link works once: it authorizes that browser tab for the running gateway, and the page continues at http://127.0.0.1:8767/ on a workstation. Reloading the tab keeps access; after restarting Heartwood, open the new link it prints.

The page is read-only until you select Use this project. Setup then offers the model sources available in this environment, the models the selected service returns, and the credential handling the platform supports. See Choose a Model for each source.

items.title: Send a Request and Review Its Actions
items.text:
Type a request in the composer and send it. The first browser conversation is the same Main session the terminal and notebook use by default; New analysis creates another persistent session.

When the agent proposes actions, the review panel lists every member with its exact command or file operation, risk label, and summary. Allow All Once runs every listed action once; Reject All runs none of them. Keyboard focus moves to a new review and returns to the composer after your decision.

Completed actions appear under Agent actions with their state, exit status, bounded result, and the project paths a typed file operation changed. An action that Heartwood allowed under a review rule is marked as allowed automatically, with the rule.

The current review mode is shown in the session header; select it, or open Settings and then Action Review, to change which actions Heartwood allows without asking. Unavailable modes are listed with the reason. See Review Modes.

Where a deployment provides outside operations, each review of an operation or result release has its own heading and a marked panel that shows what would be sent and where, without opening a disclosure.

items.title: Work With a Session
items.text:
• Send further guidance or pause while OpenHands is working.
  • Select one of up to two suggested next steps to place its full request in the composer for editing; suggestions come from the session state, not from project data.
  • Inspect task progress, model-call totals, and specialist status below the conversation.
  • Open Research to run a research workflow; Project Experiment Records there lists recorded workflow stages and scripts across the project.
  • Open Specialists to see the research specialists and Skills to see Skills.
  • Open Activity & audit for route decisions, tool results, and errors, and use Export audit to download the scrubbed audit export.
  • Use the appearance button in the session header to switch between light and dark mode.

Status labels are the same as in the other interfaces: ready, working, waiting for review, paused, complete, rejected, and recovery required. When a request cannot be applied, the browser shows a separate notice without changing the session state. OpenHands identifiers stay under Technical details.

Responses support headings, lists, tables, quotations, links, and code. Heartwood treats every response as untrusted: raw HTML and unsafe links are removed, remote images are not loaded, invisible control characters are made visible, and very large responses are truncated for display.

items.title: Inspect the Project
items.text:
Files and Changes are read-only and never offer a way to edit around action review.

Select a changed path to compare it with the Git baseline. In a project without Git, Changes shows only successful typed file-editor actions from the selected session; terminal command text is not treated as evidence of a change.

Both views exclude .heartwood/ and .git/ at every depth, refuse path traversal, symbolic links, special files, and non-UTF-8 text, and apply fixed depth, count, line, and byte limits. Truncated or unavailable content is labelled.

items.title: Models That Need a Restart
items.text:
Sign in with ChatGPT shows a one-time code; enter it on the OpenAI page, return to Heartwood, and the page updates when the account credential is stored. Sign out in the same panel removes it.

After downloading or importing a model for Heartwood to run, wait for Downloaded. Restart Heartwood to load this model., stop the launching command with Ctrl-C, and run heartwood --interface web again. Hosted and Stanford AI API Gateway connections need no restart. For an offline destination, Move a model between environments in model settings creates or inspects a verified model bundle at a path the gateway can read; follow Move a Model Into an Offline Environment.

Provider API keys and subscription tokens are never stored in browser storage. The browser stores only an explicit light or dark preference.

items.title: Keep the Interface Reachable
items.text:
Bind Heartwood to loopback unless a trusted authenticated proxy terminates access. The launch link authorizes one browser for the running gateway; other users on the machine cannot send commands or approve actions without it. It does not separate the gateway from commands that run as your own user, including approved agent commands, and your browser also sends it to other local servers on the same address, so open only local links you trust. Operators configure the ingress mode, exact origin, base path, and trusted source boundary as described in Security and Controlled Data.

Problem Next Step The browser reports HW-INGRESS-003 Stop Heartwood with Ctrl-C, run it again, and open the new link The page loads but requests fail Keep the launching terminal open and run heartwood doctor from the same project in another terminal Live updates stop The page first falls back to another live transport; if both stop, the saved conversation stays visible and Reconnect appears

See Diagnostics and Troubleshooting.

items.title: Use Heartwood From a Notebook
items.text: The notebook bridge gives Python access to the same project, model settings, sessions, action review, and audit history as the terminal and browser. Configure the model with heartwood or the browser first; the notebook is for working beside exploratory code, not for first-time setup.

items.title: Submit a First Task
items.text:
Open a notebook whose working directory is the project. On Terra, select the Python 3 (Heartwood) kernel; the default kernel and the python command in a terminal may not contain Heartwood.

from heartwood.notebook import NotebookSession

session = NotebookSession(session_id="notebook-analysis")
session.startup_plan()

NotebookSession() uses the notebook process's current directory as the project; it does not take a separate workspace path. session.project_readiness() and session.platform_capabilities() show whether a model is configured and what this platform supports.

view = session.chat(
    "Inspect the analysis code and explain the existing data-quality checks. Do not modify files."
)
view.researcher_status.label

chat() returns as soon as the background run starts. Poll the session until it reaches the next point that needs you:

import time

while view.lifecycle.status == "running":
    time.sleep(0.5)
    view = session.replay()

[(message.label, message.content) for message in view.conversation]

Call session.chat(...) again while the task runs to add guidance, and session.pause() or session.resume() to control the run.

items.title: Review an Action Set
items.text:
A pending action set appears in view.pending_approval. Inspect every member, then allow or reject the complete set by its group identifier:

pending = view.pending_approval
assert pending is not None
[(action.tool_name, action.details, action.arguments) for action in pending.actions]

view = session.approve(group_id=pending.group_id)
# Or: view = session.deny(group_id=pending.group_id)

The decision applies to every action in that set. view.actions holds every action record with its state, bounded outcome, and affected paths. An action Heartwood allowed under a review rule has that rule in automatic_rule and never appears as your approval.

The notebook runs without a deployment manifest and without an isolated worker. Review Every Action is the default, and a mode you select lasts until this notebook's gateway closes:

session.action_settings()
session.select_action_review_mode("review-changes")

See Review Modes for what each mode allows and when it is available.

items.title: Read the Session
items.text:
Attribute Contents view.researcher_status Label and detail of the current state view.task_plan Task Tracker progress view.usage, view.usage_by_purpose Model usage in total, and separately for the agent and condenser view.subagents Specialist work and its parent lineage view.suggestions Up to two editable next-step requests, the same as in the terminal and browser view.experiments Experiment records of the active session's workflow

session.specialist_settings() returns the same specialist catalog as the other interfaces.

items.title: Research Workflows
items.text:
Inspect the available workflows without starting model work:

catalog = session.research_workflows()
[(entry.definition.label, entry.available) for entry in catalog.workflows]

Availability means the workflow's checks are implemented, not that the selected model is qualified for your question.

Start a research workflow in a new session:

from heartwood.schemas.workflows import WorkflowStart

view = session.workflow(
    WorkflowStart(
        action="start",
        workflow_id="baseline-analysis",
        inputs={
            "data": "data.csv",
            "dictionary": "dictionary.json",
            "question": "Does baseline score predict the held-out outcome?",
        },
        output_directory="results",
    )
)
[(control.control_id, control.label) for control in view.workflow_controls]

Setup does not call the model. Submit the stage request you want from the controls you inspected:

run_stage = next(control for control in view.workflow_controls if control.control_id == "run")
view = session.workflow(run_stage.request)

Poll and review actions as above. After the stage settles, the controls offer result checking and any required stage review. The gateway rejects a request built from an older revision of the view.

items.title: Experiment Records, Files, and Audit Export
items.text:
records = session.experiment_records()
exported = session.export_experiments()
print(exported.sha256)

exported.jsonl holds the same verified JSON Lines as the browser download and heartwood experiments export. It can contain sensitive paths and metadata; handle it as project data, not as an anonymized or signed record. See Experiment Records.

The project views are read-only and use the same limits as the terminal and browser:

tree = session.files()
source = session.file("analysis/cohort.py")
changes = session.changes()
diff = session.diff("analysis/cohort.py")

They exclude .heartwood/ and .git/, reject unsafe paths, and label binary, truncated, unavailable, non-Git, and unsupported states.

session.audit_export() returns the scrubbed audit export with its filename and content.

items.title: Keep Required Services Running
items.text:
The notebook bridge does not supervise a downloaded model runtime or keep a token entered in another process. Start Heartwood normally so it can prepare compute and inference, keep that process running, and use a different session identifier in the notebook.

On a workstation, session.browser_url() returns the browser address; on Terra and Stanford Carina it returns None. Do not construct a proxy address manually.

items.title: Release the Session
items.text:
Only one process writes a session at a time. Close the notebook gateway before continuing the same session elsewhere:

session.close()

with NotebookSession(...) as session: releases resources and process-scoped credentials automatically.

items.title: Run a Research Workflow
items.text: A research workflow runs an analysis in stages with named inputs, output files, maintained checks, and points where you accept each stage. The agent uses its normal coding tools, and you review its actions in the conversation as usual. Start in a new session with a configured model and input files inside the project.

items.title: Choose a Workflow
items.text:
Workflow Purpose Inputs Dataset Readiness Review Inspect data quality and review a report before modeling CSV dataset and JSON data dictionary Reproducible Baseline Analysis Plan a baseline, run it, reproduce its outputs, and review the report CSV dataset, JSON data dictionary, and research question Independent Result Verification Rebuild an analysis environment, re-run the original code, and compare outputs Dataset, Python script, original results, environment record, and dependency lock

Scope of the maintained checks

The baseline checks cover a single-predictor linear model with a numeric outcome, held-out metrics, a mean-only comparator, and group-omission sensitivity checks. The data dictionary must identify separate training and test groups. Other analyses can use an ordinary conversation, but do not receive these workflow completion checks. An unavailable workflow cannot be selected in the interface. Each inspected text file must fit within 512 KiB and 10,000 lines with the default inspection settings. Use a deliberately prepared, representative extract for these bounded checks; a passing extract does not validate the full dataset.

items.title: Prepare the Inputs
items.text:
Keep original data unchanged and choose an unused output folder, such as results. A workflow does not start on an existing folder, so files from earlier work cannot count as this run's evidence. Paths are relative to your project folder, not your computer's root directory. The JSON dictionary names the data columns and their intended roles:

{
  "grouping_key": "participant_id",
  "primary_key": ["participant_id"],
  "outcome": "score",
  "permitted_predictors": ["baseline_score"],
  "excluded_predictors": {"future_score": "Measured after the outcome"},
  "split": {"column": "partition", "train": "train", "test": "test"},
  "validity": {"baseline_score": {"minimum": 0, "maximum": 100}},
  "notes": "Synthetic example; replace column names and constraints with your study definitions."
}

Every named column must exist in the CSV, except excluded predictors that are not present. For repeated observations, include all identifying columns in primary_key and keep each participant entirely within one partition. Choose the partition and analysis question before asking the agent to fit a model. The dictionary describes your intended analysis; it does not establish that the study design is valid.

Readiness counts describe the original input without dropping rows: row and arm counts include duplicates and repeated observations, while the subject count uses distinct grouping-key values.

items.title: Start and Review
items.text:
=== "Browser"

1. Open **Research** in a new session.
2. Choose the workflow, enter input paths and your question, and review **Work Limits**.
3. Select **Start Workflow** to save the setup, then **Run** for the first stage.
4. Open **Conversation** to inspect and allow or reject proposed tool actions.
5. When the agent finishes, select **Check Results** in Research.
6. Inspect the listed artifacts and checks before accepting a stage that requires review.
7. Run the next available stage until the workflow is complete.

=== "Terminal"

Run `heartwood`, then enter `/workflow` to open the keyboard-accessible workflow form.
Select a workflow and provide its inputs.
Reopen `/workflow` to inspect progress and select the next available stage action.
Tool approvals stay in the normal conversation review flow.

In plain mode, use `/workflows` to list definitions and `/workflow` to inspect the current stage:

```text
/workflow start baseline-analysis data=data.csv dictionary=dictionary.json question="Does baseline score predict the held-out outcome?" output=results
/workflow
/workflow run
```

After the agent finishes, inspect `/workflow` again and use the displayed command, such as `/workflow evaluate` or `/workflow accept`.
Decisions apply to the state you inspected; stale decisions are rejected.

=== "Notebook"

The [notebook bridge](notebooks.md#research-workflows) exposes the same definitions, run state, and available requests.
It does not run a second agent or maintain separate workflow state.

items.title: Work Limits
items.text:
Review the displayed limits before starting a stage or requesting specialist review. Each stage allows up to 15 minutes, 40 model calls, 600,000 cumulative tokens, 45 proposed actions, and $1 of reported model cost. The entire workflow also has limits: 30 minutes, 80 calls, 1.6 million cumulative tokens, 100 actions, and $4 of reported model cost. The first reached limit prevents admitting more work.

Cumulative tokens include input context sent again on later calls; they are not the model's context-window size. Elapsed time includes time waiting for action review. Specialist review and corrections share the stage's remaining allowance. An in-flight request can exceed a limit before Heartwood receives its usage, and some providers do not report cost; these are execution safeguards, not guaranteed billing caps. When a limit is reached, retain the outputs and inspect the session before starting another bounded task.

items.title: Verify an Existing Analysis
items.text:
Independent Result Verification preserves the original analysis and writes fresh reproduction outputs. The script must accept --data FILE --output-dir NEW_FOLDER and create metrics.json and predictions.csv in that folder. Heartwood compares the generated files byte for byte; matching outputs do not establish scientific validity.

Retain the original analysis's environment record and dependency lock alongside its code and results. For an existing analysis environment, select its Python executable explicitly:

heartwood experiments environment --python analysis-env/bin/python > python-environment.json

Replace analysis-env/bin/python with the executable used for the original analysis. For a notebook, session.verification_environment(python="analysis-env/bin/python") returns the same typed record. Omitting --python, or choosing Export Server Python Environment in the browser, captures Heartwood's server environment instead; use it only when that was the analysis environment. Capturing today's environment does not recover an unknown historical environment.

Prepare the dependency lock

Use a standard pylock.toml file containing the analysis's exact dependencies and wheel hashes. uv's locking tools can generate it from pinned analysis requirements:

uv pip compile requirements.txt --python analysis-env/bin/python --format pylock.toml -o pylock.toml

Review the lock against the original environment record; newly resolving unpinned requirements does not reproduce a historical environment. Heartwood accepts hash-pinned wheels from HTTPS URLs without credentials or project-relative wheel paths. Source builds, editable projects, and authenticated package indexes are not supported by reconstruction. For offline use, retain the required wheels in the project and reference them using path entries in the lock. An analysis using only the Python standard library can use a lock with lock-version = "1.0", created-by = "researcher", and packages = [].

In Independent Result Verification, select the record as Environment Record and the lock as Dependency Lock. The first stage proposes one setup action; approving it permits downloading and installing the locked packages into a fresh environment under .heartwood/runtime/. Heartwood and vLLM dependencies are not changed. Only approve dependencies from sources you trust: package hashes establish identity, not safety.

Review the observed environment before continuing. Reproduction uses its isolated Python, excluding inherited environment variables, user-site packages, and implicit project-module imports. Use installed dependencies and a self-contained entry-point script. Heartwood rechecks the observed versions immediately before execution and stops if they changed.

If setup fails, retain the failure evidence and start a new verification with a fresh output folder after resolving the cause. Missing Python versions must be installed deliberately; reconstruction never downloads an interpreter. The operating-system family and architecture must match the record. For slow or unavailable downloads, stage wheels in the project first. An interrupted setup is not reusable, and a still-running terminal command is not successful execution evidence. Stop any outstanding command before retrying; Heartwood never overwrites a previous environment or result folder.

The record includes Python implementation and version, operating-system family, architecture, and installed distribution names and versions. It does not attest binaries, native libraries, GPU drivers, or package contents. Additional packages beyond a declared requirement set are not verified. See Experiment Records for provenance and evidence boundaries.

items.title: Request an Advisory Review
items.text:
After a stage with declared specialists finishes, choose Review Analysis before moving to the next stage. Heartwood records the declared evidence and asks the selected specialists to review it through the normal agent and tool-approval flow. This uses the stage's remaining work budget; it does not grant permission to change files.

Heartwood checks the findings automatically when the review finishes. In the plain terminal, use /workflow request-review when /workflow offers it.

The assessment distinguishes verified observations, rejected claims, unsupported conditions, stale evidence, and unavailable evidence. Checks cover analysis plans that conflict with the baseline's predictor, outcome, grouping, or split requirements; invalid Python syntax; supported baseline result inconsistencies; and artifact byte mismatches. Plan findings require readable, valid input data and a data dictionary; they do not establish that the research question or statistical method is scientifically appropriate. A byte mismatch is not proof of re-execution, and a review with no findings is not proof of correctness. Missing specialist results are reported as unavailable rather than a successful review.

Each stage accepts one advisory review. Changing its conversation context invalidates the assessment; Heartwood reports that review as unavailable rather than treating redirected work as the original review. Reviewing does not automatically repair files or accept the stage. Continue to use Check Results and the normal researcher review after inspecting the findings.

items.title: Parallel Reviews
items.text:
Reviews are sequential by default. If your deployment has configured qualified parallel reviews, a stage with multiple reviewers offers Preview Parallel Review. The preview shows the worker count and work limits without starting the model. Choose the displayed parallel-review action to authorize that exact plan, or choose Review Analysis to keep the review sequential. The terminal, browser, and notebook use the same plan and controls.

Plan authorization does not approve tool actions; review the proposed specialist action set in the conversation before allowing it. The status distinguishes a preview, an authorized plan, and admitted work; admission does not mean every reviewer finished or that the findings are correct.

If the files, model route, workflow, or qualification evidence change, refresh the preview before deciding. Expired or changed authorization cannot start parallel work. After interruption, Heartwood retains the review record and does not automatically repeat an admitted batch.

A benchmark environment may instead display Experimental parallel review and Run Trial with ... Parallel Specialists. This is a bounded test, not a recommendation that the model is faster or more reliable. The same explicit plan consent and action review still apply.

items.title: Correct Verified Findings
items.text:
When a review verifies a supported defect, select Correct Findings (Up to 2 Attempts). In the terminal, use the displayed /workflow correct command or the workflow form. This authorizes a bounded correction task, not its tool actions: review each proposed action set in the conversation as usual.

Heartwood gives the agent fresh output paths and rechecks the result independently after each attempt. If the defect remains, it can make a second attempt within the stage's remaining work limits. Original evidence, accepted earlier stages, and previous attempts are preserved.

For a reproduction discrepancy, the agent receives the unchanged program's rerun command and a fresh output location. It may first propose creating the parent folder, then request approval for the rerun separately. Matching copied files do not satisfy the reproduction stage: Heartwood must have recorded the approved execution and unchanged inputs.

A successful correction means the specific checked defect is no longer observed, not that the analysis is scientifically valid. Use Check Results again and inspect the complete stage before accepting it. The original execution remains a failed experiment record; each correction has its own record linked to the source evidence.

Corrections stop when evidence is missing or changed, the conversation is redirected, or an attempt or work limit is reached. They do not silently restart after reopening a session. If an assessed attempt has remaining consent and budget, Heartwood may offer Continue Corrections; inspect the retained results before continuing. Pause active work before cancelling the workflow.

items.title: Verify and Accept Results
items.text:
Check Results reads the bound inputs and expected artifacts and compares them using maintained checks. For reproduction, the workflow also requires a separately approved execution of the unchanged analysis in a fresh process and output directory. An agent's claim that it reran the analysis is not sufficient.

Accepting a stage records your review of its current evidence. It does not grant approval for later tool actions or certify a scientific conclusion. If inputs or reviewed artifacts change, the gateway refuses to continue using stale evidence.

Experiment records connect each accepted stage's outputs to its declared inputs, code, and recorded actions. Open Experiment Records in the browser's Research tab, enter /experiments in the terminal, or read view.experiments in a notebook. See Experiment Records for evidence boundaries and project-wide export.

items.title: Recover or Stop
items.text:
Situation Next Step A check fails Inspect the failed check and artifacts; do not accept the stage as complete The agent still has pending actions Review the complete action set in Conversation before changing stages Evidence changed after review Refresh the workflow and check results again before deciding Inputs changed or the workflow cannot proceed Cancel the run and start a new session with corrected inputs You need to stop active work Pause the agent first; after it settles and pending actions are resolved, cancel the workflow

Cancellation keeps files and history; it does not undo tool actions. Inspect outputs in Files and Changes and keep the session's scrubbed action history with an audit export.

items.title: Research Skills
items.text: A Skill gives the agent reusable instructions, scripts, and reference files for a research task, in the Agent Skills format that OpenHands supports. Every release includes a small set of reviewed Skills; a deployment can offer more from a signed catalog, and anything you install is active only in the current project.

items.title: List Available Skills
items.text:
heartwood skills list

The browser Skills view shows the same list. Each entry has a source and a status:
